data.title: शव्द-स्रोत (Word Sources)
notes: शब्दको परिभाषा (Definition of Word): एउटा वा एउटाभन्दा बढी अक्षरहरू मिलेर बनेको अर्थबोधक ध्वनिमय संयोजनलाई 'शब्द' भनिन्छ। शब्द नै भाषाको सबैभन्दा सानो इकाइ हो, जसलाई अझ सानो भागमा विभाजित गर्दा अर्थ नहोस्। नेपाली भाषामा शब्दहरू विभिन्न स्रोतबाट आएका छन् जुन भाषाको समृद्धिमा योगदान पुगेका छन्।

शब्दको उद्गम (Origin of Word): शब्दको उद्गम भनेको कुन भाषा वा कुन मूलबाट शब्दले जन्म लिएको छ भन्ने कुरा हो। नेपाली भाषाको शब्दभण्डारमा संस्कृत, प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश र अन्य भाषाहरूबाट आएका शब्दहरू समावेश छन्। शब्दको स्रोत थाहा पाउनु भाषाको ऐतिहासिक विकास बुझ्न र शब्दको शुद्ध प्रयोग गर्नका लागि आवश्यक छ।

शव्दको वर्गीकरण (Classification of Words by Source): शब्दको उद्गम स्रोतको आधारमा शब्दहरूलाई मुख्यतया तीन भागमा वर्गीकरण गरिएको छ: (१) तत्सम शब्दहरू — जो संस्कृतका शुद्ध रूपमा नेपालीमा प्रयोग हुने, (२) तद्भव शब्दहरू — जो संस्कृतबाट नेपाली स्वरूपमा विकसित भएर आएका, (३) आगन्तुक शब्दहरू — जो अरबୀ-फारसी, अंग्रेजी वा अन्य भाषाबाट आएका हुन्।

तत्सम शब्दहरू (Tatsama Words): तत्सम शब्दहरू भनेको संस्कृतका ती शब्दहरू हुन् जुन उच्चारण, वर्तनी, लिङ्ग-वचन-विभक्ति सबै पक्षमा संस्कृतकै रूपमा नेपाली भाषामा प्रयोग हुन्छन्। उदाहरण: पुस्तक (पुस्तक), विद्यालय (विद्यालय), शिक्षक (शिक्षक), ज्ञान (ज्ञान), धर्म (धर्म), कर्म (कर्म), सत्य (सत्य), अस्तित्व (अस्तित्व), शासन (शासन), आत्म (आत्मा)। यी शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत नियमअनुसार हुन्छ।

तत्सम शब्दको पहिचान (Identifying Tatsama Words): तत्सम शब्दहरू पहिचान गर्नका लागि निम्न आधारहरू प्रयोग गरिन्छ: (१) चन्द्रबिन्दु (ं) र विस्गर्ग (ः) भएको शब्द तत्सम हुन्छ, (२) श, ष, ञ, ठ, ड, ण जस्ता वर्णहरू संस्कृत वर्तनीमा हुन्छन्, (३) बहुवचनमा 'हरू', 'हरू' प्रत्यय थपिन्छ, (४) शब्दको सम्पूर्ण रूप संस्कृतमै पाइन्छ। उदाहरण: 'विद्या' → 'विद्याहरू', 'शिक्षा' → 'शिक्षाहरू'।

तद्भव शब्दहरू (Tadbhava Words): तद्भव शब्दहरू भनेको संस्कृतका ती शब्दहरू हुन् जुन कालक्रममा प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश हुँदै आधुनिक नेपाली भाषामा पुगेका र आफ्नो मूल रूप त्यागेर नयाँ रूप लिएका हुन्। 'तद्भव' शब्दको अर्थ 'यसबाट भएको' वा 'यसबाट निस्किएको' हो। उदाहरण: संस्कृत 'दुग्ध' → नेपाली 'दूध', 'पत्र' → 'चिट', 'नाग' → 'साप', 'मत्स्य' → 'माछा', 'गगन' → 'आकाश', 'अश्व' → 'घोडा'।

तद्भव शब्दको पहिचान (Identifying Tadbhava Words): तद्भव शब्द पहिचान गर्ने आधारहरू: (१) चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग हुँदैन, (२) र्रे (र्), रे (रे), ककार परिवर्तन हुन्छ, (३) श, ष, ज, भ, य, र, ल, व जस्ता संस्कृत वर्णहरू नेपालीमा परिवर्तित भएर आउँछन्, (४) शब्द छोटो र सरल हुन्छ, (५) शब्दको अन्त्यमा स्वतन्त्र स्वर हुन्छ। उदाहरण: 'चिट' (पत्र), 'साँवा' (श्याम), 'आँखा' (नेत्र), 'कान' (कर्ण)।

तद्भव शब्दको परिवर्तन प्रकार (Types of Tadbhava Changes): तद्भव शब्दहरूमा निम्न प्रकारका परिवर्तनहरू देखिन्छन्: (१) स्वर परिवर्तन — जैसे: गगन → आकाश, (२) व्यञ्जन परिवर्तन — जैसे: पत्र → चिट, (३) स्वर-व्यञ्जन दुवैको परिवर्तन — जैसे: नाग → साप, (४) रूप परिवर्तन — जैसे: वक्षस् → छाती, (५) शब्द लोप — जैसे: सन्तान → सन्तान, (६) शब्द थप — जैसे: पिता → बुबा/आमा, (७) अर्थ परिवर्तन — जैसे: अश्व → घोडा।

आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Aagantuk Words): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू भनेको नेपाली भाषाको आफ्नै मूल नभएर अन्य भाषाहरूबाट लिएका शब्दहरू हुन्। यी शब्दहरू मुख्यतया दुई विभागमा पर्छन्: (क) स्वदेशी आगन्तुक — हिन्दी, उर्दू, बङ्गाली, मराठी, गुजराती, तमिल, तेलुगु, मल्यालम, सिन्धी लगायत भारतीय भाषाहरूबाट आएका, (ख) विदेशी आगन्तुक — अंग्रेजी, अरबी-फारसी, फ्रान्सेली, पोर्चुगীज, जर्मान, जापानी, चीनीबाट आएका।

अरबी-फारसी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Arabic-Persian Loanwords): इस्लामको प्रभाव र मुगलकालीन शासनकालमा अरबी-फारसी शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा प्रवेश गरे। उदाहरण: अल्लाह, अलफ़, अमीर, अद्ल, इल्म, इन्साफ, इसलाम, इकराम, इकबाल, इकरार, इज्जत, अहवाल, इबादत, हुकुम, नसीब, दौलत, जहान, फितना, किस्मत, ख्वाजा। यी शब्दहरू धर्म, प्रशासन, साहित्य र दैनिक बोलचालमा प्रयोग हुन्छन्।

अंग्रेजी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (English Loanwords): अंग्रेजी शासनकाल र आधुनिकीकरणसँगै अंग्रेजी शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा व्यापक रूपमा प्रवेश गरे। उदाहरण: अफिस (office), अलमारी (almirah/cupboard), एम्बुलेन्स (ambulance), एनिमल (animal), एजुकेशन (education), एक्ट (act), एक्टर (actor), एडिट (edit), एडमिन (admin), एप (app), बेस (base), बोर्ड (board), कम्प्यूटर (computer), डिग्री (degree), एक्साम (exam), फोन (phone), हस्पितल (hospital), इन्जिन (engine), नेटवर्क (network)।

अन्य विदेशी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Other Foreign Loanwords): पोर्चुगिसबाट: केशर (cauliflower), काजू (cashew), प्याज (pyaz/onion), बोटल (bottle), जेब (pocket), ड्रेस (dress), बेल्ट (belt)। फ्रान्सेलीबाट: गोभी (cabbage), फ्रेन्च फ्राइज, ब्रेड (bread)। जर्मनबाट: बोक्स (box), बैग (bag)। जापानीबाट: सुशी (sushi), कमि (kami), टेकि (take)। चीनीबाट: नूडल्स (noodles)। यी शब्दहरू आधुनिक जीवन, खाना, पोशाक र प्रविधिसँग सम्बन्धित छन्।

आगन्तुक शब्दको विशंस्कृतिकरण (Sanitization of Loanwords): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषाको ढाँचामा परिर्वतन भएर विशंस्कृत हुँदै आएका छन्। जस्तै: अंग्रेजी 'pocket' → 'जेब', 'bag' → 'ब्याग', 'bus' → 'बस', 'car' → 'कार', 'phone' → 'फोन', 'computer' → 'कम्प्युटर', 'electric' → 'इलेक्ट्रिक', 'radio' → 'रेडियो'। यो प्रक्रियाले आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली उच्चारण, वर्तनी र व्याकरणसँग मिल्दै जान्छन्।

आगन्तुक शब्दको उच्चारण नियम (Pronunciation Rules for Loanwords): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू उच्चारण गर्दा नेपाली ध्वनि प्रणालीअनुसार परिवर्तन हुन्छ: (१) अंग्रेजी 'th' ध्वनि → 'थ' वा 'द' (the → थ, three → थ्री), (२) 'v' ध्वनि → 'ब' वा 'भ' (very → बेरी, van → बन), (३) 'f' ध्वनि → 'फ' (farm → फार्म), (४) 'w' ध्वनि → 'व' (water → वटर), (५) 'z' ध्वनि → 'ज' (zoo → झू)। यसले आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा स्वाभाविक लाग्छ।

शब्द निर्माणका माध्यमहरू (Means of Word Formation): नेपाली भाषामा शब्द निर्माणका विभिन्न माध्यमहरू छन्: (१) उपसर्ग जोड्द्वारा — प्रति+पत्र = प्रतिलिपी, सम+गर् = समग्र, (२) प्रत्यय जोड्द्वारा — गुरु + य = गुरुय, राज + इन् = राजिन, (३) समास बनाउँद्वारा — राजा+पुरुष = राजapurush, (४) द्वन्द्व समास — राम+लक्ष्मण = रामलक्ष्मण, (५) तत्पुरुष समास — राजाको पुरुष = राजapurush, (६) कर्मधारय समास — सुन्दर घर = सुन्दरगृह।

शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धि (Enrichment of Word Bank): नेपाली भाषाको शब्दभण्डार संस्कृत, प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश, अरबो-फारसी, अंग्रेजी र स्थानीय भाषाहरूबाट आएका शब्दहरूले भरिपूर्ण छ। यी सबै स्रोतहरूले नेपाली भाषालाई समृद्ध बनाएका छन्। शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धिले भाषाको विकास र विस्तारमा मद्दत गर्छ, विभिन्न क्षेत्रहरू (विज्ञान, प्रविधि, कानून, प्रशासन) को शब्दावली विकास गर्न सहज बनाउँछ।

शब्दको उद्गम र ऐतिहासिक विकास (Historical Development of Words): शब्दहरूको उद्गम र विकास एक दीर्घ प्रक्रिया हो। मानव समुदायले सञ्चारका लागि शब्दहरूको प्रयोग सुरु गरेपछि शब्दहरूको विकास हुँदै गयो। शब्दहरू समयसँगै परिवर्तित हुँदै गए, नयाँ शब्दहरू थपिए, पुराना शब्दहरू लोप भए। नेपाली भाषामा पनि यही प्रक्रिया देखिन्छ: प्राचीन संस्कृतबाट → प्राकृत → अपभ्रंश → अवधी/बज्जिका → आधुनिक नेपाली।

शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नियम (Spelling Rules of Words): नेपाली शब्दहरूको वर्तनीका लागि निम्न नियमहरू प्रयोग हुन्छन्: (१) तत्सम शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत नियमअनुसार हुन्छ, (२) तद्भव शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नेपाली उच्चारणअनुसार हुन्छ, (३) आगन्तुक शब्दहरूको वर्तनी तिनीहरूको मूल भाषाअनुसार हुन्छ तर नेपाली उच्चारणमा ढल्किन्छ, (४) चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग तत्सम शब्दमा मात्र प्रयोग हुन्छ, (५) नेपाली वर्तनी नियम अनुसार 'क्ष' र 'ज्ञ' को प्रयोग तत्सम शब्दमा हुन्छ।

शब्दको उच्चारण र ध्वनि परिवर्तन (Pronunciation and Sound Changes): शब्दहरूको उच्चारण र वर्तनी शब्दको स्रोत र विकाससँग सम्बन्धित छ। तत्सम शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत वर्तनी अनुसार हुन्छ, तद्भव शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नेपाली उच्चारण अनुसार हुन्छ, आगन्तुक शब्दहरूको वर्तनी तिनीहरूको मूल भाषा अनुसार हुन्छ तर नेपाली उच्चारणमा ढल्किन्छ। उदाहरण: अंग्रेजी 'knowledge' → 'नोलज' (नेपाली उच्चारण), 'समुद्र' → 'समुद' (तद्भव)।

शब्द भण्डारको महत्व (Importance of Word Bank): शब्दभण्डारको ज्ञान भाषा सीपको अभिन्न अंग हो। शब्दको स्रोत थाहा हुँदा शब्दको शुद्ध वर्तनी, उच्चारण र प्रयोग गर्न सकिन्छ। NEB परीक्षामा शब्दको स्रोत (तत्सम, तद्भव, आगन्तुक) पहिचान गर्ने प्रश्नहरू प्रायः आउँछन्। शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धिले भाषाको सौन्दर्य, प्रभावकारिता र विस्तारमा महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका खेल्छ।
confusion: तत्सम र तद्भव शब्दहरू एउटै हुन् — गलत। तत्सम शब्दहरू संस्कृतका शुद्ध रूपका हुन्छन् भने तद्भव शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट विकसित भएका परिवर्तित रूपका हुन्छन्। तत्सममा चन्द्रबिन्दु/विस्गर्ग हुन्छ तर तद्भवमा हुँदैन।
आगन्तुक शब्द र तद्भव शब्दमा फरक छैन — गलत। आगन्तुक शब्दहरू अन्य भाषाहरूबाट आएका हुन्छन् भने तद्भव शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट नेपालीमा विकसित भएर आएका हुन्छन्। दुवैको उद्गम स्रोत फरक हुन्छ।
नेपाली भाषामा आएका सबै शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट आएका हुन् — गलत। नेपाली भाषामा अरबी-फारसी, अंग्रेजी, फ्रान्सेली, पोर्चुगिस, जर्मान लगायत धेरै भाषाहरूबाट शब्दहरू आएका छन्।
शब्दको स्रोत भनेको त्यसको अर्थ हो — गलत। शब्दको स्रोत भनेको त्यो शब्द कुन भाषाबाट आएको हो भन्ने हो, अर्थ होइन। स्रोत (source) = उद्गम स्थल।
आगन्तुक शब्दहरूमा चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग हुन्छ — गलत। आगन्तुक शब्दहरूमा चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग सामान्यतया हुँदैन। यी चिन्हहरू तत्सम शब्दहरूमा मात्र पाइन्छन्।
तद्भव शब्दहरू लामो र जटिल हुन्छन् — गलत। तद्भव शब्दहरू छोटो र सरल हुन्छन्, जबकि तत्सम शब्दहरू लामो र जटिल हुन्छन्। तद्भव शब्दहरू दैनिक बोलचालमा प्रयोग हुन्छन्।

data.title: कविता परिचय (Introduction to Poetry)
notes: कविता के हो? (What is Poetry?): कविता साहित्यको तात्विक विधा हो जसमा भावना, अनुभव र कल्पनालाई लय, ताल, प्रतीक र अलङ्कारको माध्यमबाट कलात्मक रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरिन्छ। कविता भनेको शब्दहरूबाट बनेको चित्र हो जसले पाठकको मनमा भावना जागाउँछ। नेपाली कवितामा प्रकृति, देशभक्ति, प्रेम, सामाजिकवाद, र दार्शनिक विचारहरूको प्रवाह देखिन्छ।

कवितिका तत्त्वहरू (Elements of Poetry): कवितामा पञ्चतत्त्वहरू छन्: (१) भावना (Emotion) — कवितार कर्ण भावना नै हो — प्रेम, वेदना, देशभक्ति, प्रकृतिको प्रति आकर्षण आदि। (२) कल्पना (Imagination) — कविले कल्पनाको सहारा लिएर वास्तविक वस्तु र घटनालाई नयाँ रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्छ। (३) लय (Rhythm) — शब्दहरूको आवृत्तिले सिर्जना गर्ने संगीतात्मक प्रवाह। (४) प्रतीक (Symbol) — वस्तु वा घटनाले अर्को गहिरो अर्थलाई संकेत गर्छ। (५) अलङ्कार (Figure of speech) — उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा आदिको प्रयोगले कवितालाई सुन्दर बनाउँछ।

कवितिका प्रकारहरू (Types of Poetry): कविता मुख्यतया दुई प्रकारकी हुन्छिन्: गद्य कविता (Free verse) जसमा नियमित लय वा तुक हुँदैन, र छन्दोबद्ध कविता (Metrical poetry) जसमा निश्चित छन्द, गति र तुक हुन्छ। विषयवस्तुक आधारमा कवितालाई प्रकृति कविता, देशभक्ति कविता, प्रेम कविता, आधुनिक कविता, योद्धा कविता, सामाजिक कविता आदिमा वर्गीकरण गर्न सकिन्छ।

कवितिका भागीहरू (Parts of a Poem): कवितामा निमन् भागीहरू छन्: (१) मुख्य भाग — जसमा कविका मुख्य विचारहरू प्रस्तुत हुन्छन्, (२) अन्तरा — जसमा भावनालाई फेरि फेरि दोहोर्याइन्छ, (३) चरण — प्रत्येक पङ्क्तिलाई चरण भनिन्छ, (४) तुक — अन्तिम शब्दहरूको ध्वनि मिलाप, (५) छन्द — लयबद्धताको नियम। कवितामा पङ्क्ति, चरण, अन्तरा, मुखडा, र सन्धि भएको देखिन्छ।

कवितिका अलङ्कारहरू (Figures of Speech in Poetry): कवितामा प्रयोग हुने मुख्य अलङ्कारहरू: (१) उपमा — दुई वस्तुको तुलना गर्न, जस्तै: 'उनको अनुहार चन्द्रमाजस्तो छ।' (२) रूपक — उपमाको 'जस्तो' हटाएर सिधै तुलना गर्न, जस्तै: 'चन्द्रमा अनुहार हो।' (३) उत्प्रेक्षा — एक वस्तुलाई अर्को वस्तु मान्न, जस्तै: 'म पनि हाँसेँ तर आँखा रा आयो।' (४) अतिशयोक्ति — वस्तुको गुणलाई अतिक्रान्त गरन। (५) प्रतीप — विपरित अर्थमा बोलन।

कवितामा भाषाको भूमिका (Role of Language in Poetry): कवितामा भाषाको भूमिका अत्यन्त महत्त्वपूर्ण हुन्छ। कविले सामान्य भाषा प्रयोग गरेर पनि गहिरो भाव व्यक्त गर्न सक्छन्। कवितामा प्रयोग हुने भाषा सरल, स्पष्ट, र प्रभावकारी हुनुपर्छ। भाषामा छन्द, लय, र तुकको सहारे कवितालाई सुन्दर बनाउन सकिन्छ। नेपाली कवितामा 'सरल भाषा' र 'गम्भीर भाव' को संयोग देखिन्छ।

कवितिका रूपहरू (Forms of Poetry): नेपाली कवितामा प्रयोग हुने प्रमुख रूपहरू: (१) पङ्क्ति — कवितार एक वाक्य वा भाग, (२) चरण — धेरै पङ्क्तिाका समूह, (३) अन्तरा — कवितार दोहोरिने भाग, (४) मुखडा — कवितार पहिलो चरण, (५) तुकबन्दी — अन्तिम शब्दहरूको ध्वनि मिलाप, (६) छन्द — लयबद्धताको नियम।

कवितामा रस (Rasa in Poetry): कवितामा रसको महत्वपर्नु हुन्छ। रस भनेको भावनाको स्वाद हो। नेपाली कवितामा मुख्यतया नौ रसहरू प्रयोग हुन्छन्: शृङ्गार, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, हस्य, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत, शान्त। प्रत्येक रसको आफ्नै विशेषता र प्रभाव हुन्छ। रस भनेको भावनाको पूर्ण र परिपक्व रूप हो जसले पाठकलाई आनन्द दिन्छ।

छन्दको परिचय (Introduction to Chhanda): छन्द भनेको कवितामा प्रयोग हुने लयबद्धताको नियम हो। छन्दले कवितालाई संगीतात्मक रूप दिन्छ। नेपाली कवितामा प्रयोग हुने प्रमुख छन्दहरू: अलङ्कार, भुजङ्ग, मनकृान्त, सरित, शारदा, आर्या, इत्यादि। छन्द भनेको कवितार लय, ताल, र गतिका नियम हो।

कवितामा मुद्रा (Mode/Mudra in Poetry): मुद्रा भनेको कवितामा प्रयोग हुने भावनात्मक र शैलीगत विशेषता हो। कविको मुद्राले कवितालाई एउटा अलग पहिचान दिन्छ। कविको जीवन अनुभव, दार्शनिक दृष्टिकोण, र भाषा प्रयोगले कविको मुद्रा निर्माण गर्छ। नेपाली कवितामा बरसड्डड्डी कविहरूको आफ्नै मुद्रा छ: बंसীधर जोशीको मार्मिकता, लक्ष्मीप्रसाद देवकोटाको गम्भीरता, प्रेम थपाको प्रकृतिप्रति आकर्षण।

नेपाली कविको ऐतिहासिक विकास (Historical Development of Nepali Poetry): नेपाली कविताको विकास तीन चरणमा बाँडिएको छ: (१) आधुनिकता पूर्वकाल (Pre-modern) — २००० साल prior, जसमा भक्ति, रसिक, र छन्दोबद्ध कविता प्रमुख थियो। (२) आधुनिक काल (Modern) — २००० देखि २०४६ साल सम्म, जसमा मुक्तक, गद्य कविता, र समकालीन विचारहरूले जन्म लिए। (३) समकालीन काल (Contemporary) — २०४६ साल पछि, जसमा सामाजिक, राजनीतिक, र दार्शनिक कविताहरू प्रमुख छन्।

प्रमुख नेपाली कविहरू (Prominent Nepali Poets): नेपाली कवितार प्रमुख कविहरू: (१) लक्ष्मीप्रसाद देवकोटा — 'महाकाव्य शिशिरको कुहिं', 'मुक्ति', 'भाइबहाइन'। (२) बंसोधर जोशी — 'सुनको फूल', 'माया', 'आँखाको आँसु'। (३) प्रेम थपा — 'प्रकृति कवि', 'सृष्टिको सपना'। (४) मोतस तुम्बाहाङ्फे — 'मिचेको माटी', 'सृजना'। (५) बालकृष्ण सम — 'शून्य', 'कविता सङ्ग्रह'। (६) भोला नेम्वाङ — 'नेपाली कविताका जनक'।

NEB पाठ्यक्रममा कविता (Poetry in NEB Curriculum): NEB (राष्ट्रिय परीक्षा बोर्ड) को नेपाली पाठ्यक्रममा कविता अध्ययनको उद्देश्य विद्यार्थीहरूमा भावनात्मक संवेदना, भाषिक सौन्दर्यबोध र आलोचनात्मक चेतना विकास गर्न हो। कविता पढ्दा भाव, भाषा, शिल्प र सन्देश — यी चार पक्षमा ध्यान दिनुपर्छ। NEB परीक्षामा कवितार अर्थ, अलङ्कार पहिचान, रस पहिचान, र विश्लेषण सम्बन्धी प्रश्नहरू आउँछन्।

कवितामा शब्दार्थ र व्याख्या (Word Meaning and Explanation in Poetry): कवितामा प्रयोग भएका शब्दहरूको अर्थ थाहा हुनु महत्त्वपूर्ण छ। कविहरूले प्रायः पुराना वा कठिन शब्दहरू प्रयोग गर्छन् जसको अर्थ थाहा हुनुपर्छ। शब्दार्थ थाहा हुँदा कवितार भाव बुझ्न सजिलो हुन्छ। NEB परीक्षामा शब्दार्थ लेख्न के प्रश्न प्रायः आउँछ।

कवितामा प्रतीकात्मकता (Symbolism in Poetry): कवितामा प्रतीकात्मकताले गहिरो अर्थ दिन्छ। एउटा वस्तु वा घटनाले अर्को गहिरो अर्थलाई संकेत गर्छ। उदाहरणका लागि: 'रातो खसरी'ले स्वतन्त्रताको प्रतीक हो, 'नीरव पहड'ले स्थिरताको प्रतीक हो, 'नदी'ले जीवन प्रवाहको प्रतीक हो। प्रतीक भनेको वस्तु वा घटना हो जसले गहिरो अर्थलाई जनाउँछ।

कविता विश्लेषणका पाँच पक्ष (Five Aspects of Poetry Analysis): कवितार विश्लेषण गर्दा निमन् पाँच पक्षहरू हेरिन्छन्: (१) भाव (Theme) — कवितार मुख्य विषय र भावना। (२) भाषा (Language) — प्रयोग भएका शब्दहरूको सरलता र प्रभावकारिता। (३) शिल्प (Technique) — छन्द, तुक, अलङ्कार, प्रतीक आदिको प्रयोग। (४) सन्देश (Message) — कवितारबाट पाठकले पाउन सक्ने सन्देश। (५) रस (Rasa) — कवितारमा प्रमुख रूपमा छाएको रस।
confusion: कवितामा छन्द हुनैपर्छ — गलत। गद्य कवितामा छन्द वा तुक हुँदैन, त्यसैले कविता छन्दोबद्ध हुनुपर्छ भन्ने आवश्यक छैन।
उपमा र रूपक एउटै हुन् — गलत। उपमामा 'जस्तो' जस्ता शब्द प्रयोग हुन्छन् तर रूपकमा 'हो' जस्ता शब्द प्रयोग हुन्छन्।
कवितामा तुक हुनैपर्छ — गलत। आधुनिक कवितामा तुक हुँदैन, अनियमित लयमा कविता लेखिन्छ।
रस र भाव एउटै हुन् — गलत। भाव सामान्य भावना हो भने रस भावनाको परिपक्व रूप हो जसले पाठकलाई आनन्द दिन्छ।
कवितामा कवि र नायक एउटै हुन् — गलत। कविले कवितामा नायक वा नायिकाको रूपमा भाव व्यक्त गर्छन्, कवि र नायक फरक हुन्छन्।
अलङ्कार र रस एउटै हुन् — गलत। अलङ्कार भनेको शब्द वा वाक्यको सौन्दर्य बढाउन सधन हो भने रस भनेको भावनाको स्वाद हो।

data.title: Angular Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Angular displacement (Δθ):** the angle through which a body rotates about a fixed axis. Measured in radians (rad). 1 rad = 57.3°, 2π rad = 360°. Angular displacement is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule): positive for anticlockwise rotation.

**Angular velocity (ω):** the rate of change of angular displacement: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average). Unit: rad/s. Direction: along the axis (right-hand rule). For uniform circular motion, ω is constant.
**Angular acceleration (α):** the rate of change of angular velocity: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt². Unit: rad/s². When α is constant, the kinematic equations mirror linear motion.

**Relationship between linear and angular quantities (for circular motion):** v = rω (linear speed = radius × angular speed), a_t = rα (tangential acceleration), a_c = v²/r = rω² (centripetal acceleration). These links connect rotational and translational motion.

**Kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration (mirror linear v = u + at, etc.):** ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; θ = (ω + ω₀)t/2. The structure is identical to linear motion — just swap x→θ, v→ω, a→α.

**Worked example — spinning wheel:** a wheel starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 rad/s² for 5 s. Angular displacement: θ = 0 + ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 rad. Final angular velocity: ω = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 rad/s. Number of revolutions: 25/(2π) ≈ 3.98 rev.

**Worked example — decelerating fan:** a fan blade rotating at 120 rpm (120 × 2π/60 = 12.57 rad/s) comes to rest in 8 s. Angular acceleration: α = (0 − 12.57)/8 = −1.57 rad/s². Angular displacement: θ = 12.57 × 8/2 = 50.27 rad ≈ 8 rev.

**NEB exam focus:** converting between rpm and rad/s; applying the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration; linking linear and angular quantities (v = rω, a = rω²); finding number of revolutions from angular displacement.

**Right-hand rule for angular quantities:** curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation; your thumb points along the angular velocity/acceleration vector. For anticlockwise rotation (as viewed from above), the vector points upward; for clockwise, it points downward.

**Angular displacement is NOT a simple angle:** while measured in radians, angular displacement has direction (along the axis). For rotations greater than 2π, the magnitude keeps increasing — unlike a simple angle which resets after 360°. This is why angular displacement is a true vector quantity.

**Non-uniform circular motion:** when angular acceleration α ≠ 0, both tangential acceleration (a_t = rα) and centripetal acceleration (a_c = rω²) are present. The total acceleration is the vector sum: a = √(a_t² + a_c²). The direction of total acceleration is at angle φ = arctan(a_c/a_t) from the tangential direction.

**Small angle approximation:** for oscillatory motion (pendulums, springs), when θ is small (θ < 0.1 rad ≈ 6°), we can approximate sin θ ≈ θ and cos θ ≈ 1. This linearizes the equations and makes them solvable analytically.

**Angular quantities as vectors — addition is NOT commutative for large angles:** while infinitesimal angular displacements dθ are vectors (they commute), finite angular displacements do NOT commute. Rotating 90° about x then 90° about y gives a different result than rotating 90° about y then 90° about x. This is why angular velocity is a true vector but finite angular displacement is not.
formulas: Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average)
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt²
Kinematic equations (constant α): ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
Linear-angular links: v = rω; a_t = rα; a_c = v²/r = rω²
rpm conversion: ω (rad/s) = rpm × 2π/60; revolutions = θ/(2π)
confusion: ❌ 'Angular displacement and angle are the same.' ✅ Angular displacement is a vector (along the axis), while angle is a scalar. For a full revolution, angular displacement = 2π rad, but the body returns to its starting position.
❌ 'Angular velocity is always constant in circular motion.' ✅ Only in UNIFORM circular motion is ω constant. In non-uniform circular motion, ω changes and there is angular acceleration.

❌ 'The direction of angular velocity is tangential.' ❌ The direction of angular velocity is ALONG THE AXIS of rotation (right-hand rule), not tangential. Tangential velocity is v = rω, but ω itself points along the axis.

❌ 'Angular acceleration means the body is speeding up.' ✅ Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity. If α and ω have the same sign, the body speeds up; if opposite signs, it slows down.
❌ 'The kinematic equations for rotation are different from linear motion.' ✅ They are IDENTICAL in form: just replace x with θ, v with ω, and a with α. The same problem-solving approach works.
❌ 'rpm and rad/s are the same.' ✅ 1 rpm = 2π/60 rad/s ≈ 0.105 rad/s. Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas.

data.title: Centripetal Acceleration and Force
notes: **Centripetal acceleration (a_c):** the acceleration directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps a body moving in a circle. Magnitude: a_c = v²/r = rω². Direction: always toward the centre (hence 'centripetal' = 'centre-seeking'). It changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.

**Centripetal force (F_c):** the net force required to produce centripetal acceleration: F_c = mv²/r = mrω². It is NOT a new force — it is the RESULTANT of real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal) pointing toward the centre.

**Why centripetal force is not a separate force:** the centripetal force is always provided by one or more real forces. For a car turning on a flat road, friction provides F_c. For a planet orbiting the Sun, gravity provides F_c. For a ball on a string, tension provides F_c.

**Derivation of a_c = v²/r:** consider a body moving at constant speed v in a circle of radius r. In a small time Δt, it moves from A to B. The change in velocity Δv points toward the centre. From similar triangles: Δv/v = Δs/r → Δv = vΔs/r. Acceleration a = Δv/Δt = v²/r (since Δs/Δt = v).

**Worked example — car turning:** a 1000 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. Required friction: F_c = mv²/r = 1000 × 400/50 = 8000 N. If μ_s = 0.6, max friction = 0.6 × 1000 × 9.8 = 5880 N — the car skids (8000 > 5880).
**Worked example — ball on a string:** a 0.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string rotates at 4 m/s. Tension = mv²/r = 0.5 × 16/1.5 = 5.33 N. If the string breaks at 10 N, max speed = √(10 × 1.5/0.5) = 5.48 m/s.

**Worked example — planet orbit:** Earth orbits the Sun at 30 km/s at a distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Centripetal acceleration = v²/r = (3×10⁴)²/(1.5×10¹¹) = 6 × 10⁻³ m/s². This is provided by the Sun's gravity.

It is always provided by some real force or combination of forces: tension (string), gravity (planets), friction (car on road), normal force (banked road), magnetic force (charged particle). It is a pseudo-force — it arises from the inertia of the body wanting to move in a straight line. In an inertial (non-accelerating) frame, there is NO outward force — only the inward centripetal force.

data.title: Relation Between Angular and Linear Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Angular displacement (Δθ):** the angle through which a body rotates about a fixed axis. Measured in radians (rad). 1 rad = 57.3°, 2π rad = 360°. Angular displacement is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule): positive for anticlockwise rotation.

**Angular velocity (ω):** the rate of change of angular displacement: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average). Unit: rad/s. Direction: along the axis (right-hand rule). For uniform circular motion, ω is constant.
**Angular acceleration (α):** the rate of change of angular velocity: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt². Unit: rad/s². When α is constant, the kinematic equations mirror linear motion.

**Relationship between linear and angular quantities (for circular motion):** v = rω (linear speed = radius × angular speed), a_t = rα (tangential acceleration), a_c = v²/r = rω² (centripetal acceleration). These links connect rotational and translational motion.

**Kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration (mirror linear v = u + at, etc.):** ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; θ = (ω + ω₀)t/2. The structure is identical to linear motion — just swap x→θ, v→ω, a→α.

**Worked example — spinning wheel:** a wheel starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 rad/s² for 5 s. Angular displacement: θ = 0 + ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 rad. Final angular velocity: ω = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 rad/s. Number of revolutions: 25/(2π) ≈ 3.98 rev.

**Worked example — decelerating fan:** a fan blade rotating at 120 rpm (120 × 2π/60 = 12.57 rad/s) comes to rest in 8 s. Angular acceleration: α = (0 − 12.57)/8 = −1.57 rad/s². Angular displacement: θ = 12.57 × 8/2 = 50.27 rad ≈ 8 rev.

**NEB exam focus:** converting between rpm and rad/s; applying the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration; linking linear and angular quantities (v = rω, a = rω²); finding number of revolutions from angular displacement.

**Right-hand rule for angular quantities:** curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation; your thumb points along the angular velocity/acceleration vector. For anticlockwise rotation (as viewed from above), the vector points upward; for clockwise, it points downward.

**Angular displacement is NOT a simple angle:** while measured in radians, angular displacement has direction (along the axis). For rotations greater than 2π, the magnitude keeps increasing — unlike a simple angle which resets after 360°. This is why angular displacement is a true vector quantity.

**Non-uniform circular motion:** when angular acceleration α ≠ 0, both tangential acceleration (a_t = rα) and centripetal acceleration (a_c = rω²) are present. The total acceleration is the vector sum: a = √(a_t² + a_c²). The direction of total acceleration is at angle φ = arctan(a_c/a_t) from the tangential direction.

**Small angle approximation:** for oscillatory motion (pendulums, springs), when θ is small (θ < 0.1 rad ≈ 6°), we can approximate sin θ ≈ θ and cos θ ≈ 1. This linearizes the equations and makes them solvable analytically.

**Angular quantities as vectors — addition is NOT commutative for large angles:** while infinitesimal angular displacements dθ are vectors (they commute), finite angular displacements do NOT commute. Rotating 90° about x then 90° about y gives a different result than rotating 90° about y then 90° about x. This is why angular velocity is a true vector but finite angular displacement is not.

Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt²
Kinematic equations (constant α): ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
Linear-angular links: v = rω; a_t = rα; a_c = v²/r = rω²
rpm conversion: ω (rad/s) = rpm × 2π/60; revolutions = θ/(2π)

❌ 'Angular velocity is always constant in circular motion.' ✅ Only in UNIFORM circular motion is ω constant. In non-uniform circular motion, ω changes and there is angular acceleration.

❌ 'The direction of angular velocity is tangential.' ❌ The direction of angular velocity is ALONG THE AXIS of rotation (right-hand rule), not tangential. Tangential velocity is v = rω, but ω itself points along the axis.

❌ 'Angular acceleration means the body is speeding up.' ✅ Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity. If α and ω have the same sign, the body speeds up; if opposite signs, it slows down.
❌ 'The kinematic equations for rotation are different from linear motion.' ✅ They are IDENTICAL in form: just replace x with θ, v with ω, and a with α. The same problem-solving approach works.
❌ 'rpm and rad/s are the same.' ✅ 1 rpm = 2π/60 rad/s ≈ 0.105 rad/s. Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas.

data.title: Conical Pendulum
notes: **Conical pendulum:** a small bob of mass m attached to a string of length L, moving in a horizontal circle at constant speed such that the string traces out a cone. The string makes angle θ with the vertical and the bob moves in a circle of radius r = L sin θ.

**Forces and geometry:** two forces act on the bob: tension T along the string, and weight mg downward. The tension has vertical component T cos θ (balances weight) and horizontal component T sin θ (provides centripetal force).

**Key equations:** T cos θ = mg (vertical equilibrium) ... (1); T sin θ = mω²r = mω²L sin θ (centripetal) ... (2). From (2): T = mω²L. Substituting into (1): mω²L cos θ = mg → cos θ = g/(ω²L). Also: ω = √(g/L cos θ) and T_period = 2π√(L cos θ/g).

**Key insight — period depends only on L cos θ:** the period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) is independent of the mass of the bob. A taller cone (larger θ, smaller cos θ) has a shorter period (faster rotation). The minimum period is when θ → 0: T_min = 2π√(L/g) (same as a simple pendulum of length L).

**Worked example:** a 0.2 kg bob on a 2 m string rotates with θ = 30°. cos 30° = 0.866. Angular speed: ω = √(9.8/(2 × 0.866)) = √5.66 = 2.38 rad/s. Period: T = 2π/2.38 = 2.64 s. Tension: T = mω²L = 0.2 × 5.66 × 2 = 2.26 N. Radius: r = 2 × sin 30° = 1 m.

**Comparison with simple pendulum:** both have period T = 2π√(L_eff/g). For a simple pendulum, L_eff = L. For a conical pendulum, L_eff = L cos θ (the vertical height of the cone). So a conical pendulum swings slower than a simple pendulum of the same string length.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving the relation cos θ = g/(ω²L); finding the period, angular speed, or tension; showing that the period is independent of mass; comparing conical and simple pendulums.
**Practical examples:** a tethered aeroplane model, a ball on a string swung in a horizontal circle, vehicles banking on a curved road (same geometry — the road provides the 'tension' component).

**Deriving the key result step by step:** from vertical equilibrium: T cos θ = mg → T = mg/cos θ. From horizontal force: T sin θ = mω²r = mω²L sin θ. Canceling sin θ (assuming θ ≠ 0): T = mω²L. Equating: mω²L = mg/cos θ → ω² = g/(L cos θ) → ω = √(g/L cos θ). This derivation is the standard NEB proof question.

**Period formula insight:** T_period = 2π/ω = 2π√(L cos θ/g). Note that L cos θ is the VERTICAL HEIGHT h of the cone. So T = 2π√(h/g) — the period depends only on the vertical height, not on the radius or the mass. A cone with height 1 m has the same period regardless of how wide it is.

**Relation to simple pendulum:** a simple pendulum of length L has period T = 2π√(L/g). A conical pendulum of string length L has period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) = 2π√(h/g). Since cos θ < 1, the conical pendulum's period is LONGER than a simple pendulum of the same string length — it swings more slowly.

**Connection to banking of roads:** the conical pendulum and a banked road share identical force geometry. In the pendulum, tension provides both vertical support and centripetal force. In a banked road, the normal force plays the same dual role. The equation tan θ = v²/(rg) for banking is equivalent to the conical pendulum's geometry.

**Watt's governor:** the conical pendulum is the basis of the centrifugal governor used in steam engines. As the engine speeds up, the bobs rise (θ increases), which mechanically reduces the steam supply. This is a real-world application that NEB sometimes references.
formulas: Vertical equilibrium: T cos θ = mg
Centripetal force: T sin θ = mω²L sin θ → T = mω²L
Angular speed: ω = √(g/(L cos θ))
Period: T_period = 2π√(L cos θ/g) — independent of mass
Radius of circle: r = L sin θ
confusion: ❌ 'The tension in the string equals mg.' ✅ The vertical component of tension equals mg. The total tension is greater: T = mg/cos θ (since cos θ < 1, T > mg).
❌ 'The bob is in equilibrium.' ✅ The bob is in vertical equilibrium (T cos θ = mg) but NOT horizontal equilibrium — it accelerates toward the centre (centripetal acceleration).
❌ 'The period depends on the mass of the bob.' ✅ The period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) is independent of mass. A heavier bob rotates at the same period (for the same θ).
❌ 'A faster rotation gives a smaller θ.' ✅ A FASTER rotation gives a LARGER θ (the cone becomes flatter). From cos θ = g/(ω²L), as ω increases, cos θ decreases, so θ increases.
❌ 'The radius of the circle is L.' ✅ The radius is r = L sin θ, which is LESS than L. Only if θ = 90° would r = L (but then cos θ = 0 and the equations break down).
❌ 'The centripetal force is a new force to add to the FBD.' ✅ The centripetal force IS the horizontal component of tension: T sin θ = mω²r. No new force is added.

data.title: Motion in a Vertical Circle
notes: **Motion in a vertical circle:** a body of mass m attached to a string moves in a vertical plane under gravity. Unlike horizontal circular motion, the speed varies with height — fastest at the bottom, slowest at the top.

**Why speed varies:** gravity does work on the body as it moves vertically. Kinetic energy is converted to gravitational PE on the way up, and back to KE on the way down. Total mechanical energy is conserved (ignoring air resistance).

**Critical distinction — string vs rigid rod:** a string can only pull (tension ≥ 0), so the body must have enough speed at the top to keep the string taut. A rigid rod can push or pull, so the body can reach the top with zero speed.

**Minimum speed at the top (string):** at the top, both tension T and weight mg point downward: T + mg = mv²/r. The minimum speed occurs when T → 0: mg = mv_min²/r → v_top(min) = √(gr). Below this, the string goes slack.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (string):** using energy conservation from bottom to top: ½mv_bottom² = ½mv_top² + mg(2r). With v_top = √(gr): ½v_bottom² = ½(gr) + 2gr → v_bottom² = 5gr → v_bottom(min) = √(5gr). This is the critical NEB result.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (rod):** since the rod can push, the body can reach the top with v_top = 0. Energy conservation: ½v_bottom² = 0 + 2gr → v_bottom(min) = √(2gr). This is lower than the string case.
**Tension at the bottom:** T_bottom − mg = mv_bottom²/r → T_bottom = mg + mv_bottom²/r. For the minimum case (string): T_bottom = mg + 5mg = 6mg. The tension at the bottom is 6 times the weight.
**Tension at the top:** T_top + mg = mv_top²/r → T_top = mv_top²/r − mg. For the minimum case (string): T_top = 0.
**Worked example:** a 0.5 kg bob on a 1.5 m string. v_top(min) = √(9.8 × 1.5) = 3.83 m/s. v_bottom(min) = √(5 × 9.8 × 1.5) = 8.57 m/s. T_bottom = 6 × 0.5 × 9.8 = 29.4 N.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving v_top(min) = √(gr) and v_bottom(min) = √(5gr); comparing string vs rod; finding tension at top and bottom; energy conservation between positions.

**Energy diagram for vertical circle:** plot KE, PE, and total E vs. height. KE is maximum at the bottom (½mv_b²), minimum at the top (½mv_t²). PE is minimum (0) at the bottom and maximum (mg·2r) at the top. Total energy E = ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + 2mgr — a horizontal line on the diagram.

**Tension variation around the circle:** at any angle θ from the bottom, T = mv²/r + mg cos θ. At the bottom (θ = 0°): T = mg + mv²/r (maximum). At the top (θ = 180°): T = mv²/r − mg (minimum). The tension difference between bottom and top is always 6mg when the minimum-speed condition holds.

**Worked example — tension at arbitrary point:** a 0.2 kg bob on a 0.8 m string has speed 6 m/s at the bottom. At the top: ½v_t² = ½ × 36 − 9.8 × 1.6 = 18 − 15.68 = 2.32 → v_t = 2.15 m/s. T_top = 0.2 × 4.62/0.8 − 1.96 = 1.16 − 1.96 = −0.80 N. Since T < 0, the string goes slack before reaching the top. The bob cannot complete the circle.

**Rod vs. string — key differences:** a rod can support compression, so the bob can reach the top with v = 0. The rod pushes upward with force mg at the top. Minimum bottom speed for a rod: √(2gr). For a string: √(5gr). The factor 5 versus 2 is the critical distinction tested in NEB.

**Complete-the-circle condition:** for a string, the condition is v_bottom ≥ √(5gr). For a rod, it is v_bottom ≥ √(2gr). If v_bottom is between √(2gr) and √(5gr), the bob completes the circle with a rod but not with a string.
formulas: Minimum speed at top (string): v_top = √(gr)
Minimum speed at bottom (string): v_bottom = √(5gr)
Minimum speed at bottom (rod): v_bottom = √(2gr)
Tension at bottom: T_bottom = mg + mv²/r

data.title: Applications of Banking
notes: **Banking of roads:** the practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road above the inner edge so that the normal reaction from the road surface provides part or all of the centripetal force needed to turn. This reduces reliance on friction and prevents skidding.

**Why banking is needed:** on a flat road, the entire centripetal force must come from friction: F_c = μmg. At high speeds or on slippery roads, friction may be insufficient and the vehicle skids outward. Banking tilts the road so the normal force has a horizontal component pointing toward the center.

**Forces on a banked road:** the road is tilted at angle θ. The normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface. Resolving N: vertical component N cos θ balances weight (N cos θ = mg); horizontal component N sin θ provides centripetal force (N sin θ = mv²/r).

**Key equation — ideal banking angle (no friction needed):** dividing the two equations: tan θ = v²/(rg). For a given radius r and design speed v, the road should be banked at angle θ = arctan(v²/(rg)). At this angle, no friction is required.

**Friction on a banked road:** if the vehicle moves faster than the design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope (preventing outward skid). If slower, friction acts UP the slope (preventing inward sliding). The general formula: tan(θ + φ) = v²/(rg), where φ = arctan(μ).
**Maximum speed on a banked road with friction:** v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]. When μ = 0 (no friction), this reduces to v = √(rg tan θ). When θ = 0 (flat road), it reduces to v = √(μrg).
**Worked example — car on banked curve:** a road of radius 100 m is banked at θ = 15°. Design speed (no friction): v = √(100 × 9.8 × tan 15°) = √(100 × 9.8 × 0.268) = √262.6 = 16.2 m/s (≈ 58 km/h).

**Railway banking (superelevation):** railways use the same principle. The outer rail is raised by height h above the inner rail. For track gauge w and banking angle θ: tan θ ≈ h/w. This prevents wear on rails and ensures passenger comfort.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving tan θ = v²/(rg); finding the design speed for a given banking angle; maximum speed with friction; railway superelevation problems.

**Force resolution on a banked road — detailed derivation:** draw the FBD with N perpendicular to the road and mg vertically down. Resolve N into: vertical component N cos θ (balances weight) and horizontal component N sin θ (provides centripetal force). From N cos θ = mg: N = mg/cos θ. From N sin θ = mv²/r: (mg/cos θ) sin θ = mv²/r → mg tan θ = mv²/r → tan θ = v²/(rg). This derivation is the standard NEB proof.

**Friction on a banked road — general case:** when friction is present, there are two limiting cases. Case 1 (going too fast): friction acts DOWN the slope, adding to the centripetal force. Case 2 (going too slow): friction acts UP the slope, preventing inward sliding. The general equation combining both: N sin θ ± f cos θ = mv²/r (horizontal) and N cos θ ∓ f sin θ = mg (vertical), where f = μN.

**Worked example — finding banking angle:** a curve of radius 150 m is designed for 90 km/h (25 m/s). Required banking angle: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 625/(150 × 9.8) = 0.425 → θ = 23.0°. At this angle, a car can negotiate the curve without any friction.

**Worked example — height of outer rail:** a railway track of gauge 1.5 m is banked at 5°. The height by which the outer rail is raised: h = w tan θ = 1.5 × tan 5° = 1.5 × 0.0875 = 0.131 m ≈ 13.1 cm. This is a typical NEB numerical problem.

**Why banking reduces tire wear:** on a flat road, friction must provide all centripetal force, causing lateral tire stress. On a banked road at the design speed, the normal force provides the centripetal component — no lateral friction needed. This dramatically reduces tire wear and fuel consumption.

Maximum speed with friction: v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]
Minimum speed with friction: v_min = √[rg(tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)]
Railway superelevation: h = w tan θ, where w = track gauge
Normal force on banked road: N = mg/cos θ
confusion: ❌ 'Banking eliminates friction entirely.' ✅ Banking REDUCES friction requirement. At the design speed (tan θ = v²/(rg)), friction is zero. At other speeds, friction is still needed.
❌ 'A steeper bank angle is always better.' ✅ Too steep a bank angle causes problems at low speeds — the vehicle may slide inward. The ideal angle depends on the design speed.
❌ 'The normal force equals mg on a banked road.' ✅ The normal force is N = mg/cos θ, which is GREATER than mg because the road is tilted.
❌ 'Banking angle depends on the mass of the vehicle.' ✅ The ideal banking angle tan θ = v²/(rg) is independent of mass — it depends only on speed and radius.
❌ 'On a banked road, friction always acts up the slope.' ✅ Friction direction depends on speed: if v > design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope; if v < design speed, friction acts UP.

data.title: Motion in a Vertical Circle
notes: **Motion in a vertical circle:** a body of mass m attached to a string moves in a vertical plane under gravity. Unlike horizontal circular motion, the speed varies with height — fastest at the bottom, slowest at the top.

**Why speed varies:** gravity does work on the body as it moves vertically. Kinetic energy is converted to gravitational PE on the way up, and back to KE on the way down. Total mechanical energy is conserved (ignoring air resistance).

**Critical distinction — string vs rigid rod:** a string can only pull (tension ≥ 0), so the body must have enough speed at the top to keep the string taut. A rigid rod can push or pull, so the body can reach the top with zero speed.

**Minimum speed at the top (string):** at the top, both tension T and weight mg point downward: T + mg = mv²/r. The minimum speed occurs when T → 0: mg = mv_min²/r → v_top(min) = √(gr). Below this, the string goes slack.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (string):** using energy conservation from bottom to top: ½mv_bottom² = ½mv_top² + mg(2r). With v_top = √(gr): ½v_bottom² = ½(gr) + 2gr → v_bottom² = 5gr → v_bottom(min) = √(5gr). This is the critical NEB result.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (rod):** since the rod can push, the body can reach the top with v_top = 0. Energy conservation: ½v_bottom² = 0 + 2gr → v_bottom(min) = √(2gr). This is lower than the string case.
**Tension at the bottom:** T_bottom − mg = mv_bottom²/r → T_bottom = mg + mv_bottom²/r. For the minimum case (string): T_bottom = mg + 5mg = 6mg. The tension at the bottom is 6 times the weight.
**Tension at the top:** T_top + mg = mv_top²/r → T_top = mv_top²/r − mg. For the minimum case (string): T_top = 0.
**Worked example:** a 0.5 kg bob on a 1.5 m string. v_top(min) = √(9.8 × 1.5) = 3.83 m/s. v_bottom(min) = √(5 × 9.8 × 1.5) = 8.57 m/s. T_bottom = 6 × 0.5 × 9.8 = 29.4 N.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving v_top(min) = √(gr) and v_bottom(min) = √(5gr); comparing string vs rod; finding tension at top and bottom; energy conservation between positions.

**Energy diagram for vertical circle:** plot KE, PE, and total E vs. height. KE is maximum at the bottom (½mv_b²), minimum at the top (½mv_t²). PE is minimum (0) at the bottom and maximum (mg·2r) at the top. Total energy E = ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + 2mgr — a horizontal line on the diagram.

**Tension variation around the circle:** at any angle θ from the bottom, T = mv²/r + mg cos θ. At the bottom (θ = 0°): T = mg + mv²/r (maximum). At the top (θ = 180°): T = mv²/r − mg (minimum). The tension difference between bottom and top is always 6mg when the minimum-speed condition holds.

**Worked example — tension at arbitrary point:** a 0.2 kg bob on a 0.8 m string has speed 6 m/s at the bottom. At the top: ½v_t² = ½ × 36 − 9.8 × 1.6 = 18 − 15.68 = 2.32 → v_t = 2.15 m/s. T_top = 0.2 × 4.62/0.8 − 1.96 = 1.16 − 1.96 = −0.80 N. Since T < 0, the string goes slack before reaching the top. The bob cannot complete the circle.

**Rod vs. string — key differences:** a rod can support compression, so the bob can reach the top with v = 0. The rod pushes upward with force mg at the top. Minimum bottom speed for a rod: √(2gr). For a string: √(5gr). The factor 5 versus 2 is the critical distinction tested in NEB.

**Complete-the-circle condition:** for a string, the condition is v_bottom ≥ √(5gr). For a rod, it is v_bottom ≥ √(2gr). If v_bottom is between √(2gr) and √(5gr), the bob completes the circle with a rod but not with a string.

Minimum speed at bottom (string): v_bottom = √(5gr)
Minimum speed at bottom (rod): v_bottom = √(2gr)
Tension at bottom: T_bottom = mg + mv²/r
Tension at top: T_top = mv²/r − mg
Energy conservation: ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + mg(2r)

data.title: Circular Motion Mindmap
notes: Circular motion: motion of a body along a circular path. Key quantities: angular displacement (θ), angular velocity (ω), angular acceleration (α), centripetal acceleration (a_c = v²/r = rω²).
Angular displacement: θ = s/r (radians); 2π rad = 360° = 1 revolution; vector along axis (right-hand rule).
Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt; uniform circular motion has constant ω; unit: rad/s; rpm conversion: × 2π/60.
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt; constant α gives kinematic equations mirroring linear motion.
Centripetal acceleration: a_c = v²/r = rω² — always directed toward the center; changes direction of velocity, not speed.
Centripetal force: F_c = mv²/r — not a new force; provided by tension, gravity, friction, or normal force.
Conical pendulum: bob moves in horizontal circle; string traces cone; period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g), independent of mass.
Vertical circle: speed varies with height; minimum top speed (string) = √(gr); minimum bottom speed = √(5gr).
Banking of roads: tan θ = v²/(rg) for ideal angle; reduces friction requirement; railway superelevation h = w tan θ.
NEB exam focus: converting rpm to rad/s; centripetal force identification; conical pendulum derivation; vertical circle min speeds; banking angle calculations.

data.title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
notes: **Ohmic conductor:** obeys Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant.
**Non-ohmic conductor:** does not obey Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is curved. Resistance changes with voltage or current.

**Examples of non-ohmic:** diode (conducts easily in one direction only), filament lamp (resistance increases with temperature as current increases), thermistor (resistance decreases with temperature).
**Why filament lamp is non-ohmic:** as current increases, the filament heats up, increasing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve bends because $R$ is not constant.
**Dynamic resistance:** $R_d = dV/dI$ at a point on the $I$-$V$ curve. For non-ohmic devices, this is the useful measure of resistance at a specific operating point.
**Forward bias diode:** current flows easily once the voltage exceeds the threshold ($\\\\approx 0.7$ V for silicon, $\\\\approx 0.3$ V for germanium). Below threshold, very little current flows.
**Reverse bias diode:** almost no current flows (except a tiny leakage current). At the breakdown voltage, current increases sharply and the diode may be damaged.
**Thermistor:** a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases sharply with temperature (NTC type). Used as temperature sensors and inrush current limiters.
**Zener diode:** operates in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage. It maintains a nearly constant voltage across it, used as a voltage regulator.

**Filament lamp $I$-$V$ curve:** starts linearly at low voltage (cool filament, low resistance). At higher voltages, the curve bends toward the voltage axis as the filament heats and resistance increases.

**Temperature coefficient of filament:** tungsten has $\\\\alpha \\\\approx 0.0045$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. A 100 W, 230 V bulb has cold resistance of about $50\\\\,\\\\Omega$ but hot resistance of $529\\\\,\\\\Omega$.
confusion: Ohm's law $V = IR$ is a definition of resistance, not a law that all materials obey. Only ohmic conductors have a linear $I$-$V$ relationship. For non-ohmic devices, $R = V/I$ is still defined but varies.

A filament lamp becomes a better conductor (lower resistance) when cold. This is why bulbs often burn out at the moment they are switched on - the initial current surge is 10 times the steady-state current.

The dynamic resistance $dV/dI$ is different from the static resistance $V/I$. For a non-ohmic device, the static resistance is $V/I$ while the dynamic resistance is the slope of the $I$-$V$ curve at that point.

A diode is not simply a 'one-way valve' for current. In reverse bias, a tiny leakage current (nA to $\\\mu$A range) still flows. In forward bias, the current is exponentially related to voltage, not linearly.

Thermistors are not simply temperature-dependent resistors. Their resistance changes exponentially with temperature: $R = R_0 e^{\ eta(1/T - 1/T_0)}$, which makes them highly sensitive to small temperature changes.

data.title: Potential Divider
notes: **Definition:** two or more resistors in series across a voltage source, used to obtain a fraction of the source voltage.
**Output voltage:** $V_{out} = V_{in} \ rac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, where $R_2$ is the resistor across which the output is taken.
**Why useful:** allows you to set any voltage between 0 and $V_{in}$ by adjusting the ratio of resistances.
**Loading effect:** if a load resistor $R_L$ is connected across $R_2$, the output voltage changes because $R_2$ is now in parallel with $R_L$, reducing the effective resistance.
**Potentiometer:** a continuous potential divider using a uniform resistance wire. The output voltage is proportional to the length of wire between the wiper and one end.
**Voltage divider rule:** for $n$ resistors in series, the voltage across resistor $R_i$ is $V_i = V_{total} \\\\cdot R_i / R_{total}$.
**Unloaded divider:** when no current is drawn from the output, the output voltage is exactly $V_{in} \\\\cdot R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$.

**Loaded divider analysis:** with load $R_L$ across $R_2$, the effective resistance of the lower branch becomes $R_2' = R_2 R_L/(R_2 + R_L)$. The new output is $V_{out} = V_{in} \\\\cdot R_2'/(R_1 + R_2')$.
**Design rule:** to minimize loading effects, choose $R_1, R_2 \\\\ll R_L$ so the divider draws much more current than the load.

**Potentiometer as voltage source:** a potentiometer can provide any fraction of the input voltage from 0 to $V_{in}$. The three terminals are the two ends of the resistive track and the sliding wiper.
**Current through the divider:** even with no load, the divider draws current $I = V_{in}/(R_1 + R_2)$, which causes power dissipation $P = V_{in}^2/(R_1 + R_2)$.
confusion: The output voltage of a potential divider changes when a load is connected. The simple formula $V_{out} = V_{in} \\\\cdot R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$ is only valid for the unloaded case.
A potential divider should not be used as a voltage source for high-current loads because the output voltage drops significantly. Use a voltage regulator or op-amp buffer instead.
The potential divider formula does not depend on the total voltage - only the ratio of resistances matters. Doubling all resistor values keeps the same output voltage but halves the current draw.
When using a potentiometer as a voltage divider, connecting the output to a load reduces the voltage because the load is in parallel with the lower portion of the potentiometer.

The power rating of the resistors in a potential divider matters. If $R_1 = R_2 = 1\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ across 12 V, each dissipates $P = V^2/R = 144/1000 = 0.144$ W. Standard 0.25 W resistors are adequate.

data.title: Resistances in Series and Parallel
notes: **Electrical work:** $W = VIt = I^2Rt = V^2t/R$. Work done by a current is the energy transferred.
**Electrical power:** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Power is the rate of energy transfer.
**Joule heating:** $P = I^2R$ is the power dissipated as heat in a resistor. This is also called $I^2R$ loss.
**Kilowatt-hour:** unit of electrical energy. $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6\\\\,\	ext{J}$. This is what electricity meters measure.
**Efficiency:** useful power output divided by total power input. Transmission lines use high voltage to reduce $I^2R$ losses because $P_{loss} \\\\propto I^2$.

**Power in different elements:** in a resistor, all electrical energy is converted to heat: $P = I^2R$. In a motor, electrical energy converts to mechanical work plus heat: $P_{input} = VI = I^2R + P_{mech}$. In a battery being charged, electrical energy is stored as chemical energy: $P_{input} = \\\\mathcal{E}I + I^2r$.

**Energy conservation in circuits:** the total electrical energy supplied equals the sum of energy dissipated as heat and energy converted to other forms: $V_{source} \\\\cdot I \\\\cdot t = I^2Rt + \	ext{other forms}$.
**Power rating of resistors:** resistors are rated by the maximum power they can dissipate without damage. Common ratings are 0.25 W, 0.5 W, and 1 W. Exceeding this causes overheating and failure.
**Domestic electrical cost:** the cost of running an appliance is $\	ext{Cost} = P(\	ext{kW}) \	imes t(\	ext{h}) \	imes \	ext{rate (per kWh)}$. A 100 W bulb running for 5 hours uses 0.5 kWh.
**Power factor:** for AC circuits, $P = VI\\\\cos\\\\phi$, where $\\\\cos\\\\phi$ is the power factor. For DC circuits, $\\\\cos\\\\phi = 1$, so $P = VI$ always.
**Heat energy in calories:** $H = 0.24 I^2 R t$ calories (mechanical equivalent of heat). In SI units, $H = I^2 R t$ joules.
confusion: Power $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$ are both correct but apply in different contexts. Use $I^2R$ when current is known (series circuits). Use $V^2/R$ when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Using the wrong one gives a wrong answer because $V$ and $I$ are not independent.
Electrical energy is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh), NOT in watts (W). Watt is a unit of power (energy per time). $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 100 W bulb connected to 230 V draws less current than a 60 W bulb (because $I = P/V$, so the 100 W bulb has $I = 0.43$ A vs $I = 0.26$ A for the 60 W bulb). The 100 W bulb actually has LOWER resistance.

In a series circuit, the higher-wattage bulb glows dimmer because it has lower resistance, and in series the same current flows through both: $P = I^2R$, so the higher resistance (60 W bulb) gets more power.
Power dissipated in internal resistance ($I^2r$) is wasted energy. This is why battery-powered devices get warm - the internal resistance converts some chemical energy to heat instead of useful work.

data.title: EMF and Internal Resistance
notes: **EMF ($\\\\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.
**Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.
**Terminal voltage:** $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \\\\mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \\\\mathcal{E}$.
**Cells in series:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}_1 + \\\\mathcal{E}_2 + \\\\ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \\\\ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.
**Cells in parallel:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.
**Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.
**Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \\\\mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.
**Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\\\\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \\\\gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.
**Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.
**Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.
**Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
confusion: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.

Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.
In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.
Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.
A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.

**Heat energy in calories:** $H = 0.24 I^2 R t$ calories (mechanical equivalent of heat). In SI units, $H = I^2 R t$ joules.
confusion: Power $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$ are both correct but apply in different contexts. Use $I^2R$ when current is known (series circuits). Use $V^2/R$ when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Using the wrong one gives a wrong answer because $V$ and $I$ are not independent.
Electrical energy is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh), NOT in watts (W). Watt is a unit of power (energy per time). $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 100 W bulb connected to 230 V draws less current than a 60 W bulb (because $I = P/V$, so the 100 W bulb has $I = 0.43$ A vs $I = 0.26$ A for the 60 W bulb). The 100 W bulb actually has LOWER resistance.

In a series circuit, the higher-wattage bulb glows dimmer because it has lower resistance, and in series the same current flows through both: $P = I^2R$, so the higher resistance (60 W bulb) gets more power.
Power dissipated in internal resistance ($I^2r$) is wasted energy. This is why battery-powered devices get warm - the internal resistance converts some chemical energy to heat instead of useful work.

data.title: Linear Momentum and Impulse
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.

Second law (general): $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$; constant mass: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$
Impulse (constant force): $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$; general: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ (area under $F$–$t$)
Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$
Average force: $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.

data.title: Application of Newton's Laws
notes: **The problem-solving framework (the 'FBD method'):** (1) isolate the body, (2) draw ALL forces acting ON it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied), (3) choose axes (one along acceleration), (4) write ΣF = ma for each axis, (5) solve. Every single NEB numerical follows this pattern.

**Elevator weight paradox:** in an accelerating upward elevator, the normal force N = m(g + a) — you feel heavier. Accelerating downward: N = m(g − a) — you feel lighter. Free fall (a = g): N = 0 (weightlessness). The weight mg never changes; what changes is the apparent weight (the normal force).

**Atwood's machine (two masses on a pulley):** acceleration a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂). The string is massless and inextensible; the pulley is frictionless — if not, extra terms appear.

**Connected bodies (push and pull):** a single force F applied to a system of masses (m₁, m₂, m₃) gives a = F/(m₁ + m₂ + m₃). The contact force between m₁ and m₂ is the force needed to accelerate the trailing masses: N = (m₂ + m₃) × a.

**Inclined plane:** weight components: mg sin θ down the slope, mg cos θ into the plane. Normal N = mg cos θ. With friction: net force down slope = mg sin θ − μmg cos θ. The body slides when sin θ > μ cos θ, i.e., tan θ > μ — the critical angle depends only on μ, NOT on mass.
**Worked example:** a 5 kg block on a 30° rough slope (μ = 0.3) — does it slide? tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.3 → yes. Acceleration: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.26) = 2.35 m/s² down the slope.

**Apparent weight in fluids:** an object submerged in a liquid appears lighter by the buoyant force (Archimedes): apparent weight = mg − ρVg. This is still a Newton's second law application: ΣF = mg − ρVg = ma.

**NEB exam focus:** elevator problems, Atwood's machine, connected bodies on horizontal surfaces, inclined plane with/without friction, apparent weight in accelerating systems — all use the same FBD → ΣF = ma framework.
formulas: Newton's second law (vector): ΣF = ma → ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y
Elevator apparent weight: N = m(g ± a) where + is upward acceleration, − is downward
Atwood's machine: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)
Smooth inclined plane: a = g sin θ down the slope; N = mg cos θ
Rough inclined plane: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); slides when tan θ > μ
confusion: ❌ 'The normal force is always mg.' ✅ N = mg only on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration. On a slope N = mg cos θ; in an accelerating elevator N = m(g ± a).

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
❌ 'The tension in a string equals the weight of the hanging mass.' ✅ Only if the system is in equilibrium. In an accelerating Atwood's machine, T ≠ mg — use ΣF = ma on each mass to find T.
❌ 'Action and reaction forces cancel each other.' ✅ They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel in a single FBD. Include only forces acting ON the body you are analyzing.
❌ 'Heavier bodies slide slower down a slope.' ✅ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) has no mass term — all bodies slide at the same rate (if μ is the same), just like free fall.
❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

Smooth inclined plane: a = g sin θ down the slope; N = mg cos θ
Rough inclined plane: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); slides when tan θ > μ

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
❌ 'The tension in a string equals the weight of the hanging mass.' ✅ Only if the system is in equilibrium. In an accelerating Atwood's machine, T ≠ mg — use ΣF = ma on each mass to find T.
❌ 'Action and reaction forces cancel each other.' ✅ They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel in a single FBD. Include only forces acting ON the body you are analyzing.
❌ 'Heavier bodies slide slower down a slope.' ✅ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) has no mass term — all bodies slide at the same rate (if μ is the same), just like free fall.
❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

data.title: Moment, Torque and Equilibrium
notes: **Torque (moment of a force):** τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application, F is the force, and θ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is Nm. Torque is positive for anticlockwise rotation, negative for clockwise.

**Equilibrium of a rigid body:** two conditions must BOTH hold: (1) translational equilibrium: ΣF = 0 (no net force → no linear acceleration); (2) rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0 (no net torque → no angular acceleration). A body at rest or rotating at constant angular velocity satisfies both.

**Couple:** two equal and opposite forces separated by a distance d produce a pure torque (independent of pivot): τ = F × d. The net force is zero, so there is no linear acceleration — only rotation. The turning effect is the same about ANY point.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the single point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For regular uniform bodies, the CG is at the geometric centre. For irregular bodies, it can be found by balancing or suspension.

**Worked example — seesaw:** a 40 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum. Where must a 50 kg child sit to balance? Torque balance: 40×9.8×2 = 50×9.8×x → x = 1.6 m. The heavier child sits closer to the fulcrum.

**Worked example — ladder:** a uniform ladder of length L leans against a smooth wall at angle θ. The wall reaction is horizontal (smooth), the ground reaction has both normal and friction components. Torque about the base eliminates the unknown ground reaction: N_wall × L sin θ = mg × (L/2) cos θ.

**Equilibrium in the NEB exam:** the standard problem is a beam/ladder/plank with multiple forces — apply ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0 (choosing the pivot wisely to eliminate unknowns). Three equations for up to three unknowns.

**Practical examples:** opening a door (push at the handle, not near the hinge — larger r gives more τ), using a spanner (longer handle = more torque for the same force), a wheelbarrow (load CG near the wheel reduces the lifting torque).
formulas: Torque of a force: τ = rF sin θ (positive = anticlockwise, negative = clockwise)
Equilibrium conditions: ΣF = 0 (translational) AND Στ = 0 (rotational)
Couple torque: τ = F × d (independent of pivot position)
Centre of gravity: x_CG = Σ(mᵢxᵢ)/Σmᵢ (weighted average of positions)
Principle of moments: for equilibrium, sum of clockwise torques = sum of anticlockwise torques
confusion: ❌ 'Torque and moment are different.' ✅ In physics problems, they are the same quantity: τ = rF sin θ. Engineers sometimes distinguish 'moment' (bending) from 'torque' (twisting), but here they are interchangeable.
❌ 'A body with zero net force is in equilibrium.' ✅ It must ALSO have zero net torque. A couple (equal and opposite forces) produces zero net force but a non-zero torque — the body rotates.
❌ 'The torque depends on the pivot chosen.' ✅ The torque of a single force depends on the pivot, but the NET torque in equilibrium is zero about ANY pivot. Choose the pivot to eliminate unknowns.
❌ 'Heavier bodies always produce more torque.' ✅ Torque depends on BOTH force and distance. A small force far from the pivot can produce more torque than a large force close to it.
❌ 'The centre of gravity is always inside the body.' ✅ For a ring, the CG is at the centre (in empty space). For an L-shaped body, it lies outside the material.
❌ 'A ladder leaning against a wall is safe if ΣF = 0.' ✅ You also need Στ = 0 AND friction at the ground to be ≤ μN. The ladder slips when the required friction exceeds μN_ground.

data.title: Solid Friction — Laws and Verification
notes: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

**Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

**Angle of friction (λ):** the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant reaction (normal + friction) when slipping is about to occur. tan λ = μ_s. The resultant reaction makes angle λ with the normal.

**Angle of repose (θ_r):** the steepest angle of a slope at which a body just remains at rest. At this angle, mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r → tan θ_r = μ_s. So θ_r = λ — the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

**Worked example — body on a slope:** a 10 kg block on a 25° slope (μ_s = 0.5). Does it slide? tan 25° = 0.466 < 0.5 → no, it stays. Static friction = mg sin 25° = 41.5 N (less than μ_sN = 0.5 × 92.4 = 46.2 N).

**Worked example — pulling a block:** a 5 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3). Pulled by a 20 N force at 30° above horizontal. Normal N = mg − F sin 30° = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Friction = 0.3 × 39 = 11.7 N. Net force = 20 cos 30° − 11.7 = 5.6 N. a = 5.6/5 = 1.12 m/s².

**NEB exam focus:** distinguish static vs kinetic friction; solve slope problems (does it slide? find acceleration); angle of repose and its equality with angle of friction; pulling/pushing at an angle (changes the normal, hence friction).
formulas: Maximum static friction: f_s(max) = μ_sN (acts just before slipping)
Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_kN (acts during sliding; μ_k < μ_s)
Slope sliding condition: body slides when tan θ > μ_s; a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ)
Angle of friction: tan λ = μ_s (angle between normal and resultant reaction)
Angle of repose: tan θ_r = μ_s → θ_r = λ (steepest angle for rest)
confusion: ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

❌ 'Friction depends on the area of contact.' ✅ For a given normal force, friction is (approximately) independent of area. A wide tyre and a narrow tyre with the same load have the same maximum friction (in the simple model).
❌ 'Static friction is always μ_sN.' ✅ Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN. Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.
❌ 'μ_k > μ_s because sliding is faster.' ✅ μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding. This is why a heavy box jerks when you first push it.
❌ 'The angle of repose depends on the mass of the body.' ✅ tan θ_r = μ_s — mass cancels out. All bodies with the same μ_s have the same angle of repose.

❌ 'Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction because the force is smaller.' ✅ Pulling upward reduces the normal (N = mg − F sin θ), which reduces friction. Pushing downward increases the normal and friction.

data.title: Hooke's Law and Force Constant
notes: **Hooke's law statement:** For small deformations, the extension (or compression) of an elastic body is directly proportional to the applied force: F = kx, where F is the applied force, x is the deformation, and k is the spring (force) constant. This linear region is called the elastic limit.

**Force (spring) constant k:** k = F/x, measured in N/m. It measures the stiffness of the spring — a stiffer spring has a larger k and needs a bigger force for the same extension. k depends on the material, the wire diameter, the number of coils and the length of the spring.

**What Spring constant really means:** a spring of k = 200 N/m requires 200 N to stretch it by 1 metre. To stretch by any x, you need F = 200x N. It is the slope of the F–x graph in the linear (Hookean) region.

**Two ways to combine springs:** series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ (softer than either); parallel: k = k₁ + k₂ (stiffer than either). Series springs stretch more for the same load — think of a long telephone-cord spring vs two short springs joined.
**Worked example:** a force of 40 N stretches a spring by 8 cm. k = F/x = 40/0.08 = 500 N/m. A 100 N force will then stretch it by x = 100/500 = 0.2 m = 20 cm.

**Hooke's law on a graph:** the F–x graph is a straight line through the origin while the elastic limit is respected. Beyond it, the graph curves; after plastic deformation, a larger force is needed for the same extension or the body does not return to its original length.

**Application — weight balance (spring balance):** the extension of a calibrated spring measures the applied weight. Since F = kx and weight = mg, the scale can be marked directly in newtons or kilograms.

**Conditions for Hooke's law to hold:** the deformation must be small, elastic (the body returns to original shape when the load is removed), and within the proportional limit. Overstretching a spring permanently changes its k.
formulas: Hooke's law: F = kx
Spring constant: k = F/x (units N/m)
Series springs: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
Parallel springs: k = k₁ + k₂
Elastic potential energy: U = ½kx²; oscillation ω = √(k/m)
confusion: ❌ 'F = kx means force depends on extension.' ✅ Precisely that — for a spring, doubling the extension doubles the stretching force needed. The spring PULLS back with force kx (restoring force) opposite to the applied load.

❌ 'k is a property only of the material.' ✅ k depends on the geometry too (length, coil radius, number of coils, wire thickness). It is the material property (Young's modulus) together with geometry that fixes k.
❌ 'A stiffer spring stretches more.' ✅ A stiffer spring stretches LESS for the same force — it has a larger k, so x = F/k is smaller.
❌ 'Extension is proportional to force at all loads.' ✅ Only within the elastic (proportional) limit. Beyond it the graph bends, and past the yield point the spring deforms permanently.
❌ 'Series springs are stiffer.' ✅ Series springs are SOFTER (smaller total k). Two identical springs in series have k/2; in parallel they have 2k.
❌ 'Force constant and friction constant (μ) are the same.' ✅ k (N/m) relates force to displacement of a spring; μ is a dimensionless friction coefficient relating friction to normal reaction.

data.title: Stress, Strain, Elasticity and Plasticity
notes: **Stress (σ):** the internal resisting force per unit area set up in a body when external forces are applied: σ = F/A. Empirical units are N/m² or Pa (pascal). Normal stress = force perpendicular to the area (tension/compression); shear stress = force parallel to the area.

**Strain (ε):** the fractional deformation produced: strain = change in dimension / original dimension. It is dimensionless. Linear strain = Δl/l, shear strain = θ (angle of shear), volumetric strain = ΔV/V.

**Elasticity and plasticity:** elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the property of remaining permanently deformed after the deforming force is removed. Bodies are elastic below the elastic limit and plastic beyond it.

**Hooke's law in stress-strain form:** within the elastic limit, stress ∝ strain: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus (N/m²). This is the generalised Hooke's law — stress and strain are proportional until the elastic limit.

**Stress-strain curve regions:** (1) linear (proportional) region up to the proportional limit; (2) elastic region up to the elastic limit (still recovers fully); (3) yielding at the yield point (permanent deformation begins); (4) plastic deformation region where the material flows; (5) ultimate tensile strength (maximum stress), then (6) fracture/breaking point.

**Worked example — a wire under tension:** a steel wire of length 2 m and cross-section 1 mm² (10⁻⁶ m²) carries a 20 kg load. F = 196 N, σ = 196/10⁻⁶ = 1.96 × 10⁸ Pa. If E_steel = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, strain ε = σ/E = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, so extension Δl = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 1.96 mm.

**Types of stress & strain (NEB focus):** tensile/compressive (longitudinal), shear (tangential), and volume (hydrostatic). Each has its own modulus: Young's modulus E = σ_t/ε_l, shear modulus G = τ/θ, bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V).

**Ductile vs brittle materials:** ductile (copper, mild steel) show a long plastic region — they deform before breaking and are used for wires. Brittle (glass, cast iron) show little or no plastic region — they break suddenly near the elastic limit, which is why glass shatters.
formulas: Stress: σ = F/A (N/m² or Pa)
Strain: ε = Δl/l (dimensionless; ε_V = ΔV/V, shear ε = θ)
Hooke's law in stress–strain form: σ = Eε
Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)
Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear modulus: G = τ/θ
confusion: ❌ 'Stress and pressure are the same.' ✅ Both have units N/m², but stress is the INTERNAL resisting force per unit area produced in a body, while pressure is an EXTERNAL force per unit area applied by a fluid.
❌ 'Strain has units.' ✅ Strain is dimensionless — it is a ratio of lengths (or volumes/angles). This is essential for dimensional analysis.
❌ 'Elasticity means materials are always elastic.' ✅ Every material is elastic only up to its elastic limit; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.
❌ 'Stress equals force.' ✅ Stress is force PER unit area (σ = F/A). Doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.
❌ 'The stress–strain graph is a straight line everywhere.' ✅ Only up to the proportional limit. After that it curves at the yield point and beyond.
❌ 'A ductile material breaks near the elastic limit.' ✅ DUCTILE materials deform plastically and stretch before fracturing; brittle materials break with little warning near the elastic limit.
