**Stress-strain curve regions:** (1) linear (proportional) region up to the proportional limit; (2) elastic region up to the elastic limit (still recovers fully); (3) yielding at the yield point (permanent deformation begins); (4) plastic deformation region where the material flows; (5) ultimate tensile strength (maximum stress), then (6) fracture/breaking point.

**Worked example — a wire under tension:** a steel wire of length 2 m and cross-section 1 mm² (10⁻⁶ m²) carries a 20 kg load. F = 196 N, σ = 196/10⁻⁶ = 1.96 × 10⁸ Pa. If E_steel = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, strain ε = σ/E = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, so extension Δl = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 1.96 mm.

**Types of stress & strain (NEB focus):** tensile/compressive (longitudinal), shear (tangential), and volume (hydrostatic). Each has its own modulus: Young's modulus E = σ_t/ε_l, shear modulus G = τ/θ, bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V).

**Ductile vs brittle materials:** ductile (copper, mild steel) show a long plastic region — they deform before breaking and are used for wires. Brittle (glass, cast iron) show little or no plastic region — they break suddenly near the elastic limit, which is why glass shatters.

Strain: ε = Δl/l (dimensionless; ε_V = ΔV/V, shear ε = θ)
Hooke's law in stress–strain form: σ = Eε
Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)
Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear modulus: G = τ/θ
confusion: ❌ 'Stress and pressure are the same.' ✅ Both have units N/m², but stress is the INTERNAL resisting force per unit area produced in a body, while pressure is an EXTERNAL force per unit area applied by a fluid.
❌ 'Strain has units.' ✅ Strain is dimensionless — it is a ratio of lengths (or volumes/angles). This is essential for dimensional analysis.
❌ 'Elasticity means materials are always elastic.' ✅ Every material is elastic only up to its elastic limit; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.
❌ 'Stress equals force.' ✅ Stress is force PER unit area (σ = F/A). Doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.
❌ 'The stress–strain graph is a straight line everywhere.' ✅ Only up to the proportional limit. After that it curves at the yield point and beyond.
❌ 'A ductile material breaks near the elastic limit.' ✅ DUCTILE materials deform plastically and stretch before fracturing; brittle materials break with little warning near the elastic limit.

data.title: Elastic Moduli — Young, Bulk, Shear
notes: **Young's modulus (E):** the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl). It measures resistance to stretching/compression. For steel, E ≈ 2×10¹¹ N/m²; for aluminium ≈ 7×10¹⁰ N/m²; for rubber ≈ 5×10⁶ N/m².

**Bulk modulus (B):** the ratio of volume stress (pressure) to volume strain: B = −P/(ΔV/V). It measures resistance to uniform compression. The minus sign keeps B positive (ΔV is negative under pressure). For water B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa; steel B ≈ 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.

**Shear modulus / modulus of rigidity (G or η):** the ratio of shear stress to shear strain: G = τ/θ = (F/A)/θ. It measures resistance to change of shape without change of volume. For steel G ≈ 8×10¹⁰ N/m².

**Key relation between moduli (for isotropic materials):** E = 2G(1 + σ) and E = 3B(1 − 2σ), where σ is Poisson's ratio. Combining them: 9/B = 3/G + 1/E or E = 9BG/(3B + G). These links let you compute one modulus from the others.

**Worked example — Young's modulus:** a wire of length 2 m and area 1 mm² extends 1 mm under a 50 kg load. F = 490 N, σ = 490/10⁻⁶ = 4.9×10⁸ Pa, ε = 10⁻³/2 = 5×10⁻⁴, E = 4.9×10⁸/5×10⁻⁴ = 9.8×10¹¹ ≈ 10¹¹ N/m².
**Worked example — bulk modulus:** 10⁵ Pa pressure on 1 m³ of water changes its volume by 4.5×10⁻⁵ m³. B = 10⁵/(4.5×10⁻⁵) = 2.2×10⁹ Pa.
**Compressibility:** the reciprocal of bulk modulus: k = 1/B. Fluids with high B are hard to compress; gases have very low B.
**Which modulus to use?** stretching a wire → Young's modulus; squeezing a sphere → bulk modulus; twisting/sliding layers → shear modulus. Choose by the type of deformation.

Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V)
Shear modulus: G = (F/A)/θ = τ/θ

❌ 'Bulk modulus applies only to liquids.' ✅ It applies to solids and gases too — any material under uniform pressure.
❌ 'Shear strain is a length ratio.' ✅ Shear strain is the ANGLE of displacement θ (radians), not a length ratio.
❌ 'Young's modulus and stiffness k are the same.' ✅ Y and k connect through geometry: E = Fl/(AΔl) while k = F/Δl, so E = kL/A.

data.title: Poisson's Ratio
notes: **Poisson's ratio (σ):** when a body is stretched (or compressed), it becomes thinner (or thicker) in the perpendicular directions. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) = −(β/α). The minus sign keeps σ positive because lateral strain is opposite in sign to longitudinal strain.
**Why it is dimensionless:** Poisson's ratio divides one strain by another — strain is dimensionless, so σ has no units and no dimensions. Its value for most materials lies between 0 and 0.5.

**Typical values:** cork ≈ 0 (no lateral change), concrete ≈ 0.1–0.2, steel ≈ 0.25–0.3, copper ≈ 0.33, aluminium ≈ 0.34, rubber ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible). A hypothetical material with σ = 0.5 would conserve volume exactly.

**Worked example — wire stretch:** a wire of length 2 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by 2 mm. Longitudinal strain = 2×10⁻³/2 = 10⁻³. If σ = 0.3, lateral strain = −0.3×10⁻³, so diameter change = 0.3×10⁻³ × 1 mm = 3×10⁻⁴ mm = 0.3 μm (a fractional diameter change of 3×10⁻⁴).

**Relation with the moduli:** σ links Young's modulus E, bulk modulus B and shear modulus G: E = 2G(1 + σ) and E = 3B(1 − 2σ). From these: 1/σ can be used to check material consistency, and σ = (3B − E)/(6B).
**Connection to volume change:** the fractional volume change under uniaxial stretch is ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ). For a perfectly incompressible material (σ = 0.5), ΔV/V = 0 — the volume is unchanged.

**Limits on σ:** the thermodynamic bound is −1 < σ < 0.5. Nearly all common materials have 0 < σ < 0.5. Materials with negative Poisson's ratio (auxetics) actually thicken when stretched — rare and exotic.

**Applications:** σ matters in designing cables, stretching films, and geological materials; cork (σ≈0) is chosen for bottle stoppers because it doesn't change width when squeezed, so it seals without expanding.
formulas: Poisson's ratio: σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain)
Relation with moduli: E = 2G(1 + σ); E = 3B(1 − 2σ)
σ from E and B: σ = (3B − E)/(6B)
σ from E and G: σ = E/(2G) − 1
Fractional volume change: ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ)
confusion: ❌ 'Poisson's ratio has units of strain.' ✅ It is a RATIO of two strains — dimensionless.
❌ 'Poisson's ratio can be greater than 1.' ✅ No — the thermodynamic limit is 0.5 for isotropic materials (a few exotic anisotropic materials exceed 0.5 but never 1).
❌ 'Lateral strain equals longitudinal strain.' ✅ Lateral strain = −σ × longitudinal strain, with σ typically between 0 and 0.5.
❌ 'When stretched, volume always increases.' ✅ If σ = 0.5 the volume is constant; for σ < 0.5 the volume increases slightly (ΔV/V = ε(1−2σ)).
❌ 'Cork and rubber have similar σ.' ✅ Cork ≈ 0, rubber ≈ 0.5 — at opposite ends of the range.
❌ 'Poisson's ratio is a force.' ✅ It is a pure, dimensionless ratio of deformation (strain) — not a force or modulus.

data.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = Gm₁m₂/r².

**The universal constant G:** G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.
**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is F₁₂ = −G(m₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: F_net = Σ Fᵢ. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.
**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** m_Earth = 6×10²⁴ kg, m_Moon = 7.4×10²² kg, r = 3.84×10⁸ m. F = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 6×10²⁴ × 7.4×10²² / (3.84×10⁸)² = 2.0×10²⁰ N — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.
**Gravitational field strength:** g = F/m = GM/r², the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface g = 9.8 m/s², which gives Earth's mass: M = gR²/G ≈ 5.97×10²⁴ kg.
**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force (GMm/r² = mv²/r) gives orbital velocity v = √(GM/r) and period T = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is ~10⁻³⁶ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.
formulas: Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r²
Gravitational field strength: g = GM/r²
Orbital velocity: v = √(GM/r)
Orbital period: T = 2π√(r³/GM)
g at height h: g' = g(R/(R+h))²
confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.
❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.
❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects (F = mg), but their acceleration is the same: a = F/m = g, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

data.title: Gravitational Field Strength
notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: V = −GM/r. At infinity V = 0, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: U = −GMm/r. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply GMm/r of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has U = −GMm/r — its total mechanical energy is E = K + U = −GMm/2r, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, U = mgh. This is the constant-g approximation of −GMm/r: since Δ(1/r) ≈ −h/R², the change matches mgh. Use mgh only for h ≪ R; use −GMm/r for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply GMm/R. Numerically for m = 1 kg: (6.67×10⁻¹¹)(5.97×10²⁴)/6.37×10⁶ ≈ 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 62.5 MJ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field g = −dV/dr (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy U = mV. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: g = −dV/dr radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.
**Superposition:** for multiple masses, V = Σ(−GMᵢ/rᵢ) and U = Σ(−GMᵢm/rᵢ) — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
formulas: Gravitational potential: V = −GM/r (J/kg)
Gravitational potential energy: U = mV = −GMm/r (J)
Near the surface: U = mgh (h ≪ R)
Field from potential: g = −dV/dr
Total orbital energy: E = −GMm/2r = U/2
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy U = mV (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ 'U = mgh and U = −GMm/r disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: mgh is the CHANGE in −GMm/r near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface (−GM/R) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ U = −GMm/r — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes −GMm/2r (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but U ≈ 0). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

data.title: Variation in g due to Altitude and Depth
notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, g' = GM/(R+h)² = g(R/(R+h))². As h increases, g decreases. For small h (h ≪ R), a binomial expansion gives g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius (R−d) contributes: g' = g(1 − d/R) — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre (d = R), g' = 0.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance (1/r² law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as (R−d)³ while distance scales as (R−d) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at h = R (one Earth radius up), g' = g(R/2R)² = g/4 = 2.45 m/s². At h = 100 km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is 2h/R = 2×100/6400 = 0.031, so g' ≈ 9.5 m/s².
**Worked example — depth:** at d = R/2 (3200 km deep), g' = g(1 − 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 m/s². At d = R (centre) → g' = 0 (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** g vs r rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as 1/r² beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by ω²R cos²λ (λ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles (≈9.832) than the equator (≈9.78); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.
**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective r = R + h: v = √(GM/(R+h)) and the orbital g is g' = GM/(R+h)² — the same g formula used at that radius.
formulas: g at altitude h: g' = g(R/(R+h))²
Small-h approximation: g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R)
g at depth d: g' = g(1 − d/R)
g at latitude λ due to rotation: g' = g − ω²R cos²λ
g inside a uniform sphere: g' = g·r/R (r ≤ R)
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as 1/(R+h)²; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by h/R.' ✅ The small-h approximation is 2h/R (from the square), not h/R. At h = 100 km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: g' = g(1 − d/R), zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At h = R, g' = g/4 — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

data.title: Centre of Mass and Centre of Gravity
notes: **Centre of mass (COM):** the point where the entire mass of a body (or system) may be considered to be concentrated for translational (linear) motion analysis. Position: R_cm = (Σ mᵢrᵢ)/(Σ mᵢ). For continuous bodies: R_cm = (∫r dm)/M.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. In a uniform gravitational field, the CG coincides exactly with the COM. If the field is non-uniform (very large bodies, varying g), the CG may shift slightly relative to the COM.

**Why CG equals COM in uniform g:** weight W = mg at each point, and since g is the same everywhere, the torque balance condition that defines the CG reduces to the same weighted average that defines the COM. The two centres coincide.
**Solved example — two masses:** masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 8 kg at x = 3 m. COM: x_cm = (2×0 + 8×3)/(2+8) = 24/10 = 2.4 m. The COM is closer to the heavier mass.

**Properties:** (1) The COM of a uniform, symmetric body lies at its geometric centre. (2) The COM of two bodies lies on the line joining them. (3) For irregular bodies the COM can lie OUTSIDE the material (e.g., a ring, a boomerang, a bent L-shape). (4) The total linear momentum of a system equals M·V_cm — external forces alone can change V_cm.

**Finding CG experimentally (NEB practical):** suspend the body from two different points; the two vertical lines through the suspension points intersect at the centre of gravity. Plumb lines are used — the intersection of the two suspension lines locates the CG.

**Applications:** designing stable structures (ships, cars, tables) keeps the CG low and inside the base; balancing acts use alignment of the CG above the support; in projectiles, the COM follows a smooth parabola even if the object rotates; spacecraft alignment uses the COM.
formulas: Centre of mass (discrete): R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ / Σmᵢ
Centre of mass (continuous): R_cm = ∫r dm / ∫ dm
Two masses: x_cm = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂)
Velocity of COM: V_cm = Σmᵢvᵢ / M
Acceleration of COM: a_cm = Σmᵢaᵢ / M = F_ext / M
confusion: ❌ 'COM and CG are always at the material centre.' ✅ Only for uniform, symmetric bodies. A ring's COM is at its empty centre; an L-shaped body has its COM outside its material.
❌ 'COM and CG are always the same point.' ✅ They coincide in a UNIFORM gravitational field. For very large objects in a non-uniform field, they differ slightly.
❌ 'COM is a force point.' ✅ COM is a mass-weighted average position — a geometric point for translational dynamics, not a force.
❌ 'To find the COM, only the largest mass matters.' ✅ All masses contribute proportionally: R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/Σmᵢ.
❌ 'The COM moves when the body spins.' ✅ The COM of an isolated system moves uniformly (or stays still); spinning happens about the COM.
❌ 'The CG of an object must lie within the object.' ✅ It can lie outside the material — ring, hollow sphere, L-shape, boomerang.

data.title: Motion of a Satellite — Orbital Velocity and Time Period
notes: **Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** K = ½mv₀² = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r. Notice K = −U/2 and E = U/2 — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).
**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m ≈ 35,800 km above the equator with v₀ ≈ 3.08 km/s.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by Δv = v₂ − v₁. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
formulas: Orbital velocity: v₀ = √(GM/r)
Near-surface orbital speed: v₀ = √(gR)
Time period: T = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM)
Kinetic energy: K = GMm/2r
Total energy: E = −GMm/2r (E = U/2, K = −U/2)
confusion: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.
❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).
❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: v₀ = √(GM/r).
❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed (v₀ = √(GM/r)) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.
❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ T ∝ r^{3/2} — the period grows faster than the radius.

❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ KE = GMm/2r DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy (+GmM·Δ(1/r)) making the total E = −GMm/2r less negative.

data.title: Geostationary Satellite
notes: **Geostationary satellite:** a satellite that appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's equator. It must satisfy three conditions: (1) orbit in the plane of the equator (equatorial plane), (2) orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west → east), and (3) have a period exactly equal to Earth's rotation period (T = 24 hours).
**Height above Earth:** using T = 2π√(r³/GM) with T = 86400 s → r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m from the centre → altitude h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km above the surface. This is about 5.6 Earth radii.
**Orbital speed:** v₀ = 2πr/T = 2π×4.22×10⁷/86400 ≈ 3.07 km/s. It matches Earth's angular speed: the satellite and the point below rotate together, so the satellite hangs over the same longitude.

**Only the equator works:** a satellite over the equator is the only way the orbit plane can contain both the satellite and Earth's rotation axis while keeping the satellite fixed over one point. An inclined orbit would carry the satellite north and south each day.
**Why 24 h is exact:** for T = T_Earth, the angular speeds match: ω_sat = ω_Earth. From r³ = GMT²/4π² the altitude is fixed (~35,800 km) — there is a unique geostationary height.

**Applications:** communications satellites (broadcast, TV, internet), weather satellites (HIMAWARI, INSAT type), and some navigation augmentation systems. Their fixed position means ground dishes never need to move.

**Geostationary vs geosynchronous:** a geosynchronous satellite has a 24-h period but may have an inclined or elliptical orbit, so it drifts north/south in the sky. A geostationary satellite is a special geosynchronous satellite confined to the equatorial plane at fixed longitude.

**Energy at geostationary orbit:** for m = 1000 kg, U = −GMm/r ≈ −9.4×10⁹ J, E_total = −GMm/2r ≈ −4.7×10⁹ J. Launching to this height needs a large boost — the standard launch uses a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) followed by an apogee burn.
formulas: Geostationary radius: r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m
Altitude: h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km
Orbital speed: v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.07 km/s
Angular speed: ω = 2π/T_Earth ≈ 7.27×10⁻⁵ rad/s
Energy: U = −GMm/r; E_total = −GMm/2r
confusion: ❌ 'Any 24-hour satellite is geostationary.' ✅ A geostationary satellite must ALSO be equatorial, circular, and west-to-east. A geosynchronous one just matches the 24-h period.
❌ 'Geostationary orbit can be at any height above the equator.' ✅ There is exactly ONE geostationary altitude: ≈ 35,800 km. It is set by Earth's rotation period.
❌ 'A geostationary satellite stays above one spot because it has no gravity.' ✅ It stays because its orbital period exactly equals Earth's rotation; gravity still holds it in orbit at v ≈ 3.07 km/s.
❌ 'The satellite is stationary in space.' ✅ It moves at 3.07 km/s; it is stationary only relative to the rotating Earth.
❌ 'At high latitudes people see it overhead.' ✅ A geostationary satellite is always over the equator — at high latitudes it appears low on the horizon, and near the poles it is not visible at all.
❌ 'The Moon is a geostationary satellite.' ✅ The Moon has a 27.3-day period and an inclined orbit — it is not geostationary.

data.title: Potential and Kinetic Energy of the Satellite
notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: V = −GM/r. At infinity V = 0, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: U = −GMm/r. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply GMm/r of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has U = −GMm/r — its total mechanical energy is E = K + U = −GMm/2r, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, U = mgh. This is the constant-g approximation of −GMm/r: since Δ(1/r) ≈ −h/R², the change matches mgh. Use mgh only for h ≪ R; use −GMm/r for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply GMm/R. Numerically for m = 1 kg: (6.67×10⁻¹¹)(5.97×10²⁴)/6.37×10⁶ ≈ 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 62.5 MJ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field g = −dV/dr (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy U = mV. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: g = −dV/dr radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.
**Superposition:** for multiple masses, V = Σ(−GMᵢ/rᵢ) and U = Σ(−GMᵢm/rᵢ) — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
formulas: Gravitational potential: V = −GM/r (J/kg)
Gravitational potential energy: U = mV = −GMm/r (J)
Near the surface: U = mgh (h ≪ R)
Field from potential: g = −dV/dr
Total orbital energy: E = −GMm/2r = U/2
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy U = mV (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ 'U = mgh and U = −GMm/r disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: mgh is the CHANGE in −GMm/r near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface (−GM/R) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ U = −GMm/r — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes −GMm/2r (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but U ≈ 0). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

data.title: Geostationary Satellite
notes: **Geostationary satellite:** a satellite that appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's equator. It must satisfy three conditions: (1) orbit in the plane of the equator (equatorial plane), (2) orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west → east), and (3) have a period exactly equal to Earth's rotation period (T = 24 hours).
**Height above Earth:** using T = 2π√(r³/GM) with T = 86400 s → r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m from the centre → altitude h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km above the surface. This is about 5.6 Earth radii.
**Orbital speed:** v₀ = 2πr/T = 2π×4.22×10⁷/86400 ≈ 3.07 km/s. It matches Earth's angular speed: the satellite and the point below rotate together, so the satellite hangs over the same longitude.

**Only the equator works:** a satellite over the equator is the only way the orbit plane can contain both the satellite and Earth's rotation axis while keeping the satellite fixed over one point. An inclined orbit would carry the satellite north and south each day.
**Why 24 h is exact:** for T = T_Earth, the angular speeds match: ω_sat = ω_Earth. From r³ = GMT²/4π² the altitude is fixed (~35,800 km) — there is a unique geostationary height.

**Applications:** communications satellites (broadcast, TV, internet), weather satellites (HIMAWARI, INSAT type), and some navigation augmentation systems. Their fixed position means ground dishes never need to move.

**Geostationary vs geosynchronous:** a geosynchronous satellite has a 24-h period but may have an inclined or elliptical orbit, so it drifts north/south in the sky. A geostationary satellite is a special geosynchronous satellite confined to the equatorial plane at fixed longitude.

**Energy at geostationary orbit:** for m = 1000 kg, U = −GMm/r ≈ −9.4×10⁹ J, E_total = −GMm/2r ≈ −4.7×10⁹ J. Launching to this height needs a large boost — the standard launch uses a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) followed by an apogee burn.
formulas: Geostationary radius: r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m
Altitude: h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km
Orbital speed: v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.07 km/s
Angular speed: ω = 2π/T_Earth ≈ 7.27×10⁻⁵ rad/s
Energy: U = −GMm/r; E_total = −GMm/2r
confusion: ❌ 'Any 24-hour satellite is geostationary.' ✅ A geostationary satellite must ALSO be equatorial, circular, and west-to-east. A geosynchronous one just matches the 24-h period.
❌ 'Geostationary orbit can be at any height above the equator.' ✅ There is exactly ONE geostationary altitude: ≈ 35,800 km. It is set by Earth's rotation period.
❌ 'A geostationary satellite stays above one spot because it has no gravity.' ✅ It stays because its orbital period exactly equals Earth's rotation; gravity still holds it in orbit at v ≈ 3.07 km/s.
❌ 'The satellite is stationary in space.' ✅ It moves at 3.07 km/s; it is stationary only relative to the rotating Earth.
❌ 'At high latitudes people see it overhead.' ✅ A geostationary satellite is always over the equator — at high latitudes it appears low on the horizon, and near the poles it is not visible at all.
❌ 'The Moon is a geostationary satellite.' ✅ The Moon has a 27.3-day period and an inclined orbit — it is not geostationary.

data.title: GPS
notes: **What GPS is:** the Global Positioning System is a satellite-based navigation system that tells a receiver its exact 3D position on Earth. It uses the same gravitational/orbital physics as any satellite, which is why it lives in the gravitation chapter.

**Principle of position fixing:** each GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal stamped with its position and precise transmission time. The receiver measures the travel time of signals from at least four satellites and solves for (x, y, z, t) — the fourth equation corrects the receiver clock offset.

**How distance is measured:** distance = speed of light × time delay. Since the receiver's clock is not atomic-precise, a fourth satellite provides the clock-error term, giving accuracy of a few metres.

**Satellite constellation:** 24+ satellites orbit at ≈ 20,200 km altitude (medium Earth orbit) in six planes inclined 55° to the equator. Each satellite has a period of ≈ 11 h 58 min (half a sidereal day) and speed ≈ 3.87 km/s — from T = 2π√(r³/GM).

**Why the orbits are chosen:** six planes × four satellites each guarantee that at least 4–6 satellites are above the horizon at any place and time. The 55° inclination covers up to the poles, unlike a geostationary belt.

**Relativity in GPS:** satellite clocks run faster than ground clocks by ~38 µs/day (7 µs from special relativity + 45 µs from general relativity). This systematic shift must be compensated, otherwise GPS positions would drift by ~10 km per day — a practical proof of relativity.

**Accuracy and sources of error:** ionospheric delays, multipath reflections, satellite clocks, and geometry (DOP). With corrections (differential GPS / WAAS / dual-frequency) accuracy reaches centimetre level for surveying.

**Applications:** navigation (cars, ships, aircraft), mapping, timing synchronisation for power grids and financial networks, agriculture, disaster relief, and scientific studies (tectonic plate motion). GPS is a direct practical payoff of satellite motion physics.
formulas: Distance from delay: d = c × Δt
GPS speed: v = √(GM/r) (r ≈ 26,600 km)
GPS period: T = 2π√(r³/GM) ≈ 12 h sidereal
Clock error mapping: Δposition = c × Δt_clock
Relativistic shift: Δt ≈ 38 µs/day (GR +45 µs, SR −7 µs)
confusion: ❌ 'GPS signal carries your position from the satellite.' ✅ The satellite only sends its OWN position + time. YOUR receiver computes your position by triangulating delays.
❌ 'Three satellites suffice for full 3D positioning.' ✅ Three give (x,y,z) only if the clock is perfect; a fourth is required for a practical unknown clock offset.
❌ 'GPS works by measuring signal strength.' ✅ It measures signal TRAVEL TIME (c × Δt), not strength.
❌ 'GPS satellites are geostationary.' ✅ They orbit at ≈ 20,200 km in inclined MEO orbits with ≈ 12 h periods — not geostationary.
❌ 'Relativistic corrections are too tiny to matter.' ✅ Without them GPS would be off by ~10 km/day. The effect is 38 µs/day — essential.
❌ 'Position accuracy is limited by the number of satellites visible.' ✅ With ≥ 4 satellites you can fix position; more satellites reduce error statistics but don't change the basic math.

data.title: Thermal Energy, Heat and Temperature
notes: **Definition:** A temperature scale is created by identifying two easily reproducible fixed points (usually the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval between them into equal divisions.

**Celsius scale (°C):** Introduced by Anders Celsius in 1742. Freezing point of water = 0°C, boiling point = 100°C at 1 atm. Has 100 equal divisions between the fixed points. The SI unit for temperature intervals is the degree Celsius.
**Fahrenheit scale (°F):** Introduced by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1720. Freezing point = 32°F, boiling point = 212°F at 1 atm. Has 180 equal divisions. Widely used in the United States.

**Kelvin scale (K):** The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, named after Lord Kelvin. It is an absolute scale with zero at absolute zero (0 K = −273.15°C). Freezing point of water = 273.15 K, boiling point = 373.15 K. The Kelvin has the same magnitude as the Celsius degree, so ΔT(K) = ΔT(°C).

**Absolute zero:** 0 K = −273.15°C = −459.67°F. The theoretical temperature at which all molecular motion ceases (classical picture). It is unreachable in practice due to quantum zero-point energy. Modern definition: 0 K is the temperature at which the triple point of water occurs at exactly 273.16 K.

**Triple point of water:** The unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and vapor phases of water coexist in equilibrium: 273.16 K (0.01°C) at 611.657 Pa. This is the defining fixed point of the Kelvin scale.
**Reaumur scale (°R or °Ré):** Freezing point = 0°Ré, boiling point = 80°Ré. Rarely used today, except historically in some European countries.
**Rankine scale (°Ra):** The absolute version of Fahrenheit. 0°Ra = 0 K = −459.67°F. Freezing point of water = 491.67°Ra, boiling point = 671.67°Ra.

**Why use Kelvin?** In gas laws (PV = nRT), temperature must be in Kelvin because the relationship P ∝ T is linear only with absolute temperature. At 0 K, the extrapolated volume of an ideal gas would be zero, making physical sense. In Celsius, this would be −273.15°C - a non-zero volume at "zero" temperature.

**Gas thermometer:** The most accurate temperature measurement uses a constant-volume gas thermometer. It measures pressure of a fixed volume of gas, which is proportional to absolute temperature. The ideal gas law PV = nRT allows extrapolation to zero pressure for perfect accuracy.

**Platinum resistance thermometer:** Uses the fact that electrical resistance of metals increases nearly linearly with temperature. R = R₀(1 + αT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. Platinum is used due to its stability and near-linear behavior.
confusion: Temperature and heat are NOT the same. Temperature is an intensive property (per unit mass); heat is energy transferred (extensive). A bathtub of 30°C water has more heat than a cup of 80°C water, but lower temperature.
A temperature difference of 1°C is NOT the same as 1°F. ΔT(°C) = (5/9)ΔT(°F). A 10°C change equals an 18°F change, so 5°C ≠ 5°F.
Kelvin is NOT written as '°K' - it is simply 'K' (e.g., 300 K, not 300°K). There is no 'degree Kelvin.' The word 'kelvin' is not capitalized when spelled out.

Absolute zero is NOT just 'really cold' - it is the state where classical thermal motion ceases entirely. At 0 K, only quantum zero-point energy remains, and all real substances have condensed to their ground states.
The triple point of water (273.16 K) and the freezing point of water (273.15 K) differ by exactly 0.01 K. Confusing these is a common source of error in metrology.

notes: **Definition:** A temperature scale is created by identifying two easily reproducible fixed points (usually the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval between them into equal divisions.

**Celsius scale (°C):** Introduced by Anders Celsius in 1742. Freezing point of water = 0°C, boiling point = 100°C at 1 atm. Has 100 equal divisions between the fixed points. The SI unit for temperature intervals is the degree Celsius.
**Fahrenheit scale (°F):** Introduced by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1720. Freezing point = 32°F, boiling point = 212°F at 1 atm. Has 180 equal divisions. Widely used in the United States.

**Kelvin scale (K):** The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, named after Lord Kelvin. It is an absolute scale with zero at absolute zero (0 K = −273.15°C). Freezing point of water = 273.15 K, boiling point = 373.15 K. The Kelvin has the same magnitude as the Celsius degree, so ΔT(K) = ΔT(°C).

**Absolute zero:** 0 K = −273.15°C = −459.67°F. The theoretical temperature at which all molecular motion ceases (classical picture). It is unreachable in practice due to quantum zero-point energy. Modern definition: 0 K is the temperature at which the triple point of water occurs at exactly 273.16 K.

**Triple point of water:** The unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and vapor phases of water coexist in equilibrium: 273.16 K (0.01°C) at 611.657 Pa. This is the defining fixed point of the Kelvin scale.
**Reaumur scale (°R or °Ré):** Freezing point = 0°Ré, boiling point = 80°Ré. Rarely used today, except historically in some European countries.
**Rankine scale (°Ra):** The absolute version of Fahrenheit. 0°Ra = 0 K = −459.67°F. Freezing point of water = 491.67°Ra, boiling point = 671.67°Ra.

**Why use Kelvin?** In gas laws (PV = nRT), temperature must be in Kelvin because the relationship P ∝ T is linear only with absolute temperature. At 0 K, the extrapolated volume of an ideal gas would be zero, making physical sense. In Celsius, this would be −273.15°C - a non-zero volume at "zero" temperature.

**Gas thermometer:** The most accurate temperature measurement uses a constant-volume gas thermometer. It measures pressure of a fixed volume of gas, which is proportional to absolute temperature. The ideal gas law PV = nRT allows extrapolation to zero pressure for perfect accuracy.

**Platinum resistance thermometer:** Uses the fact that electrical resistance of metals increases nearly linearly with temperature. R = R₀(1 + αT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. Platinum is used due to its stability and near-linear behavior.
confusion: Temperature and heat are NOT the same. Temperature is an intensive property (per unit mass); heat is energy transferred (extensive). A bathtub of 30°C water has more heat than a cup of 80°C water, but lower temperature.
A temperature difference of 1°C is NOT the same as 1°F. ΔT(°C) = (5/9)ΔT(°F). A 10°C change equals an 18°F change, so 5°C ≠ 5°F.
Kelvin is NOT written as '°K' - it is simply 'K' (e.g., 300 K, not 300°K). There is no 'degree Kelvin.' The word 'kelvin' is not capitalized when spelled out.

Absolute zero is NOT just 'really cold' - it is the state where classical thermal motion ceases entirely. At 0 K, only quantum zero-point energy remains, and all real substances have condensed to their ground states.
The triple point of water (273.16 K) and the freezing point of water (273.15 K) differ by exactly 0.01 K. Confusing these is a common source of error in metrology.

ðŸŒ¡ï¸ TEMPERATURE â€” DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot â†’ cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

ðŸ”¥ HEAT â€” DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

ðŸ’¡ KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property â€” doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property â€” depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower â€” more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

âš¡ EFFECTS OF HEAT: When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
âš–ï¸ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact â€” meaning they are at the same temperature.

ðŸ“ ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer â€” the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
ðŸ§ª THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters â€” Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
ðŸ”¬ THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

ðŸ’¡ WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP â€” ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP â€” steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree-step is. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.
ðŸ“ TABLE A1 â€” ALL 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFPâˆ’LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | Â°C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | Â°F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 â‰  ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| RÃ©aumur | Â°R (RÃ©) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |

ðŸ”‘ FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Step 1: Fundamental interval of X = 130âˆ’(âˆ’20) = 150

â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / CHANGE NUMERICALS â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL F1: A Fahrenheit thermometer reads 99Â°F when a standard Celsius thermometer reads 37Â°C. Find the error in the Fahrenheit scale.

data.title: Kinetic-Molecular Model
notes: **Kinetic theory of matter:** All matter is composed of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are in constant, random motion. The motion is thermal motion - faster at higher temperatures.

**States of matter and molecular spacing:** In gases, intermolecular spacing is much larger than molecular diameter (10× or more), so molecules move freely. In liquids, spacing is about 1 molecular diameter. In solids, molecules are tightly packed in a regular arrangement.

**Intermolecular forces:** Attractive forces between molecules (van der Waals, hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole). These forces are strongest in solids (holding molecules in fixed positions), moderate in liquids, and very weak in gases at ordinary conditions.

**Kinetic energy vs potential energy in matter:** In gases, kinetic energy dominates (molecules move freely). In solids, potential energy dominates (molecules held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces). At the melting/boiling point, energy input goes into breaking bonds (increasing PE) without changing temperature.

**Brownian motion:** Random zigzag motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, first observed by Robert Brown (1827). Explained by Einstein (1905) as the result of unequal bombardment by fluid molecules - strong evidence for the kinetic theory.

**Diffusion:** The spontaneous mixing of particles due to random molecular motion. Occurs in all states but fastest in gases and slowest in solids. Fick's law: diffusion rate $\\\propto$ concentration gradient. At higher temperature, diffusion is faster (faster molecules).

**Thermal expansion:** Matter expands when heated (generally). In gases, expansion is large (Charles's law). In liquids, expansion is moderate. In solids, expansion is small but measurable. Due to increased molecular vibration amplitudes at higher temperatures.

**Mean free path:** The average distance a molecule travels between collisions. $\\\\lambda = \ rac{1}{\\\\sqrt{2} n \\\\sigma}$, where $n$ is the number density and $\\\\sigma$ is the collision cross-section. At STP, the mean free path of air molecules is about 68 nm.

**Degrees of freedom:** The number of independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic gas: 3 translational DOF. Diatomic: 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Polyatomic: 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational) at room temperature.

**Equipartition theorem:** Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\ rac{1}{2}k_BT$ of energy per molecule, or $\ rac{1}{2}RT$ per mole. For monatomic gas ($f=3$): $U = \ rac{3}{2}nRT$. For diatomic ($f=5$): $U = \ rac{5}{2}nRT$.

**Phase transitions and energy:** During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant even though heat is added. The energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing PE), not increasing KE. This is latent heat: $Q = mL$ where $L$ is latent heat.

**Surface tension:** A consequence of intermolecular attractive forces. Molecules at the surface experience a net inward pull, creating a 'skin' effect. Surface tension $\\\\gamma$ has units of N/m or J/m$^2$. Water has high surface tension (72 mN/m at 25°C) due to hydrogen bonding.

**Viscosity:** A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow. Caused by intermolecular forces and molecular momentum transfer. Gases become more viscous at higher temperature (faster molecules, more momentum transfer). Liquids become less viscous at higher temperature (bonds break more easily).
confusion: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules, NOT the total energy. A hot object has higher average KE per molecule, but a large cold object may have more total thermal energy (more molecules).

Heat and temperature are NOT the same. Temperature is a measure of average molecular KE (intensive property). Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects due to temperature difference (extensive property). You can add heat without changing temperature (phase change).

Intermolecular forces are NOT the same as intramolecular (chemical) forces. Intermolecular forces hold molecules together in condensed phases (weak, ~1-100 kJ/mol). Intramolecular forces hold atoms together within a molecule (strong, ~100-1000 kJ/mol).
Diffusion in liquids is faster than in solids, but much slower than in gases. This is often confused with the rate of dissolving, which also involves convection and stirring.

A gas molecule at high altitude has LESS kinetic energy if it has risen (energy converts to gravitational PE). But temperature is a statistical property - individual molecules have a range of speeds given by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, not a single speed.

data.title: Molecular Properties of Matter
notes: **Kinetic theory of matter:** All matter is composed of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are in constant, random motion. The motion is thermal motion - faster at higher temperatures.

**States of matter and molecular spacing:** In gases, intermolecular spacing is much larger than molecular diameter (10× or more), so molecules move freely. In liquids, spacing is about 1 molecular diameter. In solids, molecules are tightly packed in a regular arrangement.

**Intermolecular forces:** Attractive forces between molecules (van der Waals, hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole). These forces are strongest in solids (holding molecules in fixed positions), moderate in liquids, and very weak in gases at ordinary conditions.

**Kinetic energy vs potential energy in matter:** In gases, kinetic energy dominates (molecules move freely). In solids, potential energy dominates (molecules held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces). At the melting/boiling point, energy input goes into breaking bonds (increasing PE) without changing temperature.

**Brownian motion:** Random zigzag motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, first observed by Robert Brown (1827). Explained by Einstein (1905) as the result of unequal bombardment by fluid molecules - strong evidence for the kinetic theory.

**Diffusion:** The spontaneous mixing of particles due to random molecular motion. Occurs in all states but fastest in gases and slowest in solids. Fick's law: diffusion rate $\\\propto$ concentration gradient. At higher temperature, diffusion is faster (faster molecules).

**Thermal expansion:** Matter expands when heated (generally). In gases, expansion is large (Charles's law). In liquids, expansion is moderate. In solids, expansion is small but measurable. Due to increased molecular vibration amplitudes at higher temperatures.

**Mean free path:** The average distance a molecule travels between collisions. $\\\\lambda = \ rac{1}{\\\\sqrt{2} n \\\\sigma}$, where $n$ is the number density and $\\\\sigma$ is the collision cross-section. At STP, the mean free path of air molecules is about 68 nm.

**Degrees of freedom:** The number of independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic gas: 3 translational DOF. Diatomic: 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Polyatomic: 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational) at room temperature.

**Equipartition theorem:** Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\ rac{1}{2}k_BT$ of energy per molecule, or $\ rac{1}{2}RT$ per mole. For monatomic gas ($f=3$): $U = \ rac{3}{2}nRT$. For diatomic ($f=5$): $U = \ rac{5}{2}nRT$.

**Phase transitions and energy:** During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant even though heat is added. The energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing PE), not increasing KE. This is latent heat: $Q = mL$ where $L$ is latent heat.

**Surface tension:** A consequence of intermolecular attractive forces. Molecules at the surface experience a net inward pull, creating a 'skin' effect. Surface tension $\\\\gamma$ has units of N/m or J/m$^2$. Water has high surface tension (72 mN/m at 25°C) due to hydrogen bonding.

**Viscosity:** A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow. Caused by intermolecular forces and molecular momentum transfer. Gases become more viscous at higher temperature (faster molecules, more momentum transfer). Liquids become less viscous at higher temperature (bonds break more easily).
confusion: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules, NOT the total energy. A hot object has higher average KE per molecule, but a large cold object may have more total thermal energy (more molecules).

Heat and temperature are NOT the same. Temperature is a measure of average molecular KE (intensive property). Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects due to temperature difference (extensive property). You can add heat without changing temperature (phase change).

Intermolecular forces are NOT the same as intramolecular (chemical) forces. Intermolecular forces hold molecules together in condensed phases (weak, ~1-100 kJ/mol). Intramolecular forces hold atoms together within a molecule (strong, ~100-1000 kJ/mol).
Diffusion in liquids is faster than in solids, but much slower than in gases. This is often confused with the rate of dissolving, which also involves convection and stirring.

A gas molecule at high altitude has LESS kinetic energy if it has risen (energy converts to gravitational PE). But temperature is a statistical property - individual molecules have a range of speeds given by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, not a single speed.

data.title: Boltzmann Constant and RMS Speed
notes: **Boltzmann constant:** $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K. It connects microscopic and macroscopic thermodynamics. Named after Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906).
**RMS speed:** $v_{rms} = \\\\sqrt{3RT/M}$, where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. At STP (273 K), $v_{rms}$ for air is about 479 m/s. At 300 K, about 484 m/s. Lighter gases move faster on average.

**Most probable speed:** $v_p = \\\\sqrt{2RT/M}$. This is the speed at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks. At 300 K for air: $v_p \\\\approx 364$ m/s. At 300 K for H₂: $v_p \\\\approx 1650$ m/s.
**Mean speed:** $v_{mean} = \\\\sqrt{8RT/\\\\pi M}$. The average of all molecular speeds. At 300 K for air: $v_{mean} \\\\approx 464$ m/s. At 300 K for H₂: $v_{mean} \\\\approx 1760$ m/s.

**Heat capacities - monatomic gases:** $C_V = \ rac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \ rac{5}{2}R$. The ratio $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V = 5/3 \\\\approx 1.67$. Monatomic gases (He, Ne, Ar) only have translational degrees of freedom.

**Heat capacities - diatomic gases:** $C_V = \ rac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \ rac{7}{2}R$ at ordinary temperatures ($\\\\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$). Includes 3 translational + 2 rotational DOF. At high temperature, vibration adds more, so $C_V \ightarrow 4R$, $C_P \ightarrow 5R$, $\\\\gamma \ightarrow 9/7 \\\approx 1.29$.

**Dulong-Petit law for solids:** Molar heat capacity of most solid elements at room temperature $\\\approx 3R \\\\approx 25$ J/(mol·K). This comes from 3 quadratic degrees of freedom per atom (one for each spatial axis), each contributing $R$ per mole of atoms.

**Why heat capacities differ:** The ratio $C_P/C_V = \\\\gamma$ matters for adiabatic processes ($PV^\\\gamma = \	ext{const}$). This affects everything from engine cycles to atmospheric science. $\\\gamma \\\\approx 1.4$ for air is crucial in meteorology.

**Experimental verification:** Heat capacities were measured by Regnault and others in the 19th century. The agreement with kinetic theory predictions was one of the great successes of molecular physics.
**Units:** $k_B = 1.38 \	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K. $C_P, C_V$ have units J/(mol·K). Gas constant R has the same units.
**Connection to energy:** Each degree of freedom contributes $\ rac{1}{2}R$ per mole or $\ rac{1}{2}k_B$ per molecule. 3 translational DOF $ightarrow 3 \	imes \ rac{1}{2}R = \ rac{3}{2}R$ for $C_V$
confusion: The ratio $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is NOT always 5/3 or 7/5. It depends on temperature and molecular structure. At very high temperatures, vibrational modes activate, changing $\\\\gamma$.
The formula $C_V = \ rac{3}{2}R$ applies ONLY to monatomic ideal gases. For diatomic or polyatomic gases, rotational (and sometimes vibrational) modes contribute.

Dulong's law ($C \\\\approx 3R$) for solids works well at room temperature but fails at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze out degrees of freedom). Einstein and Debye developed low-temperature models.
The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is NOT the same as the gas constant R. $k_B = 1.38 \	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K per molecule. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) per mole. $R = N_A k_B$.

Most probable speed is NOT the average speed. For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p \\\\cdot \\\\sqrt{2} < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$. The order is always $v_p < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$ at the same temperature.

data.title: Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version complements the original note with the limit-definition approach, calculus forms and graphical slope reasoning for instantaneous velocity and acceleration.

**Average quantities first:** average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ uses the whole interval; average acceleration $a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ likewise. They smooth out everything that happened in between — a car doing 100 km in 2 h has $v_{avg} = 50$ km/h regardless of traffic.

data.title: Relative Velocity
notes: **Definition of relative velocity:** The velocity of an object B as measured from the reference frame of another moving object A. It is the velocity of B relative to A.

**Same direction (one-dimensional):** If car A moves at velocity v_A and car B at v_B in the same direction, the velocity of B relative to A is v_{B/A} = v_B - v_A. If v_B > v_A, B moves ahead relative to A; if v_B < v_A, B falls behind.

**Opposite directions (one-dimensional):** If A and B move toward each other with speeds v_A and v_B, the relative speed (magnitude of relative velocity) is v_{rel} = v_A + v_B. The direction of v_{B/A} is toward A if B is moving toward A.

**Vector form (two/three dimensions):** \vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A. This is the velocity of B in the ground frame minus the velocity of A in the ground frame. In components: (v_{B/A})_x = v_{Bx} - v_{Ax}, etc.

**Relative velocity in 2D — Rain example:** If rain falls vertically downward at speed v_r and a person runs horizontally at speed v_p, the rain appears to come at the person at an angle 	heta where tan	heta = v_p / v_r. The apparent speed is \sqrt{v_r^2 + v_p^2}.

**River crossing (boat relative to water vs. ground):** Let \vec{v}_{bw} be the boat's velocity relative to the water (its heading and speed), and \vec{v}_{wg} be the water's velocity relative to ground (current). Then the boat's ground velocity is \vec{v}_{bg} = \vec{v}_{bw} + \vec{v}_{wg}. To reach a point directly across, the boat must angle upstream.

**Relative velocity of approach/separation:** For two objects approaching, the rate at which their separation decreases is v_{rel} = v_A + v_B (if opposite directions) or |v_B - v_A| (if same direction). For collision problems, relative velocity is crucial.

**Frame of reference transformation:** To transform from frame A to frame B, subtract the velocity of frame A: \vec{v}' = \vec{v} - \vec{v}_A. The laws of physics (Newton's laws) are the same in all inertial frames (Galilean relativity).

**Galilean velocity addition:** In classical mechanics, velocities add vectorially: \vec{v}_{B/C} = \vec{v}_{B/A} + \vec{v}_{A/C}. This chain rule allows finding velocity of B relative to C via an intermediate frame A.

**Relative motion on an incline:** If a block slides down an incline at speed v relative to the incline, and the incline itself moves (e.g., on a truck), the block's ground velocity is the vector sum of its velocity relative to the incline and the incline's velocity relative to ground.

**Closing speed vs. relative velocity:** Closing speed is the rate at which the distance between two objects decreases. For objects moving directly toward each other, closing speed = |v_A| + |v_B|. This is the magnitude of the relative velocity only if they are on a collision course.
confusion: Relative velocity is NOT the same as the difference in speeds. For two cars moving at 60 km/h and 40 km/h in the SAME direction, the relative speed is 20 km/h, NOT 100 km/h. For opposite directions, the relative speed is the SUM (100 km/h).

When subtracting vectors, the ORDER MATTERS: \vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A. This is the velocity of B AS SEEN BY A. \vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = -\vec{v}_{B/A}. They are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

A common mistake in river problems: students add the boat's speed to the current speed as scalars. You must add them as VECTORS: the boat's velocity relative to water PLUS water's velocity relative to ground. The angle matters!

In the rain problem, the rain does NOT change its actual velocity — it still falls vertically. Only the APPARENT velocity (relative to the moving person) is angled. The person tilts their umbrella forward to block the apparent rain.

Galilean relativity breaks down at speeds close to the speed of light (c). Einstein's special relativity replaces it with the Lorentz velocity addition formula: v = (v1 + v2)/(1 + v1v2/c^2). For everyday speeds (<< c), this reduces to Galilean addition.

data.title: Equations of Motion — Graphical Treatment
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version derives all three equations of motion graphically (from the velocity–time graph) — the derivation style NEB asks for 'using a graphical method'.

**Setup:** a body starts with initial velocity $u$ and accelerates uniformly at $a$; after time $t$ its velocity is $v$. On a $v$–$t$ graph this is a straight line from $(0, u)$ to $(t, v)$ — the straightness is exactly the meaning of uniform acceleration.
**First equation (from the slope):** slope of the line = acceleration $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$. Rearranging: $v = u + at$ — 'final velocity = initial velocity + rate of change of velocity × time'.

**Second equation (from the area):** displacement = area under the $v$–$t$ line = area of the trapezoid = area of rectangle $ut$ + area of triangle $\frac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$. Since $v - u = at$: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

**Second equation, alternate area view:** average velocity $\times$ time: $s = \left(\frac{u + v}{2}\right)t$ — the trapezoid's mean-height form. Both views give the same result and both are accepted in exams.

**Third equation (eliminating $t$):** from $t = \frac{v-u}{a}$ substitute into $s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$: $s = \frac{(u+v)(v-u)}{2a} = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$, giving $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ — the time-free equation, ideal when $t$ is neither given nor asked.

**Reading the other graphs:** on an $x$–$t$ graph, constant $a$ appears as a parabola (curvature fixed); the tangent slope at any point is $v$. On an $a$–$t$ graph, constant $a$ is a horizontal line and the area under it ($a \times t$) gives the change in velocity $v - u$.

**Displacement in the $n$-th second:** $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ — obtained from areas: distance covered between $t = n-1$ and $t = n$. For free fall from rest this gives the odd-numbers rule 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 (Galileo).

**NEB exam focus:** derive $v = u + at$ and $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with a labelled $v$–$t$ graph; derive $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$; state which equation to choose from what is given/asked; apply to braking, free fall and projected bodies.
formulas: $v = u + at$  (slope of $v$–$t$ line)
$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$  (rectangle + triangle area)
$s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$  (trapezoid mean-height form)
$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$  (time eliminated)
$s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$  (distance in the $n$-th second)
confusion: ❌ 'The area under the $v$–$t$ graph gives acceleration.' ✅ Area gives DISPLACEMENT; the SLOPE gives acceleration. Swap-proof: slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$ (m/s²), area of $v$–$t$ = $s$ (m).

❌ Using $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ for the distance in the $n$-th second directly with $t = n$. ✅ That gives the total distance in $n$ seconds. The $n$-th SECOND distance is $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$, i.e. $s(n) - s(n-1)$.

❌ Applying $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with sign errors during braking. ✅ Take one positive direction and keep it: braking at 20 m/s with $a = -5$ m/s² gives $0 = 400 + 2(-5)s \Rightarrow s = 40$ m — the minus sign is essential.
❌ 'The equations work if acceleration changes gradually.' ✅ All three equations REQUIRE constant acceleration; if $a$ varies, use graphs/areas or calculus.
❌ Treating $u$ and $v$ as interchangeable. ✅ $u$ is the velocity at $t = 0$; $v$ is at time $t$. A body dropped from rest has $u = 0$; a body thrown up has $u = +20$ m/s while $a = -10$ m/s².

❌ Confusing distance with displacement when the body reverses. ✅ The equations give displacement (vector). For total path length through a reversal, split the motion at the $v = 0$ instant and add the two parts.

data.title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version works free fall entirely through the equations of motion with sign conventions and the up-and-down symmetry argument — the pattern NEB numericals follow.

**Definition:** a freely falling body moves under gravity ALONE — no air resistance, no push after release. All bodies fall with the same acceleration $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² (take 10 m/s² in numericals) independent of mass — Galileo's famous result.

**Sign convention method:** choose upward positive. Then for a body projected up at $u$: $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$. The SAME equations with $u = 0$ describe a dropped body; with the throw downward, $u$ enters negative.

**Up–down symmetry:** a body thrown up with speed $u$ returns to the launch point with the same speed (downward); time up = time down $= u/g$; total flight $T = 2u/g$. Air resistance would break this symmetry — its absence is the point of 'free' fall.

**Key instants for a body thrown up:** at the top, $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward (never zero); height reached $h_{max} = u^2/2g$; velocities at equal heights going up and down are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
**Dropped from a height $h$:** $v = gt$, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. Time to fall: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. Falling 1:3:5:7 distances each second (Galileo's odd-number rule).

**Bodies with initial downward or upward motion from a height** (e.g. a ball thrown down at 5 m/s): $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$ with BOTH terms positive when down is the direction of travel — the third equation handles every case once signs are set.

**Relative fall problems:** a ball dropped from a descending/ascending lift, or two balls released with a time gap — write each body's position $y_i(t)$ with the same origin, then use their difference. E.g. separation between a dropped ball and one thrown down 1 s later grows as $\Delta y = \tfrac{1}{2}g + (u)t$.

**NEB exam focus:** state that $g$ is mass-independent (with the Galileo/feather-coin argument); compute maximum height, time of flight, velocity on impact; apply up–down symmetry; solve dropped/thrown-from-lift problems with one consistent sign convention.
formulas: Dropped from rest: $v = gt$, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
Thrown up (up positive): $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$
Maximum height: $h_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$ (at $v = 0$)
Times: $t_{up} = t_{down} = \dfrac{u}{g}$, total flight $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$
$n$-th second fall distance: $s_n = \tfrac{g}{2}(2n - 1)$ — ratio $1:3:5:7\ldots$
confusion: ❌ 'Heavier bodies fall faster.' ✅ In free fall ALL bodies have the same acceleration $g$; observed differences come from air resistance — demonstrated by the Apollo 15 hammer–feather drop on the Moon.
❌ 'At the top of the flight, acceleration is zero because the body stops.' ✅ $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward at ALL points of the flight. If $a$ were zero at the top, the body would stay there!

❌ Using $g = -10$ m/s² AND taking $h$ positive upward in $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. ✅ Put the sign in ONCE: either $g$ negative with up positive, or down positive with $g$ positive — never both conventions mixed.
❌ 'A body thrown up takes longer to rise than to fall.' ✅ Without air resistance the times are EXACTLY equal ($u/g$ each way); with air resistance the fall takes LONGER, not the rise.
❌ 'Velocity on returning to the thrower is less than the launch speed.' ✅ Equal in magnitude (symmetry). Only air resistance or bounce changes it.
❌ Treating 'dropped' and 'thrown down' identically. ✅ Dropped means $u = 0$; thrown down means $u \ne 0$ downward — the equations differ by that initial term.

data.title: Projectile Motion and Its Applications
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version builds projectile motion from the independence of the two components and derives all standard results step by step — the derivation chain NEB expects.

**The governing idea:** horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT. Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity stays constant ($v_x = u\cos\theta$) while the vertical motion is free fall with initial speed $u\sin\theta$. The path is the combination — a parabola.

**Component equations (up positive, launch at angle $\theta$ with speed $u$):** horizontal: $x = (u\cos\theta)t$, $v_x = u\cos\theta$; vertical: $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$.
**Time of flight:** set $y = 0$ on landing: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ — twice the time to the top ($u\sin\theta/g$).
**Maximum height:** at the top $v_y = 0$: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ — vertical throw with initial speed $u\sin\theta$.

**Horizontal range:** $R = v_x T = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$. Since $\sin 2\theta$ peaks at $2\theta = 90°$, **maximum range at $\theta = 45°$**, and complementary angles ($30°$ & $60°$, $15°$ & $75°$) give the SAME range.

**Velocity at any instant:** $v = \sqrt{(u\cos\theta)^2 + (u\sin\theta - gt)^2}$ at angle $\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{u\sin\theta - gt}{u\cos\theta}\right)$ below/above horizontal. On landing, magnitude equals $u$ (symmetry) with direction $-\theta$.
**Trajectory equation:** eliminate $t$: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ — a parabola. Also useful: $R = 4H\cot\theta$ connecting range and height.

**Applications to quote:** cannon/artillery ranges, projectile games (javelin, football), water-fountain arcs, bombing-release problems (bomb keeps the plane's horizontal velocity), and projectile on an inclined plane (extension: $R = \frac{2u^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$ for incline angle $\alpha$ — beyond syllabus but good insight).

**NEB exam focus:** state independence of motions; derive $T$, $H$, $R$; prove max range at 45°; show complementary angles share range; compute velocity (magnitude and direction) at a given time or height; draw the labelled trajectory.
formulas: Components: $v_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant); $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$
Time of flight: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$
Maximum height: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$
Range: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$; $R_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ at $\theta = 45°$
Trajectory: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ (parabola); $R = 4H\cot\theta$
confusion: ❌ 'A projectile's horizontal velocity decreases during flight.' ✅ $v_x = u\cos\theta$ is CONSTANT (no horizontal force in the ideal model); only $v_y$ changes.
❌ 'At the top of the trajectory the velocity is zero.' ✅ Only $v_y = 0$; the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ persists — speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$, the MINIMUM of the flight.
❌ 'The path is part of a circle / straight line decaying.' ✅ The trajectory is a PARABOLA — the graph of $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$.
❌ Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin 2\theta$ in the range. ✅ $R = u^2\sin 2\theta/g$; and $\sin 2\theta$ is maximal at $\theta = 45°$, not $90°$.
❌ 'Complementary angles give different ranges.' ✅ $\sin 2(90°-\theta) = \sin(180°-2\theta) = \sin 2\theta$ — $30°$ and $60°$ land at the SAME spot (the 60° shot flies higher).
❌ Doubling $u$ doubles the range. ✅ $R \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed QUADRUPLES range (and quadruples max height too).

data.title: Nucleus: Discovery, Density and Composition
notes: **Atomic mass unit (u):** $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 1.660539\	imes 10^{-27}\\\\,\	ext{kg}$. Defined as exactly $1/12$ the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. All nuclear masses are expressed in u for convenience.

**Exact mass vs mass number:** The mass number $A$ is the integer count of nucleons. The exact mass in u differs slightly from $A$ due to mass defect. For example, $^{12}\	ext{C}$ has exact mass $12\\\\,\	ext{u}$ by definition, but $^{1}\	ext{H}$ has exact mass $1.007825\\\\,\	ext{u}$, not $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$.

**Isotopes:** atoms of the same element ($Z$ same) with different mass numbers ($A$ different). They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and decay modes. Example: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ ($75.78\\\\%$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ ($24.22\\\\%$) are chlorine isotopes.

**Mass defect $\\\\Delta m$:** $\\\\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$, where $m_p \\\\approx 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the proton mass, $m_n \\\\approx 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the neutron mass, and $M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$ is the nuclear mass in u. The mass defect is always positive - the nucleus is lighter than its separated parts.

**Packing fraction:** $f = (M - A)/A$, where $M$ is the exact atomic mass in u and $A$ is the mass number. $f$ measures the fractional deviation from $A$. Negative $f$ (mass less than mass number) indicates strong binding; positive $f$ indicates weaker binding. $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ has the most negative $f$, making it the most stable nuclide.

**Binding energy:** $BE = \\\\Delta m c^2$. The energy equivalent of the mass defect. In MeV, $BE\	ext{(MeV)} \\\\approx 931.494 \	imes \\\\Delta m\	ext{(u)}$. For $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$, $BE/A \\\\approx 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, the peak of the binding-energy curve.

**Binding energy per nucleon:** $BE/A$. Rises from $\\\\sim 1\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for light hydrogen to $\\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ near iron ($A \\\\approx 56$), then slowly declines to $\\\\sim 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for uranium. This curve explains why light nuclei release energy via fusion and heavy nuclei via fission.

**Carbon-14 dating:** $^{14}\	ext{C}$ is a radioactive isotope with half-life $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. While alive, living organisms maintain $^{14}\	ext{C}/^{12}\	ext{C} \\\\approx 1.1\	imes 10^{-12}$. After death, $^{14}\	ext{C}$ decays via $\ eta^-$; measuring the remaining $^{14}\	ext{C}$ gives the time since death (archaeological dating up to $\\\\sim 50\\\\,\	ext{kyr}$).

**Isotopic abundance:** The natural abundance of each isotope (given as a percentage) determines the standard atomic weight listed in the periodic table. For chlorine, $\ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the tabulated value.

**Mass spectrometry:** A device that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$). Ions are accelerated through electric fields and deflected by magnetic fields; lighter ions deflect more. The resulting spectrum shows peaks at different $m/z$ values corresponding to different isotopes, with peak heights proportional to abundance.

**Stable vs. radioactive isotopes:** Only $\\\\sim 254$ isotopes are stable; over 3000 are known to be radioactive. Stable isotopes have balanced neutron-proton ratios; too many or too few neutrons leads to instability and radioactive decay.

**Nuclide notation:** A nuclide is written as $^{A}_{Z}\	ext{X}$, where $A$ is the mass number (protons + neutrons), $Z$ is the atomic number (protons), and $\	ext{X}$ is the element symbol. Example: $^{238}_{92}\	ext{U}$ has 92 protons and $238 - 92 = 146$ neutrons.
confusion: Misconception - Mass number $A$ is an integer count of nucleons; exact atomic mass in u is not exactly $A$. The difference is the mass defect, which is small but measurable. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes by their exact masses, not their mass numbers.

Misconception - Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ can be negative because the bound nucleus weighs less than its constituent nucleons. Students expect $M > A$ by adding individual proton and neutron masses, but binding energy release makes $M < Zm_p + Nm_n$.

Misconception - Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$; isobars share the same $A$ but have different $Z$; isotones share the same $N$ but have different $A$. These three distinctions are common exam distractors.

Misconception - Standard atomic weight (the periodic table value) is the weighted-average of all naturally occurring isotopic masses, not the mass of any single atom. A single chlorine atom has mass $\\\sim 35\\\,	ext{u}$ or $\\\sim 37\\\,	ext{u}$, never $35.45\\\,	ext{u}$.

Misconception - Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ peaks at iron ($A \\\\sim 56$) at $\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, while uranium has $BE/A \\\\approx 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Fission energy release depends on the difference between parent and daughter nuclei, not a fixed value.

Misconception - $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$ of mass defect is equivalent to $931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ of energy. This conversion factor is essential for all nuclear binding-energy calculations; omitting it produces results that are off by a factor of $\\\sim 10^8$.

Misconception - In $ eta^-$ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino: $n \ightarrow p + e^- + \ ar{\
u}_e$. The emitted electron originates from the nucleus, not from the orbital electron cloud.
Misconception - Half-life is the time required for a radioactive sample to decay to half its original amount. After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is $(1/2)^n$, not $1/(2n)$.
