data.title: Total Internal Reflection
notes: **Definition:** Total internal reflection (TIR) occurs when a ray of light traveling in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. All the light is reflected back into the denser medium — no refraction occurs.
**Two essential conditions:** (1) Light must travel from a DENSER medium to a RARER medium ($n_1 > n_2$). (2) The angle of incidence must EXCEED the critical angle ($i > \theta_c$).

**Critical angle formula:** $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$, where $n_1$ is the refractive index of the denser medium and $n_2$ is the refractive index of the rarer medium. At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary ($r = 90°$).

**Critical angle for common materials:** Glass-to-air ($n = 1.52$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.52) = 41.1°$. Water-to-air ($n = 1.33$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.33) = 48.8°$. Diamond-to-air ($n = 2.42$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/2.42) = 24.4°$.

**What happens at different angles:** If $i < \theta_c$: partial reflection + refraction (most light transmits). If $i = \theta_c$: refraction at 90° (along the boundary). If $i > \theta_c$: TOTAL internal reflection (100% reflection, no transmission).

**Why TIR is 	otal:** Unlike mirror reflection (which absorbs 5–15% of light), TIR reflects 100% of the light. This makes it far more efficient than metallic mirrors for bending light paths in optical instruments.

**Optical fibre principle:** An optical fibre consists of a core (high $n$) surrounded by cladding (lower $n$). Light entering the core at angles greater than the critical angle undergoes repeated TIR, traveling kilometers with minimal loss. This is the basis of modern telecommunications.

**Diamond sparkle:** Diamond's high refractive index ($n = 2.42$) gives a very small critical angle (24.4°). Light entering a well-cut diamond undergoes multiple TIR events before exiting, creating the characteristic brilliant flashes of color (fire).

**Mirage phenomenon:** On a hot road, air near the surface is hotter and less dense (lower $n$) than air above. Light from the sky bends away from the normal as it passes through increasingly rarer layers. At a certain height, the angle exceeds the critical angle and TIR occurs, creating the illusion of water on the road.

**Prism binoculars:** Porro prisms in binoculars use TIR at the hypotenuse face (glass-to-air at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle of ~42° for glass). This provides reflection without the need for a silvered coating — brighter images with no degradation.

**NEB exam focus:** State the two conditions for TIR. Derive the critical angle formula. Calculate critical angles for common material pairs. Explain optical fibres and mirages using TIR. Draw ray diagrams showing TIR in prisms and fibres.

**Fibre optic numbers — acceptance angle:** The maximum angle at which light can enter an optical fibre and still undergo TIR is called the acceptance angle. $\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{clad}^2}$. For typical fibres ($n_{core} = 1.48$, $n_{clad} = 1.46$): $\theta_a \approx 16°$.

**Optical fibre types:** (1) Step-index fibre: core and cladding have uniform but different indices. (2) Graded-index fibre: the core's index gradually decreases from center to edge, causing light to follow curved paths and reducing modal dispersion.

**Applications of TIR:** (1) Optical fibres for communication and endoscopy. (2) Prism reflectors in binoculars and periscopes. (3) Diamond cutting for maximum brilliance. (4) Automotive rain sensors (TIR is disrupted by water droplets on the windshield). (5) Fiber-optic sensors for temperature and pressure.

**Partial reflection at TIR:** In reality, at angles just above the critical angle, a small evanescent wave penetrates into the rarer medium (decaying exponentially over a distance of about one wavelength). This is the principle behind frustrated TIR and near-field optical microscopy.

**Energy conservation in TIR:** Since no light is transmitted, all the incident energy is reflected. The intensity of the reflected ray equals the intensity of the incident ray (ignoring absorption in the medium). This is why TIR prisms are preferred over silvered mirrors in precision optics.
confusion: ❌ TIR can occur when light goes from rarer to denser medium. ✅ TIR ONLY occurs when light travels from DENSER to RARER medium ($n_1 > n_2$). From rarer to denser, the ray always bends toward the normal and always enters the second medium.

❌ The critical angle exists for any pair of media. ✅ The critical angle only exists when $n_1 > n_2$. If light goes from air to glass ($n_1 < n_2$), there is no critical angle — refraction always occurs.

❌ At the critical angle, all light is reflected. ✅ At the critical angle ($i = \theta_c$), the refracted ray travels ALONG the boundary ($r = 90°$). TIR begins only when $i > \theta_c$, not at $i = \theta_c$.
❌ TIR produces a dimmer reflection than a mirror. ✅ TIR reflects 100% of the light — it is BRIGHTER than any metallic mirror, which typically absorbs 5–15% of incident light.

❌ Optical fibres work because light is "trapped" by the cladding. ✅ Optical fibres work because of TIR at the core-cladding interface. The cladding has a LOWER refractive index than the core, creating the condition for TIR.

❌ The critical angle for diamond is about 42°. ✅ Diamond's critical angle is about 24.4° (much smaller than glass's 42°). This small critical angle is what makes diamonds so brilliant — light undergoes multiple TIR events before exiting.

❌ TIR can occur at any interface, including solid-solid interfaces. ✅ TIR requires a boundary between two media with DIFFERENT refractive indices. It can occur at any such boundary (glass-air, water-glass, fibre core-cladding) as long as light travels from the higher-index to the lower-index medium.

data.title: Minimum Deviation Condition
notes: **Deviation angle (δ):** When a ray of light passes through a prism, it bends at both faces. The total angle between the incident ray's original direction and the emergent ray's direction is called the angle of deviation, $\delta$.
**Formula for deviation:** $\delta = i + e - A$, where $i$ is the angle of incidence, $e$ is the angle of emergence, and $A$ is the prism angle (refracting angle).

**Minimum deviation (δ_min):** As you vary the angle of incidence $i$, the deviation $\delta$ changes. There is a unique value of $i$ that gives the SMALLEST possible deviation, called the angle of minimum deviation, $\delta_{min}$.

**Symmetric path condition:** At minimum deviation, the ray passes SYMMETRICALLY through the prism: $i = e$ (angle of incidence equals angle of emergence) and $r_1 = r_2 = r$ (angles of refraction at both faces are equal).
**Geometric consequence:** At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base of the prism (for an isosceles prism). This is the shortest path through the prism.

**Finding δ_min experimentally:** Rotate the prism on a spectrometer table while viewing the emergent ray. The deviation angle decreases to a minimum and then increases. The minimum point is marked by the ray momentarily stopping and reversing direction.

**Why minimum deviation matters:** At $\delta_{min}$, the prism formula $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$ is exact and doesn't require knowing the internal ray path. This makes it the most accurate way to measure refractive index.

**Curve of δ vs. i:** Plotting deviation $\delta$ against angle of incidence $i$ gives a U-shaped curve. The lowest point is $\delta_{min}$. The curve is symmetric about the minimum point (since swapping $i$ and $e$ gives the same deviation).

**Physical intuition:** At minimum deviation, the light takes the "path of least resistance" through the prism. Any deviation from the symmetric path increases the total bending because one face does more bending while the other does less, and the net effect is larger.

**Small prism approximation:** For a thin prism (small $A$), the minimum deviation is approximately $\delta_{min} \approx (n - 1)A$. This is useful for estimating deviation without precise measurements.

**Dispersion at minimum deviation:** Since refractive index $n$ depends on wavelength ($n_{violet} > n_{red}$), each color has a different $\delta_{min}$. Violet light deviates more than red light, producing a spectrum.

**Spectrometer measurement:** In a laboratory spectrometer, $\delta_{min}$ is found by rotating the prism table until the image of the slit stops moving and reverses direction. The angle between the incident and emergent ray at this point is $\delta_{min}$.

**NEB exam focus:** State the condition for minimum deviation ($i = e$, $r_1 = r_2$). Draw the ray diagram showing the symmetric path. Explain why minimum deviation gives the most accurate refractive index measurement.

**Connection to prisms in optics:** Minimum deviation is used in spectrometers, monochromators, and prism-based optical instruments. It provides the most well-defined relationship between angle and refractive index.
confusion: ❌ Minimum deviation occurs when the ray passes straight through the prism without bending. ✅ Minimum deviation still involves bending — it's the SMALLEST possible total deviation, not zero deviation. The ray still refracts at both surfaces.

❌ At minimum deviation, the ray is perpendicular to both prism faces. ✅ At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is parallel to the BASE (for an isosceles prism), not perpendicular to the faces. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal but not necessarily 90°.

❌ Any angle of incidence gives the same deviation. ✅ Deviation varies with angle of incidence. Only at one specific value of $i$ does the deviation reach its minimum. For other values of $i$, the deviation is larger.

❌ The angle of minimum deviation is zero for a prism. ✅ For a prism with $A > 0$ and $n > 1$, the minimum deviation is always positive. Zero deviation would require no refraction, which is impossible for a prism in air.
❌ Minimum deviation means the ray doesn't bend at all. ✅ "Minimum" means the smallest possible, not zero. The ray still bends — it's just the configuration that produces the least total bending.
❌ At minimum deviation, $r_1 \neq r_2$. ✅ At minimum deviation, $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. This is one of the key conditions that defines minimum deviation.

❌ You can find δ_min without a spectrometer. ✅ While you can approximate δ_min with a simple setup, precise measurement requires a spectrometer to accurately measure the angle between incident and emergent rays.

**Curve of δ vs. i:** Plotting deviation $\delta$ against angle of incidence $i$ gives a U-shaped curve. The lowest point is $\delta_{min}$. The curve is symmetric about the minimum point (since swapping $i$ and $e$ gives the same deviation).

**Physical intuition:** At minimum deviation, the light takes the "path of least resistance" through the prism. Any deviation from the symmetric path increases the total bending because one face does more bending while the other does less, and the net effect is larger.

**Small prism approximation:** For a thin prism (small $A$), the minimum deviation is approximately $\delta_{min} \approx (n - 1)A$. This is useful for estimating deviation without precise measurements.

**Dispersion at minimum deviation:** Since refractive index $n$ depends on wavelength ($n_{violet} > n_{red}$), each color has a different $\delta_{min}$. Violet light deviates more than red light, producing a spectrum.

**Spectrometer measurement:** In a laboratory spectrometer, $\delta_{min}$ is found by rotating the prism table until the image of the slit stops moving and reverses direction. The angle between the incident and emergent ray at this point is $\delta_{min}$.

**NEB exam focus:** State the condition for minimum deviation ($i = e$, $r_1 = r_2$). Draw the ray diagram showing the symmetric path. Explain why minimum deviation gives the most accurate refractive index measurement.

**Connection to prisms in optics:** Minimum deviation is used in spectrometers, monochromators, and prism-based optical instruments. It provides the most well-defined relationship between angle and refractive index.
confusion: ❌ Minimum deviation occurs when the ray passes straight through the prism without bending. ✅ Minimum deviation still involves bending — it's the SMALLEST possible total deviation, not zero deviation. The ray still refracts at both surfaces.

❌ At minimum deviation, the ray is perpendicular to both prism faces. ✅ At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is parallel to the BASE (for an isosceles prism), not perpendicular to the faces. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal but not necessarily 90°.

❌ Any angle of incidence gives the same deviation. ✅ Deviation varies with angle of incidence. Only at one specific value of $i$ does the deviation reach its minimum. For other values of $i$, the deviation is larger.

❌ The angle of minimum deviation is zero for a prism. ✅ For a prism with $A > 0$ and $n > 1$, the minimum deviation is always positive. Zero deviation would require no refraction, which is impossible for a prism in air.
❌ Minimum deviation means the ray doesn't bend at all. ✅ "Minimum" means the smallest possible, not zero. The ray still bends — it's just the configuration that produces the least total bending.
❌ At minimum deviation, $r_1 \neq r_2$. ✅ At minimum deviation, $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. This is one of the key conditions that defines minimum deviation.

❌ You can find δ_min without a spectrometer. ✅ While you can approximate δ_min with a simple setup, precise measurement requires a spectrometer to accurately measure the angle between incident and emergent rays.

data.title: Prism Formula
notes: **Small-angle prism definition:** A prism with a refracting angle $A \leq 10°$ (typically 2°–10°) is called a thin or small-angle prism. The approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (radians) is valid for such angles.

**Derivation of $\delta = (n-1)A$:** From the prism formula at minimum deviation: $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. For small angles: $\sin x \approx x$, so $n \approx \frac{(A+\delta)/2}{A/2} = \frac{A+\delta}{A} = 1 + \frac{\delta}{A}$. Therefore: $\boxed{\delta \approx (n-1)A}$.

**Independent of angle of incidence:** Unlike the general prism formula, the thin-prism deviation $\delta = (n-1)A$ does NOT depend on the angle of incidence $i$. This is because for small $A$, the ray passes nearly symmetrically regardless of $i$.

**Why independence matters:** In a thin prism, even if the incident ray is not at the minimum deviation position, the deviation is approximately the same. This makes thin prisms useful in optical instruments where precise alignment is difficult.

**Dispersion by a thin prism:** Since $n$ varies with wavelength: $\delta_v = (n_v - 1)A$ and $\delta_r = (n_r - 1)A$. The angular dispersion (separation between violet and red) is: $\boxed{\delta_v - \delta_r = (n_v - n_r)A}$.

**Dispersive power:** The dispersive power of the prism material is $\omega = \frac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1}$, where $n_y$ is the refractive index for yellow (sodium D line). The mean deviation is $\delta_y = (n_y - 1)A$. Therefore: $\boxed{\omega = \frac{\delta_v - \delta_r}{\delta_y}}$.

**Combined thin prisms — achromatic combination:** Two thin prisms of different materials can be combined to produce deviation WITHOUT dispersion (achromatic): $(n_{v1} - n_{r1})A_1 = (n_{v2} - n_{r2})A_2$. The deviations cancel for dispersion while the mean deviations add.

**Combined thin prisms — direct-vision prism:** Two thin prisms can be arranged to produce dispersion WITHOUT net deviation (direct vision): $(n_{y1} - 1)A_1 = (n_{y2} - 1)A_2$ but $(n_{v1} - n_{r1})A_1 \neq (n_{v2} - n_{r2})A_2$. This is used in spectrometers to view a spectrum without deviating the central ray.

**Practical applications:** Thin prisms are used in (1) binoculars for image erection, (2) spectrometers for approximate dispersion measurements, (3) optical compensators in interferometers, (4) prism goggles for vision correction (prismatic lenses).

**Deviation is small but measurable:** For crown glass ($n = 1.52$) and $A = 5°$: $\delta = (1.52 - 1) \times 5° = 2.6°$. This small deviation is easily measured with a spectrometer and used to find $n$ accurately.

**Limitation of the approximation:** The formula $\delta = (n-1)A$ has about 1% error for $A = 10°$ and $n = 1.5$. For $A = 60°$ (a typical large prism), the error is ~15% — the thin-prism formula is completely inapplicable.

**Connection to lenses:** A thin prism deflects light by a constant angle. A thin lens can be thought of as many thin prisms arranged base-to-base (convex) or tip-to-tip (concave). The deviation at each "prism" varies with distance from the axis, producing focusing.

**NEB exam focus:** Derive $\delta = (n-1)A$ from the general prism formula using the small-angle approximation. Calculate angular dispersion and dispersive power for thin prisms. Solve combination problems (achromatic and direct-vision).

**Numerical example — crown glass prism:** $A = 6°$, $n_r = 1.514$, $n_y = 1.517$, $n_v = 1.523$. $\delta_r = (1.514-1) \times 6 = 3.084°$. $\delta_y = 3.102°$. $\delta_v = 3.138°$. Angular dispersion $= 3.138 - 3.084 = 0.054°$. Dispersive power $\omega = 0.054/3.102 = 0.0174$.

**Reverse calculation — finding A from known δ:** If a thin prism produces a deviation of 3° for light of wavelength 589 nm and the material has $n = 1.52$: $A = \delta/(n-1) = 3°/0.52 = 5.77° \approx 5°46'$. This is a typical prism angle for measuring refractive index.
confusion: ❌ The thin-prism formula $\delta = (n-1)A$ works for ANY prism angle. ✅ It is only valid for small $A$ (typically $A \leq 10°$). For larger angles, use the full formula $n = \sin\frac{A+\delta}{2}/\sin\frac{A}{2}$.

❌ The deviation through a thin prism depends on the angle of incidence. ✅ For a thin prism, the deviation is approximately INDEPENDENT of the angle of incidence. This is a key distinguishing feature from a thick prism.

❌ A thin prism produces no dispersion. ✅ A thin prism DOES produce dispersion — different wavelengths deviate by slightly different amounts. The dispersion is smaller than for a thick prism, but it is nonzero.

❌ Two thin prisms always cancel each other's deviation. ✅ Two thin prisms can be arranged to cancel deviation (direct-vision) or cancel dispersion (achromatic), but not both simultaneously with the same materials.

❌ The dispersive power $\omega$ depends on the prism angle $A$. ✅ Dispersive power is a PROPERTY OF THE MATERIAL, not the prism geometry. $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ depends only on refractive indices.

❌ For a thin prism, $\delta_{min} \neq (n-1)A$. ✅ For a thin prism, $\delta_{min} \approx \delta \approx (n-1)A$. The minimum deviation is approximately the same as the deviation at any angle of incidence.

❌ A combination of two thin prisms can eliminate both deviation and dispersion. ✅ This is impossible with two prisms of different materials. You can eliminate dispersion (achromatic) OR deviation (direct-vision), but not both simultaneously.

data.title: Metals, Insulators and Semiconductors – Band Theory
notes: **Intrinsic semiconductor:** A pure semiconductor crystal with no significant impurity atoms (ppm or less). Examples: pure silicon ($99.9999999\\\\%$), pure germanium. At any finite temperature, thermal excitation creates equal numbers of electrons and holes: $n = p = n_i$.

**Extrinsic semiconductor:** A semiconductor deliberately doped with a small concentration of impurity atoms (typically $10^{15}\	ext{--}10^{18}\\\\,\	ext{cm}^{-3}$) to modify its electrical properties. Doping dramatically increases conductivity by orders of magnitude.

**n-type doping:** Pentavalent donor atoms (Group V: P, As, Sb) are substituted for silicon atoms. Each donor has 5 valence electrons; 4 form covalent bonds with neighboring Si atoms, leaving 1 extra electron loosely bound. The donor ionization energy $E_d \\\\approx 0.01\	ext{--}0.05\\\\,\	ext{eV}$ (much smaller than $E_g$), so nearly all donors are ionized at room temperature. Electrons are majority carriers; holes are minority carriers.

**p-type doping:** Trivalent acceptor atoms (Group III: B, Al, Ga) replace silicon atoms. Each acceptor has 3 valence electrons, creating a vacant bond (hole) in the lattice. The acceptor ionization energy $E_a \\\\approx 0.01\	ext{--}0.05\\\\,\	ext{eV}$. Holes are majority carriers; electrons are minority carriers.

**Mass-action law:** In thermal equilibrium, $np = n_i^2$ holds for any semiconductor (intrinsic or extrinsic). For an n-type sample with donor concentration $N_d$, $n \\\\approx N_d$ and $p \\\\approx n_i^2/N_d$.

**Carrier concentration:** At room temperature, all donors in n-type are ionized (freeze-out is negligible). data.title: Linear Expansion and Its Measurement
notes: **Linear expansion definition:** When a solid is heated, its length increases. The fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature is called the coefficient of linear expansion, $\alpha$.
**Formula:** $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$, where $L_0$ is the original length, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion (unit: K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹), and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change.

**New length:** $L = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. For small $\alpha\Delta T$, this is an excellent approximation. For large temperature ranges, $\alpha$ may vary and must be treated as a function of temperature.

**Physical origin:** Heating increases the amplitude of atomic vibrations in the lattice. Because the interatomic potential is asymmetric (steeper on the compression side), the average separation increases with temperature, causing expansion.

**Coefficient of linear expansion for common materials:** Steel: $\alpha \approx 12 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Aluminum: $\alpha \approx 24 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Copper: $\alpha \approx 17 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Invar (Fe-Ni alloy): $\alpha \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Quartz: $\alpha \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹.

**Why metals expand more:** Metals with weaker interatomic bonds (larger bond length, lower melting point) tend to have larger $\alpha$. Lead ($\alpha \approx 29 \times 10^{-6}$) expands more than steel because its atomic bonds are weaker.

**Bimetallic strip:** Two metals with different $\alpha$ bonded together bend when heated — the higher-$\alpha$ metal expands more, forcing the strip to curve. Used in thermostats, circuit breakers, and temperature indicators.

**Railway tracks — expansion gaps:** Steel rails expand by $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$. For a 12 m rail and $\Delta T = 40°C$: $\Delta L = 12 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 5.76$ mm. Gaps are left between rails to accommodate this expansion, otherwise buckling occurs.

**Measuring $\alpha$ — Searle's apparatus:** A metal rod is heated uniformly. The expansion is measured by a micrometer screw gauge. $\alpha = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0 \Delta T}$. The apparatus minimizes errors from thermal expansion of the frame.

**Measuring $\alpha$ — Hoke's apparatus:** Uses a glass tube filled with liquid. As the solid rod inside expands, it displaces liquid. The volume of displaced liquid gives $\Delta L$ indirectly. This is an elegant optical-mechanical method.

**NEB exam focus:** State the formula $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$. Explain the bimetallic strip principle. Describe Searle's apparatus for measuring $\alpha$. Solve numerical problems involving expansion of rods, bridges, and railways.

**Effect on precision instruments:** Clock pendulums expand with temperature, increasing their period and causing the clock to run slow. $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, so $\Delta T/T = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$. For steel ($\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$), a 10°C rise causes the clock to lose about 5 seconds per day.

**Composite rod problem:** Two rods of different materials joined end-to-end: total expansion $\Delta L = L_{01}\alpha_1\Delta T + L_{02}\alpha_2\Delta T$. The junction shifts by the expansion of the first rod.

**Thermal stress:** If a rod is constrained from expanding, thermal stress develops: $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$, where $Y$ is Young's modulus. For steel ($Y = 200$ GPa, $\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$), a 50°C constraint gives $\sigma = 120$ MPa — significant structural stress.

**Practical consequence:** Bridges have expansion joints. Glass bottles crack when hot water is poured in because the inner surface expands faster than the outer. Telephone wires sag more in summer than in winter.
confusion: ❌ $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$ works for any temperature range. ✅ It is valid only for moderate $\Delta T$ where $\alpha$ is approximately constant. For very large temperature ranges, $\alpha$ varies and the formula becomes approximate.

❌ All solids expand at the same rate. ✅ Different materials have very different $\alpha$ values. Invar ($\alpha \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$) expands 24 times less than aluminum ($\alpha \approx 24 \times 10^{-6}$).
❌ The coefficient $\alpha$ has units of temperature. ✅ $\alpha$ has units of K⁻¹ (or °C⁻¹). It is a fractional change per degree, not an absolute change.
❌ A hole in a metal plate shrinks when heated. ✅ The hole EXPANDS — the material around it expands outward, making the hole larger. This is equivalent to a disk of the same material expanding.
❌ Linear expansion applies to liquids. ✅ Liquids do not have a fixed shape, so linear expansion is meaningless for them. Only cubical (volume) expansion is defined for liquids.
❌ The expansion gap for railway tracks should be as large as possible. ✅ The gap must be just large enough to prevent buckling. Too large a gap causes excessive noise and wear at the joints.

❌ Thermal stress depends only on $\alpha$ and $\Delta T$. ✅ Thermal stress is $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$ — it also depends on Young's modulus $Y$. A stiffer material develops more stress for the same constraint.

notes: **Linear expansion definition:** When a solid is heated, its length increases. The fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature is called the coefficient of linear expansion, $\alpha$.
**Formula:** $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$, where $L_0$ is the original length, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion (unit: K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹), and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change.

**New length:** $L = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. For small $\alpha\Delta T$, this is an excellent approximation. For large temperature ranges, $\alpha$ may vary and must be treated as a function of temperature.

**Physical origin:** Heating increases the amplitude of atomic vibrations in the lattice. Because the interatomic potential is asymmetric (steeper on the compression side), the average separation increases with temperature, causing expansion.

**Coefficient of linear expansion for common materials:** Steel: $\alpha \approx 12 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Aluminum: $\alpha \approx 24 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Copper: $\alpha \approx 17 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Invar (Fe-Ni alloy): $\alpha \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Quartz: $\alpha \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹.

**Why metals expand more:** Metals with weaker interatomic bonds (larger bond length, lower melting point) tend to have larger $\alpha$. Lead ($\alpha \approx 29 \times 10^{-6}$) expands more than steel because its atomic bonds are weaker.

**Bimetallic strip:** Two metals with different $\alpha$ bonded together bend when heated — the higher-$\alpha$ metal expands more, forcing the strip to curve. Used in thermostats, circuit breakers, and temperature indicators.

**Railway tracks — expansion gaps:** Steel rails expand by $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$. For a 12 m rail and $\Delta T = 40°C$: $\Delta L = 12 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 5.76$ mm. Gaps are left between rails to accommodate this expansion, otherwise buckling occurs.

**Measuring $\alpha$ — Searle's apparatus:** A metal rod is heated uniformly. The expansion is measured by a micrometer screw gauge. $\alpha = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0 \Delta T}$. The apparatus minimizes errors from thermal expansion of the frame.

**Measuring $\alpha$ — Hoke's apparatus:** Uses a glass tube filled with liquid. As the solid rod inside expands, it displaces liquid. The volume of displaced liquid gives $\Delta L$ indirectly. This is an elegant optical-mechanical method.

**NEB exam focus:** State the formula $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$. Explain the bimetallic strip principle. Describe Searle's apparatus for measuring $\alpha$. Solve numerical problems involving expansion of rods, bridges, and railways.

**Effect on precision instruments:** Clock pendulums expand with temperature, increasing their period and causing the clock to run slow. $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, so $\Delta T/T = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$. For steel ($\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$), a 10°C rise causes the clock to lose about 5 seconds per day.

**Composite rod problem:** Two rods of different materials joined end-to-end: total expansion $\Delta L = L_{01}\alpha_1\Delta T + L_{02}\alpha_2\Delta T$. The junction shifts by the expansion of the first rod.

**Thermal stress:** If a rod is constrained from expanding, thermal stress develops: $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$, where $Y$ is Young's modulus. For steel ($Y = 200$ GPa, $\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$), a 50°C constraint gives $\sigma = 120$ MPa — significant structural stress.

**Practical consequence:** Bridges have expansion joints. Glass bottles crack when hot water is poured in because the inner surface expands faster than the outer. Telephone wires sag more in summer than in winter.
confusion: ❌ $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$ works for any temperature range. ✅ It is valid only for moderate $\Delta T$ where $\alpha$ is approximately constant. For very large temperature ranges, $\alpha$ varies and the formula becomes approximate.

❌ All solids expand at the same rate. ✅ Different materials have very different $\alpha$ values. Invar ($\alpha \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$) expands 24 times less than aluminum ($\alpha \approx 24 \times 10^{-6}$).
❌ The coefficient $\alpha$ has units of temperature. ✅ $\alpha$ has units of K⁻¹ (or °C⁻¹). It is a fractional change per degree, not an absolute change.
❌ A hole in a metal plate shrinks when heated. ✅ The hole EXPANDS — the material around it expands outward, making the hole larger. This is equivalent to a disk of the same material expanding.
❌ Linear expansion applies to liquids. ✅ Liquids do not have a fixed shape, so linear expansion is meaningless for them. Only cubical (volume) expansion is defined for liquids.
❌ The expansion gap for railway tracks should be as large as possible. ✅ The gap must be just large enough to prevent buckling. Too large a gap causes excessive noise and wear at the joints.

❌ Thermal stress depends only on $\alpha$ and $\Delta T$. ✅ Thermal stress is $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$ — it also depends on Young's modulus $Y$. A stiffer material develops more stress for the same constraint.

data.title: Scalars and Vectors
notes: **Scalars and vectors:** a scalar has only magnitude (mass, time, speed, energy, temperature); a vector has magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, electric field). Vectors are written $\vec{A}$ or bold **A**, with magnitude $|\vec{A}| = A$.

**The three addition laws** answer one question — 'what is the single vector that has the same effect as several together?' (1) **Triangle law** (two vectors): place them head-to-tail; the resultant runs from the free tail to the free head. (2) **Parallelogram law** (two vectors from one point): draw both from a common origin; the diagonal through that origin is the resultant. (3) **Polygon law** (three or more): place all head-to-tail in order; the closing side taken in reverse is the resultant.

**The master formula** (obtained from either the triangle or parallelogram derivation): $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$ with direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$. Every special case follows from it.

**Special cases from the master formula:** $\theta = 0°$: $R_{max} = P + Q$; $\theta = 90°$: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ (Pythagoras); $\theta = 180°$: $R_{min} = |P - Q|$; $P = Q$: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$ and the resultant bisects the angle; $P = Q$, $\theta = 120°$: $R = P$ — three equal forces at 120° are in equilibrium.

**Equilibrium:** vectors placed head-to-tail that close into a polygon give $\vec{R} = \vec{0}$ — the body is in equilibrium. For three concurrent forces this is the triangle of forces; quantitatively, **Lami's theorem**: $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$ (each force over the sine of the angle between the other two).

**Resultant vs equilibrant:** the resultant $\vec{R}$ replaces all vectors; the equilibrant $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$ balances them. Equal magnitude, opposite direction — a favourite 2-mark definition pair in NEB.

**Resolution connects the laws:** for many vectors the fastest route is resolving each into $x$ and $y$ components, then $R_x = \sum F_{ix}$, $R_y = \sum F_{iy}$, $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$. The polygon law is the graphical twin of this algebraic method.

**Bounds on the resultant:** $|P - Q| \le R \le P + Q$ for any angle — a quick sanity check and a frequent MCQ. For three vectors, $R$ lies between the sum and appropriate differences; a closed triangle guarantees $R = 0$.

data.title: Addition of Vectors — Same and Opposite Directions
notes: **Definition:** The cross product (vector product) of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is a vector $\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ whose magnitude is $AB\sin\theta$ and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Magnitude:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$).

**Direction — right-hand rule:** Point the fingers of your right hand in the direction of $\vec{A}$, then curl them toward $\vec{B}$. Your thumb points in the direction of $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$. The result is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Unit vector form:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, given by the right-hand rule.

**Case 1 — Parallel vectors ($\theta = 0°$ or $180°$):** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$. Parallel (or anti-parallel) vectors have zero cross product. This is the condition for parallelism: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0 \iff \vec{A} \parallel \vec{B}$.
**Case 2 — Perpendicular vectors ($\theta = 90°$):** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB$ (maximum possible magnitude). Perpendicular vectors produce the largest cross product.

**Non-commutative property:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order reverses the direction. The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE, unlike the dot product which is commutative.

**Cross products of unit vectors:** $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0$. Cyclic: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$. Anti-cyclic: $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$.
**Distributive property:** $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{A} \times \vec{C}$. The cross product distributes over vector addition.

**Physical applications:** (1) Torque: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. (2) Magnetic force: $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$. (3) Angular momentum: $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. (4) Linear velocity: $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$.

**NEB exam focus:** Define the cross product. State the right-hand rule. Calculate cross products of given vectors. Distinguish between dot product (scalar result) and cross product (vector result). Solve torque and magnetic force problems.

**Comparison with dot product:** Dot product: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ (scalar, commutative). Cross product: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$ (vector, anti-commutative). The dot product measures "sameness" (projection); the cross product measures "perpendicularity" (area).
**Geometric interpretation:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$ equals the AREA of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. The direction of the cross product is normal to this parallelogram.

**Cross product and motion:** If $\vec{v}$ is the velocity and $\vec{r}$ is the position vector, then $\vec{r} \times \vec{v}$ is twice the areal velocity (area swept per unit time). This is the basis of Kepler's second law.

**Scalar triple product:** $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ gives the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors. It is cyclic: $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = \vec{B} \cdot (\vec{C} \times \vec{A}) = \vec{C} \cdot (\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$.
confusion: ❌ The cross product gives a scalar. ✅ The cross product gives a VECTOR. The result is perpendicular to both input vectors. The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a vector.
❌ $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$. ✅ The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order flips the direction by 180°.

❌ The cross product is defined for any number of vectors. ✅ The cross product is defined only for EXACTLY TWO vectors in 3D space. You cannot take $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} \times \vec{C}$ without parentheses — it is not associative.

❌ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ must be zero vectors. ✅ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then either $\vec{A} = 0$, $\vec{B} = 0$, OR $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are PARALLEL. Any one of these conditions makes the cross product zero.

❌ The right-hand rule is arbitrary and any convention works. ✅ The right-hand rule is a CONVENTION, but it must be consistent throughout physics. Using the left-hand rule would flip the sign of torque, angular momentum, and magnetic force, causing contradictions.

❌ $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. ✅ The cross product is NOT ASSOCIATIVE. In general, $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) \neq (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. The vector triple product identity is: $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{C})\vec{B} - (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B})\vec{C}$.

❌ The cross product exists in 2D. ✅ The cross product is defined in 3D (and 7D with special structure). In 2D, you can compute a "pseudo-cross product" that gives a scalar ($A_x B_y - A_y B_x$), but this is not a true vector cross product.

data.title: Scalar and Vector Products
notes: **Scalars and vectors:** a scalar has only magnitude (mass, time, speed, energy, temperature); a vector has magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, electric field). Vectors are written $\vec{A}$ or bold **A**, with magnitude $|\vec{A}| = A$.

**The three addition laws** answer one question — 'what is the single vector that has the same effect as several together?' (1) **Triangle law** (two vectors): place them head-to-tail; the resultant runs from the free tail to the free head. (2) **Parallelogram law** (two vectors from one point): draw both from a common origin; the diagonal through that origin is the resultant. (3) **Polygon law** (three or more): place all head-to-tail in order; the closing side taken in reverse is the resultant.

**The master formula** (obtained from either the triangle or parallelogram derivation): $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$ with direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$. Every special case follows from it.

**Special cases from the master formula:** $\theta = 0°$: $R_{max} = P + Q$; $\theta = 90°$: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ (Pythagoras); $\theta = 180°$: $R_{min} = |P - Q|$; $P = Q$: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$ and the resultant bisects the angle; $P = Q$, $\theta = 120°$: $R = P$ — three equal forces at 120° are in equilibrium.

**Resultant vs equilibrant:** the resultant $\vec{R}$ replaces all vectors; the equilibrant $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$ balances them. Equal magnitude, opposite direction — a favourite 2-mark definition pair in NEB.

data.title: Resolution of a Vector
notes: **Definition:** The cross product (vector product) of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is a vector $\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ whose magnitude is $AB\sin\theta$ and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Magnitude:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$).

**Direction — right-hand rule:** Point the fingers of your right hand in the direction of $\vec{A}$, then curl them toward $\vec{B}$. Your thumb points in the direction of $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$. The result is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Unit vector form:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, given by the right-hand rule.

**Case 1 — Parallel vectors ($\theta = 0°$ or $180°$):** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$. Parallel (or anti-parallel) vectors have zero cross product. This is the condition for parallelism: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0 \iff \vec{A} \parallel \vec{B}$.
**Case 2 — Perpendicular vectors ($\theta = 90°$):** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB$ (maximum possible magnitude). Perpendicular vectors produce the largest cross product.

**Non-commutative property:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order reverses the direction. The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE, unlike the dot product which is commutative.

**Cross products of unit vectors:** $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0$. Cyclic: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$. Anti-cyclic: $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$.
**Distributive property:** $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{A} \times \vec{C}$. The cross product distributes over vector addition.

**Physical applications:** (1) Torque: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. (2) Magnetic force: $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$. (3) Angular momentum: $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. (4) Linear velocity: $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$.

**NEB exam focus:** Define the cross product. State the right-hand rule. Calculate cross products of given vectors. Distinguish between dot product (scalar result) and cross product (vector result). Solve torque and magnetic force problems.

**Comparison with dot product:** Dot product: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ (scalar, commutative). Cross product: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$ (vector, anti-commutative). The dot product measures "sameness" (projection); the cross product measures "perpendicularity" (area).
**Geometric interpretation:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$ equals the AREA of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. The direction of the cross product is normal to this parallelogram.

**Cross product and motion:** If $\vec{v}$ is the velocity and $\vec{r}$ is the position vector, then $\vec{r} \times \vec{v}$ is twice the areal velocity (area swept per unit time). This is the basis of Kepler's second law.

**Scalar triple product:** $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ gives the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors. It is cyclic: $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = \vec{B} \cdot (\vec{C} \times \vec{A}) = \vec{C} \cdot (\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$.
confusion: ❌ The cross product gives a scalar. ✅ The cross product gives a VECTOR. The result is perpendicular to both input vectors. The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a vector.
❌ $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$. ✅ The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order flips the direction by 180°.

❌ The cross product is defined for any number of vectors. ✅ The cross product is defined only for EXACTLY TWO vectors in 3D space. You cannot take $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} \times \vec{C}$ without parentheses — it is not associative.

❌ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ must be zero vectors. ✅ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then either $\vec{A} = 0$, $\vec{B} = 0$, OR $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are PARALLEL. Any one of these conditions makes the cross product zero.

❌ The right-hand rule is arbitrary and any convention works. ✅ The right-hand rule is a CONVENTION, but it must be consistent throughout physics. Using the left-hand rule would flip the sign of torque, angular momentum, and magnetic force, causing contradictions.

❌ $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. ✅ The cross product is NOT ASSOCIATIVE. In general, $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) \neq (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. The vector triple product identity is: $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{C})\vec{B} - (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B})\vec{C}$.

❌ The cross product exists in 2D. ✅ The cross product is defined in 3D (and 7D with special structure). In 2D, you can compute a "pseudo-cross product" that gives a scalar ($A_x B_y - A_y B_x$), but this is not a true vector cross product.

data.title: Unit Vector — Definition and Worked Example
notes: **Scalars and vectors:** a scalar has only magnitude (mass, time, speed, energy, temperature); a vector has magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, electric field). Vectors are written $\vec{A}$ or bold **A**, with magnitude $|\vec{A}| = A$.

**The three addition laws** answer one question — 'what is the single vector that has the same effect as several together?' (1) **Triangle law** (two vectors): place them head-to-tail; the resultant runs from the free tail to the free head. (2) **Parallelogram law** (two vectors from one point): draw both from a common origin; the diagonal through that origin is the resultant. (3) **Polygon law** (three or more): place all head-to-tail in order; the closing side taken in reverse is the resultant.

**The master formula** (obtained from either the triangle or parallelogram derivation): $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$ with direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$. Every special case follows from it.

**Special cases from the master formula:** $\theta = 0°$: $R_{max} = P + Q$; $\theta = 90°$: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ (Pythagoras); $\theta = 180°$: $R_{min} = |P - Q|$; $P = Q$: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$ and the resultant bisects the angle; $P = Q$, $\theta = 120°$: $R = P$ — three equal forces at 120° are in equilibrium.

**Equilibrium:** vectors placed head-to-tail that close into a polygon give $\vec{R} = \vec{0}$ — the body is in equilibrium. For three concurrent forces this is the triangle of forces; quantitatively, **Lami's theorem**: $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$ (each force over the sine of the angle between the other two).

**Resultant vs equilibrant:** the resultant $\vec{R}$ replaces all vectors; the equilibrant $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$ balances them. Equal magnitude, opposite direction — a favourite 2-mark definition pair in NEB.

**Resolution connects the laws:** for many vectors the fastest route is resolving each into $x$ and $y$ components, then $R_x = \sum F_{ix}$, $R_y = \sum F_{iy}$, $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$. The polygon law is the graphical twin of this algebraic method.

**Bounds on the resultant:** $|P - Q| \le R \le P + Q$ for any angle — a quick sanity check and a frequent MCQ. For three vectors, $R$ lies between the sum and appropriate differences; a closed triangle guarantees $R = 0$.

**Choosing a method:** (1) two vectors with a known angle → master formula; (2) perpendicular components → Pythagoras; (3) three or more vectors, roughly at right angles → component method; (4) checking equilibrium → closed polygon / Lami's theorem; (5) graphical answer required → scale drawing (parallelogram or polygon).

**NEB exam focus:** state and prove the triangle/parallelogram law; derive $R$ and $\alpha$; solve numericals on resultant and equilibrium; state Lami's theorem; define equilibrant; find the angle between two equal vectors whose resultant equals either vector ($120°$).
formulas: Master formula: $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$
Direction: $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$
Equal vectors: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$; $R = P$ when $\theta = 120°$
Bounds: $|P - Q| \le R \le P + Q$
Lami's theorem (equilibrium of 3 concurrent forces): $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$
Equilibrant: $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$
confusion: ❌ 'The triangle law and parallelogram law give different resultants.' ✅ They are mathematically EQUIVALENT — the triangle is half the parallelogram, so the same diagonal/resultant appears in both.

❌ Measuring the angle between the two sides INSIDE the parallelogram. ✅ $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors placed TAIL-TO-TAIL at the common origin — not the parallelogram's obtuse interior angle.

❌ 'The resultant of three vectors is always bigger than each.' ✅ Not necessarily — vectors can partially or fully cancel; a closed polygon gives $\vec{R} = \vec{0}$, smaller than every individual magnitude.
❌ 'The equilibrant is another name for the resultant.' ✅ They are OPPOSITE: equilibrant $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$. Same magnitude, opposite direction — the force that balances the system.
❌ Applying Lami's theorem to any three forces. ✅ Lami's theorem applies ONLY to three CONCURRENT forces IN EQUILIBRIUM; each force is divided by the sine of the angle between the OTHER two.
❌ 'Adding vectors means adding magnitudes.' ✅ $|\vec{P} + \vec{Q}| \ne P + Q$ in general; only the cross-term $2PQ\cos\theta$ distinguishes vector addition from arithmetic addition.

data.title: Cross Product — Component Form and Area of Parallelogram
notes: **Component form of cross product:** For $\vec{A} = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B_1\hat{i} + B_2\hat{j} + B_3\hat{k}$: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ A_1 & A_2 & A_3 \\ B_1 & B_2 & B_3 \end{vmatrix}$.
**Expanded form:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (A_2B_3 - A_3B_2)\hat{i} + (A_3B_1 - A_1B_3)\hat{j} + (A_1B_2 - A_2B_1)\hat{k}$. Note the cyclic pattern and the negative sign on the $\hat{j}$ component.

**Memory trick (Sarrus' rule):** Write the first two columns again to the right: $\begin{array}{ccc|cc} A_1 & A_2 & A_3 & A_1 & A_2 \\ B_1 & B_2 & B_3 & B_1 & B_2 \end{array}$. The $\hat{i}$ component comes from the diagonal $A_2B_3 - A_3B_2$. The $\hat{j}$ component uses the middle diagonal with a minus sign: $-(A_1B_3 - A_3B_1)$. The $\hat{k}$ component uses $A_1B_2 - A_2B_1$.

**Area of parallelogram:** The magnitude of the cross product equals the AREA of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors: $\text{Area} = |\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$. This is because the base is $A$ and the height is $B\sin\theta$.

**Area of triangle:** The area of the triangle formed by two vectors is HALF the parallelogram area: $\text{Area}_{\triangle} = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$. This is because the triangle is exactly half of the parallelogram.

**Worked example:** Find $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ for $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$. $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i}(4 - 6) - \hat{j}(8 + 3) + \hat{k}(-4 - 1) = -2\hat{i} - 11\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$.

**Area calculation example:** For $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i}(8 + 9) - \hat{j}(4 - 6) + \hat{k}(-3 - 4) = 17\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$. Area of parallelogram $= \sqrt{289 + 4 + 49} = \sqrt{342} \approx 18.5$ sq units. Area of triangle $= \sqrt{342}/2 \approx 9.25$ sq units.

**Perpendicularity property:** The cross product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ is perpendicular to BOTH $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. This can be verified: $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) = 0$ and $\vec{B} \cdot (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) = 0$. This property is used to find normal vectors to planes.

**Normal to a plane:** If two non-parallel vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ lie in a plane, then $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ is normal (perpendicular) to that plane. This is used to find the equation of a plane: $\vec{n} \cdot (\vec{r} - \vec{r_0}) = 0$, where $\vec{n} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$.

**NEB exam focus:** Compute cross products using the determinant method. Calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles using cross products. Find normal vectors to planes. Verify perpendicularity using dot products.

**Physical application — torque:** Torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. The magnitude $\tau = rF\sin\theta$ gives the turning effect. The direction (along the axis of rotation) follows the right-hand rule. A wrench applying force perpendicular to its handle ($\theta = 90°$) gives maximum torque.

**Physical application — magnetic force:** The magnetic force on a moving charge is $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$. The force is perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field. This causes charged particles to move in circular or helical paths in magnetic fields.

**Physical application — angular momentum:** $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p} = m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$. Angular momentum is conserved in the absence of external torque. This conservation explains why ice skaters spin faster when they pull their arms in.

**Physical application — linear velocity in rotation:** For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$, the linear velocity of a point at position $\vec{r}$ is $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$. This relates rotational motion to translational motion.

**Cross product in 2D:** In 2D, the cross product of $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = B_x\hat{i} + B_y\hat{j}$ gives $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (A_x B_y - A_y B_x)\hat{k}$. The scalar $A_x B_y - A_y B_x$ is called the 2D "perp dot product" and equals the signed area of the parallelogram.
confusion: ❌ The cross product of two vectors is a scalar. ✅ The cross product is a VECTOR. Its magnitude is a scalar (the area), but the result itself is a vector perpendicular to both input vectors.

❌ $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$. ✅ The cross product is anti-commutative: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. The two results have the same magnitude but opposite directions.

❌ The area of the parallelogram is $|\vec{A}| \cdot |\vec{B}|$. ✅ The area is $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$. The dot product $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ gives a different quantity (projection-related, not area).

❌ You can cancel vectors in a cross product: if $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{A} \times \vec{C}$, then $\vec{B} = \vec{C}$. ✅ You CANNOT cancel. $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} - \vec{C}) = 0$ means $\vec{B} - \vec{C}$ is parallel to $\vec{A}$, not necessarily zero. $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{C}$ could be different vectors both parallel to $\vec{A}$.
❌ The $\hat{j}$ component of the cross product has a positive sign. ✅ The $\hat{j}$ component has a NEGATIVE sign: $-(A_1B_3 - A_3B_1) = A_3B_1 - A_1B_3$. This is a common source of sign errors.

❌ The cross product is associative: $(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C} = \vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$. ✅ The cross product is NOT associative. The two expressions give different results. Always use parentheses to specify the order.

❌ If $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = 0$, then both vectors must be zero. ✅ If the cross product magnitude is zero, the vectors are PARALLEL (or one is zero). Non-zero parallel vectors have zero cross product.

data.title: Work Done by a Constant Force and a Variable Force
notes: **Definition of work (constant force):** $W = F s \\\\cos\	heta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the constant force, $s$ is the displacement, and $\	heta$ is the angle between the force vector and displacement vector. Work is a scalar quantity - it has magnitude but no direction.

**Sign of work:** Work is POSITIVE when $0^\\\\circ \\\\le \	heta < 90^\\\\circ$ (force component along displacement). Work is ZERO when $\	heta = 90^\\\\circ$ (force perpendicular to displacement, e.g., centripetal force, normal force on horizontal surface). Work is NEGATIVE when $90^\\\\circ < \	heta \\\\le 180^\\\\circ$ (force opposes displacement, e.g., kinetic friction, gravity when lifting).

**Work by multiple forces:** Total work is the sum of works by individual forces: $W_{\	ext{net}} = \\\\sum W_i = \\\\sum F_i s \\\\cos\	heta_i$. This is equivalent to the work done by the net force: $W_{\	ext{net}} = F_{\	ext{net}} s \\\\cos\	heta_{\	ext{net}}$.

**Variable force definition:** When force varies with position, work is the integral of force over the displacement: $W = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \\\\, dx$ (for 1D motion). Graphically, this is the area under the $F$ vs $x$ curve between the initial and final positions.

**Work by a spring force (Hooke's law):** For an ideal spring, $F = -kx$. Work done BY the spring when moving from $x_i$ to $x_f$: $W_{\	ext{spring}} = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} (-kx) dx = \ rac{1}{2}k x_i^2 - \ rac{1}{2}k x_f^2$. Work done ON the spring (by external agent) is the negative of this.

**Work by gravity (near Earth):** Gravity is a constant force $F_g = mg$ downward. If an object moves vertically by $\\\\Delta y$ (up positive), $W_g = -mg \\\\Delta y$. If it moves horizontally, $W_g = 0$. For a path with vertical drop $h$, $W_g = +mgh$ (gravity does positive work).

**Work by a constant force in 2D/3D:** $W = \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot \\\\vec{s} = F_x s_x + F_y s_y + F_z s_z$. Only the component of force parallel to displacement contributes. This dot product form is frame-independent.

**Work-energy connection (preview):** The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\	ext{net}} = \\\\Delta K = \ rac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \ rac{1}{2}mv_i^2$. This is the work-energy theorem, derived from Newton's second law.

**Path dependence for variable forces:** For a variable force, work depends on the path taken. For conservative forces (gravity, spring), work is path-independent and equals $-\\\\Delta U$. For non-conservative forces (friction), work depends on the actual path length.

**Graphical interpretation:** The area under the $F$-$x$ curve (with sign) gives the work. Positive area = positive work; negative area = negative work. For a spring, the $F$-$x$ graph is a straight line through origin with slope $k$, and the area is a triangle $\ rac{1}{2}kx^2$.

**Work by a varying force in 2D:** $W = \\\\int_C \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r} = \\\\int_C (F_x dx + F_y dy)$. This is a line integral. For a force $\\\\vec{F}(x,y)$, the work along path C depends on the specific curve C unless $\\\\vec{F}$ is conservative ($\
abla \	imes \\\\vec{F} = 0$).

**Constant force vs variable force summary:** Constant force: $W = F s \\\\cos\	heta$ (simple product). Variable force: $W = \\\\int F(x) dx$ (area under curve). Both are special cases of the general definition $W = \\\\int \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r}$.

**Example - work by gravity on an incline:** Block slides down incline of angle $\	heta$, length $L$. Vertical drop $h = L \\\\sin\	heta$. Work by gravity: $W_g = mgh = mgL \\\\sin\	heta$. This equals force component parallel to incline ($mg\\\\sin\	heta$) times distance $L$.

**Example - work by external agent stretching a spring:** Slowly stretch spring from 0 to $x$ (quasi-static, acceleration $\\\\approx 0$). Applied force $F_{\	ext{app}} = +kx$ (matches spring force). Work done: $W = \\\\int_0^x kx dx = \ rac{1}{2}kx^2$. This energy is STORED as elastic potential energy in the spring.
confusion: Work is NOT force times distance in general - it is force component in the direction of displacement times distance. $W = F s$ only when force and displacement are parallel ($	heta = 0$). Many students forget the $\\\cos\	heta$ factor.

Work done BY a force vs work done ON an object: $W_{\	ext{by}} = -W_{\	ext{on}}$. The work-energy theorem uses $W_{\	ext{net}}$ (work done BY all forces ON the object). Work done BY the object on something else is the negative.

Holding a heavy object stationary: You exert a force, but displacement is zero, so $W = 0$! You get tired because your muscles do internal biochemical work (energy conversion), not mechanical work on the object. This is a classic misconception.

Centripetal force does NO work: $F_c$ is always perpendicular to velocity (displacement), so $\\\\cos 90^\\\\circ = 0$. It changes direction, not speed. A planet in circular orbit around the Sun has zero work done by gravity.

For a variable force, you CANNOT just multiply 'average force' by distance unless you know the average is the integral average. The correct method is always integration or graphical area. A common error: averaging endpoints $\ rac{F_i + F_f}{2}$ only works for linear forces.

data.title: Conservation of Energy
notes: **Law of conservation of energy:** Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another or transferred between systems. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant over time.

**Mechanical energy conservation:** When only conservative forces (gravity, spring force, electrostatic force) act on a system, mechanical energy E = K + U is conserved: ΔK + ΔU = 0, or K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

**Potential energy types:** Gravitational PE near Earth: U_g = mgh (h = height above reference). Elastic PE of a spring: U_s = ½kx² (x = compression/extension from natural length). For a universal gravitational field: U = -GMm/r.

**Non-conservative forces and energy loss:** Friction, air resistance, and viscous drag are non-conservative. They convert mechanical energy into thermal energy (heat). Work done by non-conservative forces: W_nc = ΔE_mech = E_final - E_initial.

**Total energy conservation including heat:** Even with friction, total energy is conserved if you include thermal energy: ΔK + ΔU + ΔE_thermal = 0. The first law of thermodynamics: ΔU_internal = Q - W, where Q is heat added, W is work done BY the system.

**Pendulum energy conservation:** For a simple pendulum (mass m, length L, angle θ): At the bottom, K = ½mv², U = 0. At the extremes, v = 0, K = 0, U = mgL(1-cosθ). With no air resistance: ½mv² + mgL(1-cosθ) = constant.
**Spring-mass system:** For a mass m on a spring with constant k: At equilibrium, K = ½mv², U = 0. At max extension x = A, v = 0, K = 0, U = ½kA². Energy oscillates: ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA² = constant.

**Roller coaster physics:** At the top of a hill, the car has maximum PE (mgh) and minimum KE. At the bottom, maximum KE and minimum PE. Total energy constant (neglecting friction). Minimum speed at top of vertical loop: v ≥ √(gr) to stay on track.

**Energy in collisions:** In elastic collisions, both momentum and KE are conserved. In inelastic collisions, momentum is conserved but KE is not (some converts to heat/sound). In perfectly inelastic collisions, objects stick together and KE loss is maximum.

**Conservation of energy in nuclear reactions:** Mass-energy equivalence E = mc² shows mass is another form of energy. In nuclear fission/fusion, the total mass of products is less than reactants — the mass defect Δm appears as kinetic energy of products: ΔE = Δmc².
**Power and energy relationship:** Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = dE/dt. If power is constant, E = Pt. If power varies, E = ∫P dt. Energy delivered is the area under the P-t curve.

**Real-world energy transformations:** Chemical energy (fuel) → thermal (burning) → mechanical (engine) → electrical (generator) → electromagnetic (light) → thermal (absorber). At each step, some energy becomes heat (second law).

**Reference point for potential energy:** Gravitational PE is defined relative to a chosen zero level. The choice is arbitrary — only differences in PE matter. Usually we set U = 0 at the lowest point in the problem or at ground level.
formulas: Mechanical energy conservation: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f (only conservative forces)
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²
Work by non-conservative forces: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i)
Gravitational PE: U_g = mgh (near Earth); U = −GMm/r (universal)
Elastic PE: U_s = ½kx²; total spring energy: ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA²
confusion: Energy is NOT created or destroyed — it only transforms. When a pendulum stops swinging due to friction, the energy doesn't 'disappear'; it becomes thermal energy in the air and the pivot. The FIRST law of thermodynamics says energy is conserved in all processes.

Conservation of mechanical energy (K + U = constant) ONLY holds when ALL forces are conservative. If there is ANY friction, air resistance, or non-conservative force, mechanical energy is NOT conserved. You must include W_nc or track thermal energy.

Potential energy is NOT absolute — it is defined relative to an arbitrary zero point. A ball on a table has U = mgh relative to the floor, but U = mg(h+H) relative to the basement. Only PE differences matter physically.

In a collision, momentum is ALWAYS conserved (if no external forces). Kinetic energy is ONLY conserved in perfectly ELASTIC collisions. Many students think KE is always conserved in collisions — it is NOT. Real collisions are usually somewhat inelastic.

The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) and energy conservation (ΔK + ΔU = -W_nc) are DIFFERENT. The first is about NET work changing kinetic energy. The second is about total mechanical energy. With conservative forces, W_net = -ΔU, so W_net + ΔU = ΔK, which is the work-energy theorem.

data.title: Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces
notes: **Conservative force definition:** A force is conservative if the work done by it depends ONLY on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. Equivalently, the work done around any closed loop is zero: ∮F·dr = 0.

**Path independence:** For a conservative force, W = U_i - U_f = -(U_f - U_i) = -ΔU. The work is the negative of the change in potential energy. This means we can define a potential energy function U(r) such that F = -∇U (force is the negative gradient of potential).
**Examples of conservative forces:** Gravity (near Earth: F = -mg, U = mgh), spring force (F = -kx, U = ½kx²), electrostatic force (F = kQq/r², U = kQq/r), uniform electric field (F = qE, U = qEy).

**Non-conservative force definition:** A force is non-conservative if the work done depends on the path taken. The work around a closed loop is NOT zero: ∮F·dr ≠ 0. Energy is dissipated as heat or sound.

**Examples of non-conservative forces:** Kinetic friction (F_f = μN, work = -μN × distance traveled — depends on path length!), air resistance/viscous drag (proportional to v or v², opposes motion), rolling friction, human muscle force (metabolic energy not recoverable).

**Potential energy association:** Conservative forces ALLOW the definition of potential energy because the work done against them is stored and recoverable. Non-conservative forces do NOT have an associated potential energy — the energy is lost from the mechanical system.

**Closed loop test:** Take any closed path. For gravity: lift a mass up height h (W = -mgh), lower it down (W = +mgh). Net work = 0. For friction: slide a block around a closed square (perimeter = 4L). Each side does work = -μmgL. Net work = -4μmgL ≠ 0.

**Mixed force systems:** When both conservative and non-conservative forces act, use: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) - (K_i + U_i). This is the most general energy equation for mechanical systems. If W_nc = 0, mechanical energy is conserved.

**Energy dissipated by friction:** For a block sliding distance d with kinetic friction μ_k, the thermal energy generated is Q = μ_k N d. This comes from the work done BY friction: W_f = -μ_k N d. The mechanical energy lost equals the heat generated.

**Conservative force and curl:** In 3D, a force F is conservative iff its curl is zero: ∇ × F = 0 (everywhere in a simply connected region). This is a mathematical test — if the force field has no circulation, it is conservative.

**Electrostatic force is conservative:** The work done by an electrostatic field depends only on endpoints. This allows defining electric potential V = U/q and voltage differences. The electric field is the negative gradient: E = -∇V.

**Why it matters for problem solving:** If all forces are conservative, use K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f (simple). If non-conservative forces are present, use W_nc = ΔE_mech. Always identify which forces are conservative and which are not.
formulas: Conservative force: work depends only on endpoints; ∮F·dr = 0 (closed loop)
Non-conservative force: work depends on path; ∮F·dr ≠ 0
Work-energy relation: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i)
Conservative force and PE: W = −ΔU (work = negative change in potential energy)
Friction work: W_f = −μNd (always negative; energy dissipated as heat)
confusion: Friction does NOT have a potential energy. Many students try to write U_friction = μmgx or something similar. This is WRONG — friction is non-conservative, and the energy it 'removes' from the mechanical system becomes heat, not stored potential energy.

A force being 'conservative' does NOT mean the total energy of the system is conserved. It means mechanical energy can be conserved IF that force is the ONLY force doing work. If you have conservative forces PLUS non-conservative forces, mechanical energy is not conserved even though some forces are conservative.

Normal force and tension are NOT conservative forces — they are constraint forces that do zero work (they are perpendicular to displacement). They don't appear in the energy equation because W = 0, not because they have potential energy.

The term 'non-conservative' does NOT mean 'energy is destroyed.' It means mechanical energy is converted to other forms (heat, sound) that are NOT tracked by potential energy. Total energy is ALWAYS conserved (first law).
Air resistance (drag) is non-conservative. The work done by drag depends on the path (speed profile). You CANNOT define a 'drag potential energy.' The energy lost to drag becomes heat in the air.

data.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
notes: **Elastic collision:** A collision in which both total momentum AND total kinetic energy are conserved. The bodies rebound without permanent deformation, no sound/heat is produced. The relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation: v₂ - v₁ = u₁ - u₂.

**Inelastic collision:** A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is NOT conserved. Some kinetic energy is converted to internal energy (heat, sound, deformation). The coefficient of restitution e < 1.

**Perfectly inelastic collision:** The extreme case where the colliding bodies stick together after collision and move with a common velocity. Momentum is conserved; KE loss is maximum (but not 100% because momentum must be conserved, so some KE remains as center-of-mass motion).

**One-dimensional elastic collision formulas:** For masses m₁, m₂ with initial velocities u₁, u₂: v₁ = (m₁-m₂)u₁/(m₁+m₂) + 2m₂u₂/(m₁+m₂), v₂ = (m₂-m₁)u₂/(m₁+m₂) + 2m₁u₁/(m₁+m₂). These come from conservation of momentum + conservation of KE.

**Special case — equal masses (m₁ = m₂) in elastic collision:** The masses exchange velocities! v₁ = u₂, v₂ = u₁. If m₂ was initially at rest (u₂ = 0), then v₁ = 0 (first mass stops) and v₂ = u₁ (second mass moves off with the first mass's original speed).

**Special case — very massive m₁, stationary m₂ (m₁ ≫ m₂, u₂ = 0):** m₁ barely slows: v₁ ≈ u₁. m₂ shoots forward at v₂ ≈ 2u₁ (twice the initial speed). This is how a golf club hits a ball, or a bat hits a baseball.

**Coefficient of restitution (e):** e = (relative speed of separation) / (relative speed of approach) = (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂). For perfectly elastic: e = 1. For perfectly inelastic: e = 0. For inelastic: 0 < e < 1. e depends on the materials (e.g., tennis ball on concrete: e ≈ 0.75; steel on steel: e ≈ 0.9; putty: e ≈ 0).

**Energy loss in inelastic collisions:** ΔK = K_f - K_i = -½ μ v_rel² (1 - e²), where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) is the reduced mass and v_rel = u₁ - u₂ is the relative velocity. The energy lost goes to heat, sound, and permanent deformation.

**Two-dimensional collisions:** Momentum is conserved as a vector: p_x and p_y separately. For elastic collisions, KE is also conserved. The scattering angles depend on the impact parameter. Center-of-mass frame analysis often simplifies 2D collisions.

**Center-of-mass frame:** In the CM frame, total momentum is zero. In an elastic collision, the speeds of particles don't change, only their directions change. The scattering is isotropic for identical particles in the CM frame.

**Real-world applications:** Car crash safety (crumple zones increase collision time, reduce force — KE is dissipated controllably). Billiards (nearly elastic). Newton's cradle (demonstrates momentum and energy transfer through elastic collisions). Sports (baseball, tennis, golf — coefficient of restitution of ball/racket/club matters).

**Explosion — reverse collision:** An object at rest splits into fragments with kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved (total momentum before = 0, after = 0). KE after > KE before — the energy comes from internal chemical/nuclear energy stored in the object. This is a 'reverse' inelastic collision.
formulas: Elastic collision (1D): v₁ = [(m₁−m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁+m₂); v₂ = [(m₂−m₁)u₂ + 2m₁u₁]/(m₁+m₂)
Perfectly inelastic: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁+m₂)v (common velocity v)
Coefficient of restitution: e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂) = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach
KE loss in inelastic collision: ΔK = ½μv_rel²(1 − e²), where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)
Equal mass elastic (one at rest): v₁ = 0, v₂ = u₁ (velocities exchanged)
confusion: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects DO NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy. They lose the MAXIMUM possible KE consistent with momentum conservation. The center-of-mass kinetic energy (½Mv_cm²) MUST remain because momentum is conserved. Only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.

The coefficient of restitution e is NOT the ratio of final to initial KE. e = (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂) is the ratio of relative speeds. The fraction of KE retained is e² (for equal masses) or a more complex formula for unequal masses. Many students confuse e with KE ratio.

Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in an isolated system (no external forces). Kinetic energy is ONLY conserved in perfectly elastic collisions. Students often think KE is always conserved in collisions — it is NOT. Real collisions are usually somewhat inelastic (0 < e < 1).

For a ball bouncing on the floor: The floor/earth is so massive it doesn't move. The ball's speed before and after impact relates by e = v_after/v_before. The ball loses (1-e²) of its KE each bounce. The floor provides the impulse to change momentum; the earth's recoil is negligible.

A collision where kinetic energy is 'gained' (superelastic) is possible if internal energy is released (explosion, chemical reaction, spring release). These are NOT standard collisions and require tracking internal energy changes.

data.title: Work Done by Constant and Variable Force
notes: **Work done by a constant force:** W = F·d·cos θ = Fd cos θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, J = N·m). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (θ < 90°), negative when opposite (θ > 90°), and zero when perpendicular (θ = 90°).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the F-x graph, or mathematically, W = ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂. For a spring force F = −kx, the work done by the spring when stretched from x₁ to x₂ is W = ½k(x₁² − x₂²).

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f), where Δh is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls (h decreases) and negative work when it rises (h increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** W_s = ½kx² (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by x). The spring does work W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) when it returns from x_i to x_f. At the natural length (x = 0), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** W_f = −f_k·d = −μ_k·N·d. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length d, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force (W = Fd cos θ), work done by a spring (W = ½kx²), work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK), area under F-x graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.
formulas: Work by constant force: W = Fd cos θ (positive when θ < 90°, negative when θ > 90°, zero when θ = 90°)
Work by variable force: W = ∫ F(x) dx (area under F-x graph)
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu²
Work by gravity: W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f) (path-independent)
Work by spring: W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) (spring force F = −kx)
confusion: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.
❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).
❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.
❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).
❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.
