data.title: Cell Biology & Biomolecules
notes: **Cell theory:** all living organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
**Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells:** prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, ER, Golgi bodies.
**Mitochondrion:** powerhouse of the cell — site of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis; has its own circular DNA (semi-autonomous organelle).

**Biomolecules:** carbohydrates (energy source; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆), proteins (made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds), lipids (fats/oils; concentrated energy store), nucleic acids (DNA/RNA carry hereditary information).
**Enzymes** are globular protein catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy; they are substrate-specific and work best at optimum temperature and pH.
confusion: ❌ 'Prokaryotes lack all organelles.' ✅ They lack *membrane-bound* organelles (nucleus, mitochondria), but possess non-membrane-bound organelles like ribosomes.
❌ 'Nucleotide and nucleoside are the same.' ✅ Nucleotide = Nucleoside (sugar + base) + Phosphate. Nucleoside lacks the phosphate group.
❌ 'Enzymes are consumed in the reaction.' ✅ Enzymes are catalysts; they speed up reactions by lowering activation energy but are NOT consumed (they are regenerated).
❌ 'Mitochondria are purely eukaryotic.' ✅ While found in eukaryotes, their circular DNA and structure suggest an endosymbiotic origin related to prokaryotes.

data.title: Faunal Diversity, Evolution & Environment
notes: **Porifera (sponges):** pore-bearing aquatic animals with canal system; skeleton of spicules.
**Arthropoda:** largest phylum — jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, open circulatory system (insects, crabs).
**Chordata characters:** notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail at some stage of life.

**Oparin–Haldane theory:** life originated from non-living organic molecules in the primitive reducing atmosphere ('primordial soup'); Miller–Urey experiment (1953) supported it by producing amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O with electric discharge.
**Darwinism:** natural selection — survival of the fittest; variations that help survival are inherited.

**Ecology levels:** organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome. Food chain shows energy flow; ~10% energy transfers to each trophic level. **Conservation:** in-situ (national parks) and ex-situ (zoos, seed banks).
confusion: ❌ 'Natural selection means the physically strongest survive.' ✅ Natural selection means the 'fittest'—those best *adapted* to the current environment—survive and reproduce.
❌ 'Energy in a food chain is destroyed at each step.' ✅ Energy is *transformed* (largely into heat) per the 10% law, not destroyed (conservation of energy applies).
❌ 'Humans evolved directly from monkeys seen today.' ✅ Humans and modern monkeys share a common ancestor; humans did not evolve from the monkeys seen today.

data.title: Floral Diversity & Microbiology
notes: **Binomial nomenclature** was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus — every organism gets two names: generic name + specific epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica).
**Five kingdom classification (Whittaker):** Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation and nutrition.

**Algae:** chlorophyll-bearing, aquatic thalloid organisms; green algae (Spirogyra) have ribbon-shaped spiral chloroplasts; brown algae (Laminaria) have fucoxanthin; red algae (Polysiphonia) contain r-phycoerythrin.
**Bryophytes:** amphibians of the plant kingdom; need water for fertilisation; e.g. mosses and liverworts.
**Bacteria:** prokaryotic, reproduce by binary fission; useful forms fix nitrogen (Rhizobium) and ferment milk into curd (Lactobacillus).
**Virus:** acellular obligate parasite with DNA or RNA core and protein coat (capsid); e.g. TMV, HIV.
**Fungi:** heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin; yeast is unicellular and used in fermentation; Penicillium gives the antibiotic penicillin.
confusion: ❌ 'All bacteria are harmful.' ✅ Many (e.g., Rhizobium, Lactobacillus) are essential for nitrogen fixation, food fermentation, and gut/health functions.
❌ 'Fungi are plants.' ✅ Fungi are heterotrophic, have cell walls made of *chitin* (not cellulose like plants), and lack chlorophyll.
❌ 'Viruses are living cells.' ✅ They are acellular, obligate parasites that only show life characteristics (like replication) *inside* a host cell.
❌ 'Bryophytes are ferns.' ✅ Bryophytes (mosses) are *non-vascular* (lack xylem/phloem) and reproduce by spores; ferns are *vascular* plants.

data.title: Atomic Structure
notes: **Dalton's atomic theory:** matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; compounds form by combination of atoms in fixed ratios.

**Sub-atomic particles:** electron (e⁻, discovered by J.J. Thomson, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass ≈ 1/1837 u); proton (p⁺, Goldstein/Rutherford, +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 u); neutron (n, Chadwick, neutral, 1 u).

**Bohr's model:** electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) with quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = hν. Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å; energy E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

**Defects of Bohr's model:** cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms, fine structure (splitting of spectral lines), Zeeman and Stark effects, and the dual nature/wave character of the electron (de Broglie) or Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

**Quantum numbers:** principal (n), azimuthal (l = 0 … n−1: s, p, d, f), magnetic (m_l = −l … +l) and spin (m_s = ±½). **Pauli exclusion:** no two electrons in an atom have identical sets of four quantum numbers. **Hund's rule** and Aufbau principle govern filling order.
confusion: ❌ 'Bohr orbits are the same as orbitals.' ✅ Orbits are 2D fixed circular paths; orbitals are 3D regions in space where electron finding probability is high.
❌ 'Only s-orbitals are spherical.' ✅ Yes, s-orbitals are spherical; p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped; d-orbitals have complex double-dumbbell shapes.
❌ 'An electron in an atom jumps orbits without emitting/absorbing energy.' ✅ Bohr's model states energy change (ΔE = hν) *must* occur for any orbital jump.
❌ 'Principal quantum number n tells about energy only.' ✅ n primarily dictates size and energy, while l dictates shape.

data.title: Chemical Bonding & Shapes of Molecules (VSEPR)
notes: **Ionic bond:** electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by transfer of electrons (e.g. NaCl). High melting point, conducts electricity in molten/solution state.
**Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs (e.g. H₂, CH₄). Directional; low melting/boiling point compared with ionic solids.
**Coordinate (dative) bond:** shared pair donated by one atom only (e.g. NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).

**VSEPR theory:** electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and arrange to be as far apart as possible. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

Shapes: AX₂ linear (BeCl₂), AX₃ trigonal planar (BF₃), AX₄ tetrahedral (CH₄), AX₃E pyramidal (NH₃, 107°), AX₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°), AX₅ trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅), AX₆ octahedral (SF₆).

**Hybridisation:** intermixing of orbitals of comparable energy to form equivalent hybrid orbitals — sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (octahedral).
confusion: ❌ 'Ionic bonds are always stronger than covalent bonds.' ✅ Ionic bonds are strong in crystal lattices, but covalent bonds can be stronger in individual molecules (e.g., C≡C triple bond is very strong).
❌ 'VSEPR considers all electron pairs equally.' ✅ VSEPR accounts for different repulsion strengths: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp, which distorts bond angles from ideal values.
❌ 'NH₃ is trigonal planar because it has 3 bond pairs.' ✅ NH₃ has 3 bp + 1 lp → tetrahedral electron geometry, but molecular shape is PYRAMIDAL (not planar) due to the lone pair.
❌ 'Hybridisation determines geometry; geometry determines hybridisation.' ✅ Hybridisation is a model used to *explain* observed geometries; it is not a physical process that happens before bonding.

data.title: Chemical Equilibrium & Organic Fundamentals
notes: **Chemical equilibrium:** the stage at which rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction; concentrations remain constant. Dynamic in nature.
**Le Chatelier's principle:** if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.
**Equilibrium constant K_c** = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff. For gas reactions K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn.
**Acids & bases (Bronsted-Lowry):** acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14.

**Organic chemistry basics:** catenation, tetravalency of carbon, homologous series, functional groups, isomerism (chain, position, functional), IUPAC nomenclature rules for alkanes/alkenes/alkynes and simple derivatives.
confusion: ❌ 'Equilibrium means equal amounts of reactants and products.' ✅ Equilibrium means *constant* concentrations, not equal ones. The position of equilibrium depends on K, which can heavily favour either side.
❌ 'Le Chatelier's principle shifts equilibrium to re-establish old rates.' ✅ It shifts to oppose the *change in conditions* (concentration, pressure, temperature), not to restore old rates.
❌ 'K changes when concentration or pressure changes.' ✅ K is constant at a given temperature. Only temperature changes alter the value of K.
❌ 'Catenation is unique to carbon.' ✅ Carbon shows the *greatest* catenation, but silicon and sulfur also exhibit it to lesser degrees.

data.title: Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Reactions
notes: **Oxidation:** loss of electrons / gain of oxygen / increase in oxidation number. **Reduction:** gain of electrons / loss of oxygen / decrease in oxidation number.
**Oxidising agent** accepts electrons (is reduced); **reducing agent** donates electrons (is oxidised).

**Oxidation number rules:** free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is +1 with non-metals and −1 with metals; the sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule is 0.
**Balancing redox equations** — ion-electron (half-reaction) method or oxidation-number method; in acidic medium balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺.
**Applications:** electrochemical cells, electrolysis, corrosion, bleaching and titrations (redox titrations of KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇).
confusion: ❌ 'Oxidation always involves oxygen.' ✅ Modern definition: oxidation is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number — oxygen need not be involved.
❌ 'The oxidising agent gets oxidised.' ✅ The oxidising agent accepts electrons and is therefore REDUCED. The reducing agent is oxidised.
❌ 'Oxygen always has oxidation number −2.' ✅ Almost always −2, but −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂), +2 in OF₂, and 0 in O₂.

❌ 'A reaction with no visible colour change cannot be redox.' ✅ Many redox reactions are colourless (e.g., Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu has visible change, but H⁺ + OH⁻ is not redox — check oxidation numbers, not appearance).

data.title: Periodic Table
notes: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
s-block: groups 1-2; p-block: groups 13-18; d-block: groups 3-12.
Trends: atomic radius decreases across a period, increases down a group.
Ionization energy increases across a period; electronegativity follows the same pattern.

data.title: States of Matter (Gaseous State)
notes: **Boyle's law:** at constant T, V ∝ 1/P. **Charles' law:** at constant P, V ∝ T. **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at same T and P.
**Ideal gas equation:** PV = nRT, R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

**Kinetic theory of gases:** molecules are in continuous random motion; collisions are perfectly elastic; volume of molecules is negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular attraction; average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
**Graham's law of diffusion:** rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√(molar mass).
**Real gases** deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature; van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume and attraction.
confusion: ❌ 'Ideal gases exist in reality.' ✅ Ideal gas is a theoretical model. Real gases approximate ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure where intermolecular forces are negligible.

❌ 'Boyle's law and Charles' law apply to real gases under all conditions.' ✅ They are exact only for ideal gases. Real gases deviate at high pressure/low temperature (described by van der Waals equation).

❌ 'Graham's law applies to rate of effusion but not diffusion.' ✅ Graham's law applies to both effusion (through a pinhole) and diffusion, though diffusion is more complex due to molecular collisions.
❌ 'At 0 K, all molecular motion stops completely.' ✅ At absolute zero, translational motion ceases but zero-point quantum energy remains. Also, no real gas reaches 0 K.

data.title: Basic Concepts of Chemistry & Stoichiometry
notes: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. One mole = **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro's number, N_A).
**Molar mass:** mass of one mole of a substance in grams; numerically equal to its molecular/atomic weight. n = given mass / molar mass.
**Laws of chemical combination:** law of conservation of mass, law of definite (constant) proportions, law of multiple proportions and Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
**Empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; **molecular formula** = n × empirical formula where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass.
**Limiting reagent:** the reactant that is completely consumed first and therefore limits the amount of product formed.
**Percentage yield:** (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100.
confusion: ❌ 'One mole of any substance has the same mass.' ✅ One mole has the same NUMBER of particles (6.022 × 10²³), but different masses depending on molar mass (e.g., 1 mol H₂ = 2 g, 1 mol O₂ = 32 g).

❌ 'Empirical and molecular formulas are always the same.' ✅ Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula is the actual count. They differ when n > 1 (e.g., empirical CH₂, molecular C₆H₁₂).

❌ 'The limiting reagent determines the mass of all products equally.' ✅ The limiting reagent determines the maximum amount of *each* product formed, but different products have different molar ratios from the balanced equation.
❌ 'Percentage yield can exceed 100%.' ✅ Theoretical yield is the maximum possible. Yield > 100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying, not an error in calculation.

data.title: Q: 12 g of carbon reacts with 32 g of hydrogen to produce 44 g of methane — which chemical law do these data illustrate?
notes: Reactants: carbon (12 g) + hydrogen (32 g)
Total mass of reactants = 12 + 32 = 44 g
Total mass of product (methane) = 44 g
Since the mass before the reaction (44 g) equals the mass after (44 g), mass is neither created nor destroyed
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Conservation of Mass**

data.title: Q: 20 g of CaCO₃ is heated and produces 11.2 g of CaO — calculate the weight of CO₂ produced
notes: Reaction: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: mass of CaCO₃ = mass of CaO + mass of CO₂
20 g = 11.2 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 20 − 11.2 = 8.8 g**

data.title: Q: 6.3 g of NaHCO₃ added to 10 g of HCl solution leaves a 12 g residue — what is the mass of CO₂ released?
notes: Reaction: NaHCO₃ + HCl → Residue + CO₂↑
Total mass of reactants: 6.3 g (NaHCO₃) + 10 g (HCl) = 16.3 g
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products
16.3 g = 12 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 16.3 − 12 = 4.3 g**

data.title: Q: Two samples of common salt contain different masses of chlorine — show these results agree with the law of constant proportion
notes: **Data:** 0.25 g of sample 1 contains 0.1518 g of chlorine; 0.24 g of sample 2 contains 0.1458 g of chlorine
Since the percentage of chlorine is nearly identical in both samples (≈ 60.7%), regardless of sample size, this confirms the **Law of Constant (Definite) Proportion**

data.title: Q: Two copper oxide reduction experiments — show they illustrate the law of definite proportions
notes: **Experiment 1:** 1.375 g of CuO is reduced to 1.098 g of copper by dry hydrogen gas
**Experiment 2:** 1.179 g of metallic copper is formed from 1.476 g of copper oxide
The percentage of copper is essentially constant (≈ 79.9%) across both experiments, verifying the **Law of Definite Proportions**

data.title: Q: Determine the weight of oxide formed by heating 1 g of a carbonate (using the law of definite proportions)
notes: **Data:** 0.36 g of a metal burnt in oxygen yields 0.60 g of oxide; the carbonate of that metal contains 28.57% of the metal
From the oxide experiment: mass of metal = 0.36 g, mass of oxide = 0.60 g → ratio (mass of metal)/(mass of oxide) = 0.36/0.60 = **0.6**
From the carbonate experiment: 1 g of carbonate contains 28.57% metal → mass of metal in 1 g carbonate = 0.2857 g
By the Law of Definite Proportions, the metal-to-oxide ratio stays fixed at 0.6, so: 0.2857 / (mass of oxide) = 0.6
Mass of oxide = 0.2857 / 0.6
**Answer: mass of oxide = 0.4762 g**

data.title: Q: Hydrogen and oxygen react separately to give H₂O₂ and H₂O — what law of stoichiometry is illustrated?
notes: Two elements (hydrogen and oxygen) combine to form more than one compound: H₂O and H₂O₂
For a fixed mass of hydrogen (2 g), the masses of oxygen that combine are 16 g (in H₂O) and 32 g (in H₂O₂)
Ratio of oxygen masses = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2** — a simple whole-number ratio
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: A metal forms two oxides (11.9% and 21.2% oxygen) — show these data illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Oxide 1: oxygen = 11.9%, metal = 100 − 11.9 = 88.1% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 11.9/88.1 = **0.135 g**
Oxide 2: oxygen = 21.2%, metal = 100 − 21.2 = 78.8% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 21.2/78.8 = **0.269 g**
Ratio of oxygen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of metal: 0.135 : 0.269 ≈ **1 : 2**
Since 1:2 is a simple whole-number ratio, this confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Element X forms three binary compounds with chlorine (50.08%, 66.73%, 74.95% Cl) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Compound 1: Cl = 50.08%, X = 49.92% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 50.08/49.92 = **1.003 g**
Compound 2: Cl = 66.73%, X = 33.27% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 66.73/33.27 = **2.006 g**
Compound 3: Cl = 74.95%, X = 25.05% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 74.95/25.05 = **2.992 g**
Ratio of chlorine masses combining with a fixed mass of X: 1.003 : 2.006 : 2.992 ≈ **1 : 2 : 3**
The simple whole-number ratio confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Four hydrocarbons with % compositions (C 75%/H 25%, C 80%/H 20%, C 85.7%/H 14.3%, C 92.3%/H 7.7%) — prove the law of multiple proportions
notes: Find the mass of hydrogen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of carbon in each: (a) 25/75 = 0.333 g; (b) 20/80 = 0.250 g; (c) 14.3/85.7 = 0.167 g; (d) 7.7/92.3 = 0.083 g
**Ratio of hydrogen masses = 4 : 3 : 2 : 1**
This simple whole-number ratio proves the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Three oxides of lead reduced in hydrogen — show this illustrates the law of multiple proportions
notes: **Data:** (i) 1.393 g of litharge gave 1.293 g of lead; (ii) 2.173 g of lead peroxide gave 1.882 g of lead; (iii) 1.712 g of red lead gave 1.552 g of lead
Find the mass of oxygen in each oxide by subtracting the lead mass from the total oxide mass: (i) 1.393 − 1.293 = 0.100 g; (ii) 2.173 − 1.882 = 0.291 g; (iii) 1.712 − 1.552 = 0.160 g
Find the mass of Pb combining with 1 g of O in each: (i) 1.293/0.100 = 12.93 g; (ii) 1.882/0.291 = 6.467 g; (iii) 1.552/0.160 = 9.700 g
Ratio: 12.93 : 6.467 : 9.700 — dividing all terms by 6.467 gives 2 : 1 : 1.5
Clearing the decimal by multiplying by 2: **4 : 2 : 3**
This simple whole-number ratio validates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Nitrogen forms five oxides with oxygen (0.572 g, 1.14 g, 1.73 g, 2.28 g, 2.85 g of O per 1.09 g of N) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Fixed mass of nitrogen = 1.09 g in all five oxides
**Ratio of oxygen masses = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5**
This simple whole-number ratio illustrates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: State the observations and conclusions of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil undeflected → most of the atom's volume is empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very small fraction bounced almost straight back → these particles must have encountered something small, dense, and positively charged
**Conclusion:** the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons occupying the mostly empty space around it

data.title: Q: Why does Rutherford's nuclear model fail to explain the stability of an atom?
notes: Maxwell's theory states that any accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic energy
An electron orbiting the nucleus is constantly changing direction, so it is constantly accelerating, and by Maxwell's theory it should continuously lose energy as radiation

Losing energy means the electron's orbital radius should shrink, causing it to spiral inward and collapse into the nucleus within a fraction of a second — but real atoms are stable, which Rutherford's model cannot account for

data.title: Q: How exactly did Bohr's model resolve the stability crisis left unsolved by Rutherford?
notes: Bohr proposed that electrons can only exist in specific 'stationary' orbits where they do NOT radiate energy, regardless of their acceleration — this postulate directly overrides the classical prediction that orbiting charges must radiate
Energy changes only happen in discrete jumps between these fixed orbits (ΔE = hν), not continuously, so there's no mechanism for a gradual energy loss and inward spiral

data.title: Q: Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but fails for helium — why does adding one more electron break the model?
notes: Bohr's postulates and resulting equations were derived by balancing the electrostatic attraction between a single electron and the nucleus against the centripetal force needed for circular motion — a clean two-body problem

With two or more electrons, electron–electron repulsion enters the picture, making it a multi-body problem that Bohr's simple circular-orbit model has no mechanism to account for — this is why it accurately predicts the spectra of H, He⁺, and Li²⁺ (all single-electron species) but not neutral He or heavier atoms

data.title: Q: What do the Zeeman and Stark effects reveal about the limits of Bohr's model?
notes: **Zeeman Effect:** spectral lines split into multiple closely spaced lines when the atom is placed in a magnetic field
**Stark Effect:** spectral lines split when the atom is placed in an electric field

Bohr's model treats each orbit as having a single fixed energy, so it cannot explain why a magnetic or electric field would split a single spectral line into several — this splitting requires additional quantum numbers (like the magnetic quantum number) that only came with the more advanced quantum mechanical model of the atom

data.title: Q: State the three main observations of Rutherford's gold foil experiment and their corresponding conclusions
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the foil undeflected → **Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected through small-to-moderate angles → **Conclusion:** there is a concentration of positive charge somewhere in the atom that repels the positively charged α-particles

**Observation 3:** a very small fraction (about 1 in 8000) bounced back at large angles, close to 180° → **Conclusion:** this positive charge, along with almost all of the atom's mass, is concentrated in an extremely small volume — the nucleus

data.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the radius of the electron in the 2nd orbit of a Li²⁺ ion
notes: Bohr radius formula: r_n = (0.529 Å)·n²/Z, where n = orbit number and Z = atomic number
For Li²⁺: Z = 3, n = 2
**Answer: r₂ ≈ 0.705 Å**

data.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the wavelength of the series limit of the Lyman series for hydrogen
notes: The series limit occurs as n₂ → ∞, so 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 0) = R_H/n₁²
For the Lyman series, n₁ = 1: 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 1 = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
**Answer: λ ≈ 91.15 nm** — deep ultraviolet, consistent with the Lyman series being a UV series

data.title: Q: Which hydrogen spectral series falls entirely within the visible region of light, and why is it the only one?
notes: The **Balmer series** (n₁ = 2) is the only series entirely visible to the human eye
Its emitted wavelengths (transitions from n₂ = 3, 4, 5... down to n₁ = 2) happen to fall in the roughly 400–700 nm range that human eyes detect

The Lyman series (n₁ = 1) is higher-energy and shorter-wavelength (ultraviolet), while Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund (n₁ = 3, 4, 5) are lower-energy and longer-wavelength (infrared) — both fall outside the visible window

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Negative Energy & Bohr Critique (Page 108)
notes: **Q1. Why is the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit taken as negative?** Because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Q2. State two major defects of Bohr's atomic model.** (1) It could not explain why only certain orbits are allowed (quantization was assumed, not derived). (2) It could not explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron (e.g. helium), nor the fine structure of spectral lines.

**Q3. What is the significance of E = mc² in the development of quantum mechanics?** It links mass and energy, and combined with Planck's E = hν it leads to the de Broglie relation λ = h/(mv), showing that matter has wave-like properties.

**Q4. How did Schrödinger's 1926 work shift the atomic model?** Schrödinger replaced Bohr's definite circular orbits with a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the probabilistic orbital concept.

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Duality & Principle Deflections (Page 111)
notes: **Q1. Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.** An orbit is a definite circular path of the electron (Bohr model), planar and described by one quantum number n. An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high probability of finding the electron (quantum mechanics), described by three quantum numbers (n, l, m) and obeying the uncertainty principle.

**Q2. What is the physical significance of the wave function ψ and of ψ²?** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; ψ² gives the probability density of finding the electron in a small volume around a point, which is used to map the electron cloud.

**Q3. Why did the wave-mechanical model replace Bohr's definite orbits?** Because the uncertainty principle forbids knowing position and momentum simultaneously, a definite orbit is impossible; the electron must instead be described by a probability distribution (orbital).

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Numerical Verifications & Degeneracy Mappings (Page 114)
notes: **Q1. How many orbitals are present in the subshell with l = 2? What is its maximum electron capacity?** Number of orbitals = 2l + 1 = 2(2) + 1 = 5. Maximum electron capacity = 2(2l + 1) = 10. So the d subshell has 5 orbitals and holds up to 10 electrons.

**Q2. Write the four quantum numbers that completely describe an electron in the 3p orbital.** Principal n = 3, azimuthal l = 1, magnetic m = −1, 0 or +1 (three possible values), spin s = +½ or −½. Any one of the six possible combinations (3 values of m × 2 spins) describes an electron in 3p.

**Q3. How many degenerate orbitals are there in a p subshell, and why are they called degenerate?** There are three (pₓ, pᵧ, p_z). They have the same energy (they are degenerate) in the absence of an applied magnetic field.

**Q4. For the d subshell, verify the degeneracy mapping.** With l = 2, m takes the values +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, giving 2l + 1 = 5 degenerate orbitals; each holds 2 electrons, so the d subshell accommodates 10 electrons in total.

data.title: Q (worked examples): de Broglie Wavelength & Uncertainty Principle
notes: **Q1. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.** Using λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and v = 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s: λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.006 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

**Q2. Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.15 kg) not observable?** Using λ = h/(mv), for even a small ball travelling at 30 m/s the wavelength is λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m — far smaller than the size of a nucleus and completely unobservable; the wavelength is negligible for macroscopic objects (λ ∝ 1/m).

**Q3. If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, what is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity?** Using Δx · Δv ≥ h/(4πm): Δv = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (4 × 3.14 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1.143 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s.

**Q4. Explain why Bohr's definite orbits contradict the uncertainty principle.** A definite orbit requires both position and momentum to be exactly known at every instant, but Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π forbids simultaneous exact knowledge — so the electron cannot follow a sharply defined circular path.

data.title: Q (worked examples): Atomic Number, Mass Number & Isotopes
notes: **Q1. For the atom ₁₂Mg²⁴, find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.** Atomic number Z = 12, so protons = 12 and electrons = 12 (neutral atom). Mass number A = 24, so neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12.

**Q2. The magnesium ion Mg²⁺ has atomic number 12. How many protons and electrons does it contain?** Protons = Z = 12 (unchanged). Since the ion has lost 2 electrons, electrons = 12 − 2 = 10. Its atomic number remains 12.

**Q3. Protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²) and tritium (₁H³) are isotopes. How do they differ?** All three have the same atomic number Z = 1 (one proton and one electron) but different mass numbers. Protium has 0 neutrons, deuterium has 1 neutron, and tritium has 2 neutrons. Protium is most abundant (99.98%), deuterium about 0.015%, and tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ % (radioactive).

**Q4. Show that ₁₈Ar⁴⁰, ₁₉K⁴⁰ and ₂₀Ca⁴⁰ are isobars.** All three atoms have the same mass number A = 40 but different atomic numbers (18, 19, 20). Hence they are isobars — atoms of different elements with the same mass number.

**Q5. Show that ₆C¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵ and ₈O¹⁶ are isotones.** For ₆C¹⁴: neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8. For ₇N¹⁵: neutrons = 15 − 7 = 8. For ₈O¹⁶: neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8. All have the same number of neutrons (8) but different atomic and mass numbers, hence they are isotones.

**Q6. Verify that ₁₉K³⁹ and ₉F¹⁹ are isodiaphers.** For ₁₉K³⁹: neutrons − protons = (39 − 19) − 19 = 20 − 19 = 1. For ₉F¹⁹: neutrons − protons = (19 − 9) − 9 = 10 − 9 = 1. Both have the same isotopic excess (1), hence they are isodiaphers.

data.title: Self-Practice — Rutherford's Model Diagnostic Questions (Page 102)
notes: **Q1. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the nucleus of an atom contains the entire mass of the atom?** The fact that a minute fraction of alpha particles (about 1 in 20,000) were reflected back suffering a deflection of 180° shows that the nucleus must possess considerable mass — only a massive, dense centre could reflect alpha particles of considerable mass.

**Q2. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the central part (nucleus) of an atom is positively charged?** Some alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected by as much as 90° or even larger angles. Since alpha particles are positively charged, they could only be repelled by a positively charged centre — proving the nucleus is positively charged.

**Q3. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the atom consists mostly of hollow or empty space?** The vast majority of alpha particles (about 99%) passed straight through the gold foil completely undeflected, showing that most of the space inside the atom is empty.

**Q4. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the volume occupied by the nucleus is very small compared to the total volume of the atom?** Only a very small number of alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected through 90° or larger angles, indicating that the positively charged centre (nucleus of radius 10⁻¹³ cm) occupies a tiny volume compared to the whole atom (radius 10⁻⁸ cm).

**Q5. Why did Rutherford select gold foil for the α-particle scattering experiment?** Gold can be beaten into an extremely thin sheet (0.00006 cm thickness), thin enough for alpha particles to pass through and interact with individual atoms; gold is also a heavy element with a highly charged nucleus, producing measurable deflections.

data.title: English Grammar & Composition Essentials
notes: **Tenses:** 12 forms built from present/past/future × simple/continuous/perfect/perfect-continuous. Watch time markers: *since/for* with perfect, *yesterday/tomorrow* fixing the frame.
**Articles:** 'a/an' before singular countable nouns (an + vowel *sound*); 'the' for specific or previously mentioned nouns and superlatives.
**Active & passive voice:** object of active becomes subject in passive; verb changes to be + past participle. E.g. 'She writes a letter' → 'A letter is written by her'.
**Direct & indirect speech:** reporting statements shifts tense back one step; questions use if/whether or wh-word order; imperatives use infinitive with told/requested/ordered.

**Paragraph writing:** one controlling idea per paragraph — topic sentence, supporting details (examples, facts), concluding sentence. **Essay structure:** introduction → body paragraphs → conclusion.
**Comprehension strategy:** skim for gist first, scan for keywords from the question, then read the relevant lines closely; answer in your own words.

**The 12 Tense System — complete map:** (1) Present Simple: habitual actions, general truths — 'She walks to school every day.' (2) Present Continuous: ongoing now, temporary situations — 'She is walking to school.' (3) Present Perfect: past action with present result — 'She has walked to school today.' (4) Present Perfect Continuous: duration up to now — 'She has been walking for an hour.' (5) Past Simple: completed past action — 'She walked to school yesterday.' (6) Past Continuous: ongoing past action — 'She was walking when it rained.' (7) Past Perfect: action before another past action — 'She had walked before the rain started.' (8) Past Perfect Continuous: duration before past point — 'She had been walking for an hour when she fell.' (9) Future Simple: prediction, instant decision — 'She will walk tomorrow.' (10) Future Continuous: ongoing future action — 'She will be walking at 6 AM.' (11) Future Perfect: completed before future point — 'She will have walked 5 km by noon.' (12) Future Perfect Continuous: duration before future point — 'She will have been walking for 2 hours by noon.' Master all 12 forms and their time markers.

**Time markers — the tense key:** Simple present: always, usually, often, never, every day. Present continuous: now, at the moment, currently, today. Present perfect: already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for. Past simple: yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago. Past continuous: while, when, as. Future simple: tomorrow, next week, in 2030, soon. These markers are your biggest help in choosing the correct tense.

**Reported speech — the backshift rule:** When converting direct to indirect speech, shift the tense ONE STEP BACK: present simple → past simple; past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could. Exceptions: general truths stay in present ('He said the sun rises in the east'), and commands/requests use infinitive ('He told me to go'). Questions: Yes/No questions use 'if/whether'; Wh- questions keep the wh-word with statement word order ('She asked where I was going', NOT 'where was I going').

**Voice transformation — the 6 rules:** (1) Object becomes subject. (2) Main verb becomes past participle. (3) Add correct form of 'be' (is/am/are → was/were; will → would; can → could). (4) 'By' + original subject. (5) Impersonal passive for general opinions: 'It is said that…' / 'People say that…' (6) Not all verbs can be made passive (intransitive verbs like 'happen', 'sleep' cannot). Practice: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built by them.' 'Someone stole my pen' → 'My pen was stolen.'

**Conditional sentences — the 4 types:** Type 0 (general truth): If + present, present — 'If you heat water, it boils.' Type 1 (real future): If + present, will + base — 'If it rains, I will stay home.' Type 2 (unreal present): If + past, would + base — 'If I were rich, I would travel.' Type 3 (unreal past): If + past perfect, would have + past participle — 'If I had studied, I would have passed.' Inversion without 'if': 'Were I rich…' / 'Had I known…' / 'Should you need help…'

**Modal verbs — the nuance guide:** Ability: can (present), could (past), be able to (all tenses). Permission: may (formal), can (informal), could (polite). Obligation: must (internal), have to (external), should (advice). Prohibition: mustn't (forbidden), don't have to (not necessary). Possibility: may/might/could (varying degrees of certainty). Deduction: must be (near certainty), can't be (impossibility), might be (uncertainty). Master the difference between 'must' (strong obligation) and 'have to' (external obligation), and between 'should' (advice) and 'ought to' (moral duty).

**Gerund vs. Infinitive — the verb pattern chart:** Gerunds (-ing) after: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, keep, practice, consider, admit, deny, risk, feel like, can't help. Infinitives (to + base) after: want, hope, decide, plan, agree, refuse, learn, pretend, seem, appear, offer, afford, manage, expect, need, needn't, must. Special cases (change meaning): stop smoking (= quit the habit) vs. stop to smoke (= pause in order to smoke); remember to call (= don't forget) vs. remember calling (= recall the memory). This distinction is heavily tested.

**Prepositions — the invisible connectors:** Time: at (specific time: at 5 PM), on (day/date: on Monday, on May 5th), in (month/year/period: in May, in 2025, in the morning). Place: at (point: at the door), on (surface: on the table), in (enclosure: in the room). Movement: to (direction: go to school), into (entry: walk into the room), onto (surface: jump onto the chair). Other common prepositions: depend ON, interested IN, good AT, afraid OF, proud OF, responsible FOR, different FROM, similar TO. Each verb/adjective pairs with a specific preposition — memorise the pairs.

**Conjunctions — joining ideas with purpose:** Coordinating (FANBOYS): for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — join equal clauses. Subordinating: because, although, if, when, while, since, unless, until, as, before, after — join dependent to independent. Correlative pairs: both…and, either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, whether…or. These pairs MUST be used symmetrically: 'Not only did he study, but he also passed.' NOT: 'Not only he studied, but he also passed.'

**Common grammar errors in exams:** (1) Subject-verb agreement: 'The list of items are long' → 'is long' (subject is 'list', not 'items'). (2) Wrong article: 'I saw a elephant' → 'an elephant'. (3) Double negative: 'I don't need nothing' → 'I don't need anything'. (4) Wrong tense sequence: 'If I will go, I will tell you' → 'If I go, I will tell you.' (5) Wrong preposition: 'I am good in English' → 'good at English'. (6) Fragment: 'Because he was late.' → needs a main clause. (7) Comma splice: 'I was tired, I slept early' → fix with conjunction or semicolon.

**Essay proofreading checklist — the final 3 minutes:** After finishing your essay, spend the last 3 minutes checking: (1) Subject-verb agreement in every sentence. (2) Consistent tense throughout (no unexpected shifts). (3) Correct article usage (a/an/the/none). (4) Proper punctuation — especially commas before FANBOYS, after introductory phrases, and around non-restrictive clauses. (5) Spelling of commonly misused words: its/it's, their/there/they're, your/you're, affect/effect, affect/effect, principal/principle. (6) Every sentence has a subject and a verb. (7) No fragments or run-ons.

data.title: Subject-Verb Agreement — Tricky Cases
notes: **Subject-Verb Agreement** is one of the most tested grammar topics in NEB English. The basic rule is: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs. However, many nouns break this rule — they look plural but take singular verbs, or look singular but take plural verbs.
## 🔹 Looks Plural, Takes a Singular Verb
These nouns end in **-s** but are actually singular and take **is/was**:
### 📘 School Subjects / Science
- **Physics** is my favorite subject.
- **Mathematics** is not difficult if you practice.
- **Economics** is a popular choice for commerce students.
- **Genetics** is a branch of biology.
- **Robotics** is an emerging field.
### 🩺 Diseases
- **Measles** is a contagious childhood disease.
- **Mumps** is caused by a virus.
- **Diabetes** is a chronic condition.
- **Rabies** is fatal if not treated.
### 🎲 Games / Sports
- **Darts** is a popular pub game.
- **Billiards** is played on a large table.
- **Dominoes** is a game of tiles.
- **Gymnastics** requires great flexibility.
### 🌍 Countries / Places
- **The United States** is a large country.
- **The Netherlands** is known for tulips.
- **The Philippines** is an archipelago.
- **Headquarters** is located in the city center.
### 💰 Measurement Units (Time / Money / Distance)
- **Ten dollars** is too much for a coffee.
- **Five miles** is a long distance to run.
- **Three hours** is a long flight.
### 📰 Other Words
- **News** is broadcast at 6 PM.
- **Series** is my favorite TV genre.
- **Species** is a biological classification.
- **Crossroads** is a busy intersection.
> **Rule:** Words ending in **-s** that are names of academic subjects, diseases, games, countries, measurements, or abstract concepts often take **singular verbs**.
## 🔹 Looks Singular, Takes a Plural Verb
These nouns have no **-s** but are actually plural and take **are/were**:
### 👥 Groups of People
- **Police** are investigating the crime.
- **People** are waiting outside.
- **Clergy** were present at the ceremony.
- **Gentry** are known for their generosity.
- **Folk** are traditional and colorful.
### 🐄 Animals / Livestock
- **Cattle** are grazing in the field.
- **Poultry** are kept for eggs and meat.
- **Vermin** are pests that destroy crops.
### 💼 Work Groups (when focusing on members)
- The **staff** are having a meeting.
- The **crew** are working hard.
> **Rule:** Collective nouns that refer to groups of individuals often take **plural verbs** when emphasizing the members.
## 🔹 Compound Subjects Joined by 'And'
### 🍽️ One Single Meal / Dish → Singular Verb
These foods are served and eaten together as one dish:
- **Bread and butter** is my daily breakfast.
- **Rice and curry** is a popular meal in Asia.
- **Fish and chips** is a famous British dish.
- **Bacon and eggs** is a heavy breakfast.
- **Macaroni and cheese** is comfort food.
- **Strawberries and cream** is served at tennis matches.
### 🛒 Separate Food Items / Groceries → Plural Verb
Same-sounding pairs, but here they're two separate items:
- Bread and butter **are** both on the shopping list.
- Milk and cookies **are** in the kitchen.
- Apples and oranges **grow** on trees.
### 🤝 One Concept or Idiom → Singular Verb
- **Law and order** is important for a safe city.
- **Peace and quiet** is all I need.
- **Trial and error** is a great way to learn.
- **Slow and steady** wins the race.
- **All work and no play** makes Jack a dull boy.
### 👫 Distinct People or Roles → Plural Verb
- My mom and dad **are** coming.
- The teacher and the student **were** talking.
- Fire and water **do not** mix.
### 🏹 Two Objects Working as One Unit → Singular Verb
- A horse and carriage **was** outside.
- A needle and thread **is** needed.
- A bow and arrow **was** used.
### 🎒 Different Objects / Tools → Plural Verb
- A pen and a pencil **are** on the desk.
- The hammer and the wrench **are** in the box.
- Shoes and socks **are** in the closet.
### 🔍 How to Tell the Difference Quickly
Look at the little word **"the"** or **"a"** in the sentence — it's a major clue:
- **One article = Singular idea:** "The chef and owner is here." (one person, two jobs)
- **Two articles = Plural people:** "The chef and the owner are here." (two different people)
> **Example:** _Rice and curry is my favorite dish._ (one meal) vs. _Rice and curry are both sold at the market._ (two items)
## 🔹 Plural-Only Nouns: Clothing & Tools
These items have no singular form — they are always plural:
### 👖 Clothing and Underwear
- **Pants** — The pants **are** on the bed.
- **Jeans** — Blue jeans **look** great.
- **Shorts** — Running shorts **are** comfortable.
- **Trousers** — Black trousers **match** any shirt.
- **Pajamas** — My pajamas **feel** soft.
- **Leggings** — Yoga leggings **stretch** a lot.
- **Tights** — Warm tights **keep** you cozy.
- **Briefs / Boxers / Underpants** — These boxers **are** new.
- **Overalls** — Denim overalls **are** trendy.
- **Slacks** — Dress slacks **are** required for work.
- **Suspenders** — Clip-on suspenders **hold** up pants.
### ✂️ Tools and Instruments
- **Scissors** — Large scissors **cut** thick paper.
- **Pliers** — Needle-nose pliers **grip** wires tightly.
- **Tweezers** — Metal tweezers **pick** up small items.
- **Tongs** — Ice tongs **are** in the bucket.
- **Shears** — Hedge shears **trim** the bushes.
- **Clippers** — Nail clippers **are** sharp.
- **Forceps** — Medical forceps **hold** the bandages.
- **Handcuffs** — Steel handcuffs **lock** tight.
- **Nutcrackers** — Wooden nutcrackers **crack** walnuts easily.
- **Bellows** — Fireplace bellows **blow** air onto logs.
### 🕶️ Gear for Eyes and Ears
- **Glasses / Spectacles** — Reading glasses **help** you see.
- **Sunglasses** — Dark sunglasses **block** the sun.
- **Goggles** — Safety goggles **protect** your eyes.
- **Binoculars** — Heavy binoculars **make** birds look close.
- **Headphones / Earphones** — Wireless headphones **play** music clearly.
> **Rule:** Two-part items that are always plural — no singular form exists. Use **are/were**, never **is/was**.
## 🔹 Indefinite Pronouns — The Agreement Rules
### 👤 SINGULAR (take singular verbs)
- **Each, every, either, neither** → singular: 'Each of the students **is** present.'
- **Someone, someone else, anyone, anyone else, no one, nobody, everyone, everybody** → singular: 'Everyone **is** here.'
- **Something, anything, nothing, everything** → singular: 'Nothing **is** impossible.'
- **One** → singular: 'One **must** follow the rules.'
### 👥 PLURAL (take plural verbs)
- **Both, few, several, many** → plural: 'Both of them **are** coming.'
- **All** → depends on what follows: 'All of the cake **is** gone.' (singular) vs. 'All of the students **are** gone.' (plural)
> **Rule:** Words like each, every, anyone, everyone, nobody, somebody ALWAYS take singular verbs — even when followed by 'of the students/people'.
## 🔹 'Of' Phrases — Finding the Real Subject
In sentences like 'The list of items **is** long,' the subject is NOT 'items' — it's 'list.' The phrase 'of items' is just additional information. Common patterns:
- The **number** of students **is** large. (The number = singular; a specific quantity)
- **A number** of students **are** absent. (A number = plural; many students)
- The **majority** of the work **is** done. (The majority = singular when referring to a whole)
- **Half** of the pie **is** eaten. / **Half** of the students **are** absent.
- One **third** of the population **lives** in cities. / One **third** of the voters **support** the plan.
- None of the money **has** been spent. / None of the students **have** arrived.
> **Rule:** In 'The [noun] of [plural noun]' constructions, the FIRST noun (not the one after 'of') is the subject. 'The number of' = singular. 'A number of' = plural.
## 🔹 Headings, Titles, and Quotations as Subjects
- The **title** of the book **is** 'Harry Potter.' (singular — title = subject)
- '**Himalaya**' **is** a mountain range. (singular — the word itself)
- '**Les Misérables**' **is** a famous novel. (singular — one title)
- '**The Rajiv Gandhi Award**' **was** established in 1991. (singular)
- '**War and Peace**' **is** Tolstoy's longest novel. (singular — one book)
- '**Tom and Jerry**' **is** a classic cartoon. (singular — one show)
> **Rule:** Titles, names of books/movies, and single entities take singular verbs — even if they contain 'and' or look plural.
## 🔹 Words That Are Always Singular
- **Mathematics, physics, economics, ethics, measles, mumps, tennis, billiards** → singular
- **The poor, the rich, the elderly, the young, the deaf, the blind** → plural (referring to groups): 'The poor **need** help.'
- **Dias, weeks, months, years, miles** (as measurement) → singular: 'Ten miles **is** a long walk.'
- **Measles, diabetes, malaria, gymnastics** → singular: 'Malaria **is** a serious disease.'
## 🔹 Collective Nouns — When Singular, When Plural

Collective nouns like 'team', 'family', 'committee', 'government', 'class', 'board' can take EITHER singular or plural verbs depending on whether you mean the GROUP as a unit or the INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS:
- **Singular (unit):** 'The team **wins** the championship.' (the team as one entity)
- **Plural (members):** 'The team **are** arguing among themselves.' (individual members disagreeing)
- **Singular:** 'The government **has** announced a new policy.'
- **Plural:** 'The government **are** divided on this issue.'
- **Singular:** 'The class **is** going to the museum.'
- **Plural:** 'The class **are** wearing their uniforms.'
> **Rule:** If the group acts as ONE UNIT → singular verb. If the members act INDIVIDUALLY → plural verb. Look for clues: 'themselves' often signals plural.
## 🔹 Inversion and Questions — Finding the Subject
In inverted sentences (where the verb comes before the subject), find the REAL subject to get agreement right:
- **There is** a book on the table. / **There are** books on the table. (subject follows the verb)
- **Here comes** the bus. / **Here come** the buses. (subject follows the verb)
- **Where is** the manager? / **Where are** the managers?
- **Under the tree sits** a old man. / **Under the tree sit** three old men.
- **On the wall hangs** a painting. / **On the wall hang** three paintings.
> **Rule:** In 'There is/are' and 'Here comes/come' constructions, the subject comes AFTER the verb. Match the verb to the subject that follows.
## 🔹 'And' vs. 'Or' / 'Nor' / 'Either…or' / 'Neither…nor'
### AND — always plural (unless one idea)
- Ram and Shyam **are** coming. (plural — two people)
- Bread and butter **is** my breakfast. (singular — one dish)
### OR / NOR / EITHER…OR / NEITHER…NOR — verb agrees with NEAREST subject
- Neither the teacher nor the students **are** present. (nearest = 'students' → plural)
- Neither the students nor the teacher **is** present. (nearest = 'teacher' → singular)
- Either the boys or the girl **has** won. (nearest = 'girl' → singular)
- Either the girl or the boys **have** won. (nearest = 'boys' → plural)
- Neither the captain nor the players **were** happy. (nearest = 'players' → plural)
> **Rule:** With 'or/nor/either…or/neither…nor', the verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST to it. Always check which subject is nearest.
## 🔹 Quantifiers and Agreement
- **Many a** + singular noun + singular verb: 'Many a student **has** failed.' (literary/formal)
- **A number of** + plural noun + plural verb: 'A number of students **are** absent.'
- **The number of** + plural noun + singular verb: 'The number of students **is** increasing.'
- **Some, most, all, half** + of + singular/plural noun → verb matches the noun: 'Some of the water **is** dirty.' / 'Some of the students **are** late.'
- **None of** + singular/plural → both acceptable, but singular is more formal: 'None of the answers **is** correct.' / 'None of the answers **are** correct.'
## 📝 Quick Reference Table
| Category | Examples | Verb | Example Sentence |
| Ends in -s but singular | Physics, Math, Economics | **is** | Physics **is** easy. |
| Diseases ending in -s | Measles, Mumps, Diabetes | **is** | Measles **is** contagious. |
| Games ending in -s | Darts, Billiards, Gymnastics | **is** | Darts **is** fun. |
| Countries with 'The' | The United States, The Philippines | **is** | The Philippines **is** an island nation. |
| Measurements | Ten dollars, Five miles | **is** | Ten dollars **is** enough. |
| Group nouns (plural) | Police, Cattle, People | **are** | The police **are** coming. |
| Compound (one idea) | Bread and butter, Law and order | **is** | Bread and butter **is** delicious. |
| Compound (two things) | A pen and a pencil, Mom and dad | **are** | Mom and dad **are** here. |
| Always plural | Scissors, Pants, Glasses | **are** | Scissors **are** sharp. |
| Indefinite pronouns | Each, everyone, nobody | **is** | Everyone **is** ready. |
| 'A number of' | A number of students | **are** | A number of students **are** absent. |
| 'The number of' | The number of students | **is** | The number of students **is** 50. |
| Collective noun (unit) | The team wins | **wins** | The team **wins** the match. |
| Collective noun (members) | The team argue | **argue** | The team **are** arguing. |
| 'Or/Nor' nearest subject | Neither teacher nor students | **are** | Neither the teacher nor the students **are** here. |
## ✅ Practice Questions
1. Physics _____ my favorite subject. (is/are)
2. The police _____ investigating the case. (is/are)
3. Bread and butter _____ my breakfast. (is/are)
4. My scissors _____ missing. (is/are)
5. The United States _____ a large country. (is/are)
6. Measles _____ a viral disease. (is/are)
7. The staff _____ having a meeting. (is/are)
8. Law and order _____ everyone's responsibility. (is/are)
9. Five miles _____ a long distance. (is/are)
10. The glasses _____ on the table. (is/are)
11. Each of the students _____ a textbook. (has/have)
12. Neither the boys nor the girl _____ at home. (is/are)
13. The number of applicants _____ increased. (has/have)
14. A number of reasons _____ given. (has/have)
15. The news _____ very encouraging. (is/are)
16. The couple _____ buying a new house. (is/are)
17. Rice and curry _____ my favorite meal. (is/are)
18. Ten dollars _____ too much to pay. (is/are)
19. There _____ a book and two pens on the desk. (is/are)
20. Neither the principal nor the teachers _____ aware of the plan. (was/were)

**Answers:** 1. is, 2. are, 3. is, 4. are, 5. is, 6. is, 7. are, 8. is, 9. is, 10. are, 11. has, 12. is, 13. has, 14. have, 15. is, 16. are, 17. is, 18. is, 19. is (nearest = 'a book'), 20. were (nearest = 'teachers')

data.title: Comprehension and Unseen Passage — answering in your own words
notes: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.

**Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

**Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.
**Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**The four-step comprehension method:** (1) SKIM — read the passage once quickly (60 seconds) to get the gist. Don't stop for unknown words. (2) SCAN — read the questions FIRST, then scan the passage for keywords related to each question. (3) LOCATE — find the exact sentence(s) that contain the answer. Underline them. (4) RESTATE — write the answer in YOUR OWN WORDS using complete sentences. Never copy the passage verbatim.

**Why copying is the #1 comprehension error:** Examiners explicitly penalise copied sentences. If the passage says 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' and you write 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' you get ZERO marks for that answer. You must PARAPHRASE: 'Industrial waste had contaminated the river.' This proves you UNDERSTOOD the meaning, not just your ability to copy.

**Paraphrasing techniques for exam success:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'happy' → 'joyful', 'big' → 'large', 'sad' → 'sorrowful'. (2) *Word class change*: 'The government decided' → 'The government's decision was…' (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built by them.' (4) *Clause reduction*: 'Although it was raining heavily, they went out' → 'Despite the heavy rain, they went out.' (5) *Active to passive*: 'The teacher gave the students homework' → 'The students were given homework by the teacher.'

**Question type mastery — WH questions:** (1) *What* — answer with a noun or clause: 'What caused the flood?' → 'Heavy rainfall caused the flood.' (2) *Why* — answer with a reason: 'Why did she refuse?' → 'She refused because she had lost faith in the system.' (3) *How* — answer with a method or manner: 'How did they solve the problem?' → 'They solved it by combining traditional knowledge with modern techniques.' (4) *When/Where/Who* — direct factual answers. ALWAYS use complete sentences unless told otherwise.

**Question type mastery — true/false/not given:** (1) *True* — the passage explicitly confirms the statement. (2) *False* — the passage explicitly contradicts the statement. (3) *Not Given* — the passage doesn't mention the information at all. 'Not Given' is different from 'False' — it means the information is simply absent, not wrong. This distinction is heavily tested.

**Question type mastery — short answer vs. long answer:** (1) *Short answer* (1 mark): one sentence, direct to the point. (2) *Long answer* (2-3 marks): answer + supporting evidence/reason from the passage. For 2-mark questions, always include BOTH the answer AND the evidence. Format: 'X happened because Y [evidence from passage].' Don't just state the answer — justify it.

**Vocabulary-in-context questions:** When asked 'What does the word X mean in the passage?', do NOT write a dictionary definition. Write what the word means IN THAT CONTEXT. 'In the passage, "reluctant" means unwilling or hesitating because the character had no choice but to agree despite her reservations.' Always anchor your answer in the passage's context.

**Inference questions — reading between the lines:** Inference questions ask you to deduce something NOT explicitly stated. 'What can you infer about the author's attitude?' Strategy: (1) Find the sentence with the relevant information. (2) Ask 'what does this imply?' (3) Write the implication as your answer. Don't go beyond the text — stay close to the passage. 'The author's use of the word "heartbreaking" suggests they feel deep sorrow about the situation.'

**Reference questions — what does 'it/this/that' refer to?** These questions ask you to identify what a pronoun or demonstrative refers to in context. Strategy: (1) Find the pronoun in the passage. (2) Look at the preceding sentence(s). (3) Identify the noun that the pronoun replaces. Answer: 'It refers to [the specific noun from the passage].' Never answer with another pronoun.

**Tone and attitude questions:** 'What is the author's tone?' Possible answers: formal, informal, objective, subjective, sympathetic, critical, sarcastic, hopeful, pessimistic, nostalgic, indifferent. 'What is the author's attitude towards…?' Possible answers: positive, negative, neutral, ambivalent, critical, admiring. Always support your answer with a specific word or phrase from the passage.

**Main idea and title questions:** (1) *Main idea*: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph. The main idea is what connects ALL paragraphs. (2) *Title*: Choose a title that covers the WHOLE passage, not just one paragraph. A good title is specific but not too narrow. Bad title: 'Pollution in Kathmandu' (only covers one paragraph). Good title: 'Environmental Challenges in Urban Nepal' (covers all paragraphs).

**Comprehension time management:** For a 30-mark comprehension section with a 300-400 word passage and 10-12 questions: (1) Spend 2 minutes skimming. (2) Read questions in 1 minute. (3) Each question takes 2-3 minutes (locate + restate + verify). (4) Leave 2 minutes for review. Total: ~30 minutes. Don't spend 10 minutes on one question — move on and come back. Speed and accuracy matter.

**The verification check — your last step:** After writing every answer, go back to the passage and ask: (1) Does my answer match the passage? (2) Have I answered the question asked, not a different one? (3) Is my answer in my own words? (4) Is it in a complete sentence? (5) Does it fit the word limit? If any answer fails these checks, rewrite it. Verification catches 60% of comprehension errors.
confusion: Copying vs. paraphrasing: Copying = writing the exact words from the passage (0 marks). Paraphrasing = expressing the SAME MEANING in YOUR OWN WORDS (full marks). Example: Passage says 'The children played joyfully in the garden.' Copy: 'The children played joyfully in the garden' (wrong). Paraphrase: 'The kids had fun playing outdoors in the garden' (correct). Always paraphrase unless the question says 'quote from the passage.'

Inference vs. opinion: An inference is a LOGICAL conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage. An opinion is YOUR PERSONAL belief that may or may not be supported by the passage. Inference: 'The character was likely anxious because she kept checking her watch.' Opinion: 'I think the character was anxious because I get nervous too.' Inferences use passage evidence; opinions use personal experience. Examiners want inferences.

True vs. Not Given: True = the passage CONFIRMS the statement. False = the passage CONTRADICTS the statement. Not Given = the passage NEITHER confirms nor contradicts — the information is simply absent. Example: Passage says 'Rahul went to school.' Statement: 'Rahul walked to school.' This is NOT GIVEN — we know he went, but not HOW. Don't assume; stick to what's in the passage.

Short answer vs. long answer format: A short answer (1 mark) is one complete sentence that directly answers the question. A long answer (2-3 marks) is answer + evidence/reason. Format for long answers: 'The answer is X because Y [with reference to the passage].' For short answers, skip the 'because' — just state the answer directly. Over-answering short questions wastes time; under-answering long questions loses marks.

Main idea vs. topic: The TOPIC is what the passage is about (one word or phrase: 'deforestation'). The MAIN IDEA is what the passage says ABOUT the topic (a complete sentence: 'Deforestation in Nepal is accelerating due to population pressure and policy failures'). Don't confuse them — a topic is a label; a main idea is a claim.

data.title: Essay Writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, expository
notes: **What it is:** an essay argues, describes, narrates or explains a topic in organised paragraphs. The examiner marks STANCE + STRUCTURE + evidence, not length.

**Universal skeleton:** Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (ONE reason each: topic sentence → explanation → example) → optional counter-argument (acknowledge, then rebut) → Conclusion (restate thesis + consequence).

**Four types:** *Argumentative* (clear side, reasons, admit the other side), *Descriptive* (5 senses, spatial order, show-don't-tell), *Narrative* (one incident: setup → conflict → climax → reflection), *Expository* (explain causes/process in numbered factors, no opinion).
**Tense logic:** essays live in PRESENT for general truths; past only inside narrative examples; predictions use will/would.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Argumentative essay deep dive:** The argumentative essay requires you to take a clear position on a debatable issue. Start with a provocative hook — a startling statistic, a rhetorical question, or a bold claim. Your thesis statement must be specific and arguable (not a fact). Each body paragraph follows the T.E.E.L. structure: Topic sentence → Explanation → Evidence → Link back to thesis. Use transition phrases like 'Furthermore', 'Moreover', 'On the other hand' to signal your reasoning. Always include a counter-argument paragraph: acknowledge the opposing view fairly, then refute it with evidence. End with a conclusion that extends the thesis into a broader implication — what are the consequences if your view is accepted or rejected?

**Argumentative essay — power phrases:** 'It is widely believed that… however, evidence suggests…'; 'While critics argue that…, the reality is…'; 'The implications of this policy are far-reaching…'; 'To dismiss this concern would be irresponsible because…'. These phrases demonstrate sophisticated argumentation and earn higher marks.

**Descriptive essay — sensory writing:** A descriptive essay paints a picture using all five senses: sight (colour, shape, light), sound (loudness, rhythm, tone), smell (fragrance, stench), taste (sweet, bitter, savoury), touch (texture, temperature, weight). Use spatial organisation — move the reader's eye from left to right, top to bottom, near to far, or general to specific. Employ 'show, don't tell': instead of 'The market was busy', write 'Vendors shouted over each other, children darted between stalls, and the air hung thick with the smell of frying spices'. Use present tense to make the description immediate and vivid.

**Descriptive essay — figurative language toolkit:** Simile ('The lake was as smooth as glass'), metaphor ('The city is a concrete jungle'), personification ('The old house groaned under the weight of years'), hyperbole ('I waited for an eternity'), onomatopoeia ('The bacon sizzled and popped'), alliteration ('The silent, silver snow fell softly'). Each device should serve the overall atmosphere — do not scatter them randomly. If describing a peaceful scene, use soft, flowing language; if describing a war zone, use sharp, broken sentences.

**Narrative essay — the art of storytelling:** A narrative essay retells a personal experience with a clear arc: exposition (who, when, where) → rising action (complications build) → climax (the decisive moment) → falling action (aftermath) → resolution (what you learned). The most important rule: ONE central incident. Do not cram an entire year into one essay. Focus on the turning point — the moment everything changed. Use dialogue to bring scenes alive ('I couldn't believe what she said'). End with reflection: what did this experience teach you? How did it change your perspective?

**Narrative essay — tense and pacing:** Past simple drives the plot forward ('I walked into the room'). Past continuous sets the scene ('The rain was pouring outside'). Past perfect marks earlier events ('I had never felt so afraid'). Short sentences at the climax create tension ('The door opened. A shadow appeared. My heart stopped.'). Longer sentences in the resolution slow the pace and create calm. Mastering tense shifts and sentence length is what separates a good narrative from a great one.

**Expository essay — explaining without bias:** The expository essay explains a process, concept, or phenomenon without taking sides. Use logical organisation: chronological (for processes), cause-effect (for analysis), compare-contrast (for two subjects), or problem-solution (for issues). Each paragraph should open with a clear topic sentence and develop with facts, examples, and definitions. Avoid 'I think' or 'In my opinion' — the expository essay presents information objectively. Use transition words: 'First', 'Second', 'In addition', 'Consequently', 'Finally'. The goal is clarity, not persuasion.

**Expository essay — common topics and approaches:** 'How does photosynthesis work?' (process), 'What causes climate change?' (cause-effect), 'Democracy vs. Authoritarianism' (compare-contrast), 'The effects of social media on youth' (problem-analysis). For process essays, use imperative voice or numbered steps. For cause-effect, clearly distinguish between causes (reasons something happened) and effects (results). For compare-contrast, use either the block method (all of A, then all of B) or the point-by-point method (A1 vs B1, A2 vs B2). Choose based on what makes the comparison clearest.

**Introduction strategies — hooking the reader:** (1) Startling fact: 'Every year, 8 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean.' (2) Rhetorical question: 'What would you do if you had only one day left?' (3) Quotation: 'As Martin Luther King Jr. said, "Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere."' (4) Anecdote: 'When I was ten, I discovered a hidden truth about my neighbourhood.' (5) Bold statement: 'Education is the most powerful weapon you can use to change the world.' After the hook, add 1-2 sentences of context, then your thesis. Never start with 'In this essay I will discuss…' — it is weak and wastes words.

**Body paragraph structure — T.E.E.L. method:** **T**opic sentence (states the paragraph's main point) → **E**xplanation (explains the point in detail) → **E**vidence (example, fact, quote, or statistic) → **L**ink (connects back to the thesis). Example: 'Social media isolates young people from real relationships. (T) When teenagers spend hours scrolling through feeds, they miss opportunities for face-to-face interaction, which is essential for developing empathy. (E) A 2023 study found that teenagers who use social media for more than 3 hours daily report 40% higher rates of loneliness. (E) This data confirms that the digital world, despite its promise of connection, often creates the opposite. (L)'

**Conclusion — beyond repetition:** A strong conclusion does more than restate the thesis. It: (1) Signals closure with a transition ('In conclusion', 'Ultimately', 'Taking everything into account'); (2) Restates the thesis in fresh words; (3) Synthesises — shows how your points work together; (4) Extends — asks 'What next?' or 'What are the broader implications?' Avoid introducing new evidence, apologising ('This is just my opinion'), or ending with a weak summary. The final sentence should resonate — leave the reader thinking.

**Counter-argument paragraph — the mark of mature writing:** In an argumentative essay, dedicating one paragraph to the opposing view shows intellectual honesty. Structure: (1) Acknowledge the opposing view fairly ('Some people believe that…'); (2) Explain why it has some merit ('This is understandable because…'); (3) Refute with evidence or reasoning ('However, recent data shows…' / 'This argument overlooks the fact that…'); (4) Reaffirm your position. This paragraph typically comes after your main arguments and before the conclusion.

**Essay planning — the 5-minute blueprint:** Before writing, spend 5 minutes planning: (1) Circle the key words in the question; (2) Choose your essay type; (3) Write your thesis statement in one sentence; (4) List 3 body paragraph topics; (5) Note one example/evidence for each; (6) Draft a counter-argument if argumentative. This plan prevents rambling, ensures every paragraph has a purpose, and typically saves more time than it costs. A well-planned essay always scores higher than a hastily written one, no matter how good the ideas are.

**Common essay mistakes and how to avoid them:** (1) No clear thesis → write one sentence that states your position before you begin; (2) One giant paragraph → break into 4-6 focused paragraphs; (3) Repetition → each paragraph must add a NEW point; (4) Informal language → no slang, contractions (in formal essays), or 'you/I' unless the prompt allows first person; (5) No evidence → every claim needs support; (6) Weak conclusion → end with impact, not apology; (7) Copying the question → rephrase in your own words. Check these seven points in your final read-through.
confusion: Argumentative vs. Persuasive essay: An argumentative essay presents balanced reasoning and acknowledges the opposition before refuting it. A persuasive essay focuses on convincing the reader using emotional appeals and may not fairly represent the other side. For exams, write argumentative essays — they demonstrate higher-order thinking.

Descriptive vs. Narrative essay: A descriptive essay focuses on painting a vivid picture of a person, place, or thing using sensory details — it is static, like a photograph. A narrative essay tells a story with a beginning, middle, and end — it is dynamic, like a film. A descriptive essay may lack a clear plot; a narrative essay always has a sequence of events.

Expository vs. Argumentative essay: An expository essay explains something objectively without taking a stance. An argumentative essay takes a clear position and defends it with evidence. If the prompt says 'Explain' or 'Discuss', write expository. If it says 'Do you agree?' or 'Argue for/against', write argumentative.

Thesis statement vs. Topic sentence: A thesis statement appears in the introduction and covers the ENTIRE essay — it is the central argument. A topic sentence appears at the start of each body paragraph and covers only THAT paragraph's point. The thesis is the umbrella; topic sentences are the ribs.

Introduction hook vs. Introduction background: The hook grabs attention (a fact, question, or story). The background provides context (what the issue is, why it matters). A strong introduction has both: hook → 1-2 context sentences → thesis. Skipping the hook makes the essay feel flat; skipping the background leaves the reader confused.

data.title: Formal & Informal Letters — two registers, two formats
notes: **The core idea — REGISTER:** a letter is formal or informal depending on the RELATIONSHIP with the reader. Same information, different clothes. Choosing the wrong register loses more marks than any grammar slip.

**FORMAL letter — used for:** applications (jobs, scholarships), letters to editors, complaints to authorities, inquiries to institutions, official requests. Reader = someone you do NOT know personally or someone with authority.

**Formal format (in order):** sender's address (top-right or top-left) → date → recipient's name/designation/address → SUBJECT line (one line, the letter in miniature) → salutation 'Dear Sir/Madam' → body (intro → details → expected action) → 'Yours faithfully/sincerely' → full name. NO first names, NO contracted forms.

**Formal body plan — the 3-paragraph rule:** P1 states purpose ('I am writing to apply for...'), P2 gives supporting detail/facts, P3 requests action and closes politely ('I look forward to your response'). Never mix purposes across paragraphs.

**Formal language kit:** 'I am writing to inquire/apply/complain...', 'I would be grateful if you could...', 'Thank you for your consideration.' Replace contractions: cannot, do not, I am. Replace casual words: get→receive, buy→purchase, help→assist.
**INFORMAL letter — used for:** letters to friends, siblings, cousins, close relatives. Reader = someone you address by first name.

**Informal format:** address (top-right) → date → salutation 'Dear Raksha,' → body → closing 'Yours lovingly / With love / Your friend' → first name only. NO subject line, NO recipient's full address, NO formal titles.

**Informal body plan:** open with warmth and acknowledgement ('It's been ages since I heard from you... I was thrilled to get your letter'), develop the main news/topic in a friendly, flowing style, close with regards and an invitation to reply ('Write back soon and tell me all about...').
**Contractions are correct here:** it's, I'm, can't, won't — contractions are a signal of informality and are expected. Formal letters forbid them.

**Compare side by side — asking for information:** Formal: 'I would be grateful if you could send me the prospectus for the coming session.' Informal: 'Could you send me the prospectus when you get a chance? Really curious about the courses!'

**Compare — complaint:** Formal: 'I wish to draw your attention to the poor condition of the road outside our school, which has caused several accidents.' Informal (to a friend about the same): 'You won't believe how terrible the road outside school has become — Rajan actually fell off his bike there last week!'

**Exam marking:** format ~2 (all parts present, correct order), register & tone ~2 (formal stays formal, informal stays warm), content & organisation ~2, grammar ~1. The subject line in formal letters is scored content — never omit it.
confusion: ❌ 'Dear Sir' in a letter to your friend. ✅ Informal letters use first names: 'Dear Sita,'.
❌ 'Yours lovingly' in a job application. ✅ Formal closings: 'Yours faithfully' (name unknown) or 'Yours sincerely' (name known).
❌ Subject line in an informal letter. ✅ Subject lines exist ONLY in formal letters.
❌ Contractions in formal letters ('I can't attend'). ✅ Write in full: 'I cannot attend'.
❌ 'Dear Mr. Ram Sir' — mixing title and 'Sir'. ✅ Either 'Dear Mr. Sharma' or 'Dear Sir', never both.
