data.title: Grammar for Writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
notes: **Sentence types as tools:** simple (one clause — POWER), compound (two main clauses via and/but/so or a semicolon — equal weight), complex (main + subordinate clause via because/although/when/if — shows the relation between ideas). Mix them: examiners reward rhythm.

**Clauses vs phrases:** a phrase has no subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone; a dependent clause has one but leans on the main clause ('Because it rained.' alone is a fragment). Relative clauses (who/which/that) add noun detail — commas only for extra information.

**Punctuation logic:** full stop ends a thought; comma separates list items, follows openers, precedes and/but/so between full sentences; semicolon joins balanced sentences; colon introduces; apostrophe = possession or contraction (its vs it's is the classic trap). Comma splice = two full sentences joined by only a comma — fix it.

**Tense + agreement discipline:** pick a tense zone per paragraph (essays: present; reports: past); subjects agree with verbs ('Each of the students WAS present'); a/an by SOUND ('an hour', 'a university').
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**The three sentence types — when to use each:** (1) *Simple* (one independent clause): 'The boy ran.' 'She passed the exam.' Use for: emphasis, punchy statements, climactic moments. (2) *Compound* (two independent clauses): 'The boy ran, and he caught the bus.' Use for: equal ideas, contrasts, adding information. (3) *Complex* (one independent + one dependent): 'Although the boy was tired, he ran.' Use for: showing cause-effect, condition, contrast, time. Mix all three for rhythm — exams reward variety.

**Subordinating conjunctions — the complex sentence toolkit:** These words join independent and dependent clauses: CAUSE (because, since, as), CONTRAST (although, though, even though, whereas, while), CONDITION (if, unless, provided that), TIME (when, while, before, after, until, as soon as, once), PURPOSE (so that, in order that). Master these 15+ conjunctions — they are the backbone of complex sentences and essential for high grammar scores.

**Compound sentences — the joiners:** Two ways to join independent clauses: (1) *Coordinating conjunction* (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so): 'He studied hard, so he passed.' (2) *Semicolon* (for closely related ideas): 'She studied hard; she passed.' Remember: a semicolon joins TWO complete sentences — it cannot join a clause to a phrase. Always use a comma BEFORE FANBOYS when joining two independent clauses.

**Relative clauses — adding detail without starting new sentences:** Relative clauses begin with who (people), which (things), that (people/things — restrictive), where (places), when (times), whose (possession). Example: 'The girl who won the race is my sister.' 'The book which I read was fascinating.' 'The house where I grew up has been sold.' Use commas for NON-RESTRICTIVE clauses (extra info): 'My sister, who won the race, is in the photo.' No commas for RESTRICTIVE clauses (essential info): 'The girl who won the race is my sister.'

**Punctuation deep dive — the full-stop family:** (1) *Full stop (.)*: ends a declarative sentence. (2) *Question mark (?)*: ends a direct question. (3) *Exclamation mark (!)*: ends a strong emotion. (4) *Comma (,)*: separates items in a list, follows introductory phrases, sets off non-restrictive clauses, joins independent clauses with FANBOYS. (5) *Semicolon (;)*: joins two related independent clauses. (6) *Colon (:)*: introduces a list, explanation, or quote. (7) *Apostrophe (')*: possession (Rahul's book) or contraction (don't, it's). (8) *Quotation marks (" ")*: direct speech. (9) *Hyphen (-)*: joins compound words (well-known, high-speed).

**Comma rules — the top 5 tested in exams:** (1) List commas: 'I bought apples, oranges, and bananas.' (Oxford comma optional but recommended). (2) Introductory phrase comma: 'After the exam, we celebrated.' (3) Compound sentence comma: 'She studied hard, and she passed.' (4) Non-restrictive clause comma: 'My brother, who lives in Pokhara, is visiting.' (5) Quotation comma: 'I am leaving,' she said. NEVER use a comma between subject and verb, or between verb and object.

**Common punctuation errors — the killer mistakes:** (1) *Comma splice*: 'I was tired, I went to bed.' → Fix: 'I was tired, so I went to bed.' (2) *Missing comma after introductory phrase*: 'After the rain stopped we went out.' → Fix: 'After the rain stopped, we went out.' (3) *Wrong apostrophe*: 'The dog wagged its tail' (its = possessive, correct) vs. 'It's a beautiful day' (it's = it is, correct). 'The dog wagged it's tail' (wrong!). (4) *Missing comma before FANBOYS*: 'She ran but she fell' → 'She ran, but she fell.' (5) *Fragment*: 'Because he was late.' → 'Because he was late, he missed the bus.'

**Subject-verb agreement — the golden rule:** The verb must agree with the SUBJECT in number (singular/plural). (1) Singular subject → singular verb: 'The boy runs.' (2) Plural subject → plural verb: 'The boys run.' (3) Compound subject with 'and' → plural: 'Rahul and Sita are coming.' (4) 'Each/every/no' + singular noun → singular verb: 'Each of the students is present.' (5) 'Either/or' → verb agrees with NEAREST subject: 'Either the teacher or the students are wrong.' (6) Collective nouns: 'The team is winning' (unit) vs. 'The team are arguing' (individuals).

**Articles — a, an, the mastery:** (1) *a/an* (indefinite): use before singular, countable, non-specific nouns. 'A' before consonant SOUND ('a university' — sound is /j/; 'a hour' — wait, it's 'an hour' because 'h' is silent). (2) *an* before vowel SOUND ('an apple', 'an honest man', 'an MBA'). (3) *the* (definite): use before specific, previously mentioned, or unique nouns. 'The sun rises in the east.' 'I read the book you recommended.' (4) No article: general plural nouns ('Cats are mammals'), abstract nouns ('Love is powerful'), meals ('I had breakfast'), languages ('I speak Nepali').

**Tense sequence — keeping your timeline clear:** (1) *Reported speech*: backshift tense (present → past, past → past perfect). 'I am happy' → He said he was happy. (2) *Conditional*: Type 0 (general truth): present+present. Type 1 (real future): if+present, will+base. Type 2 (unreal present): if+past, would+base. Type 3 (unreal past): if+past perfect, would have+past participle. (3) *Time clauses*: after when/before/until, use present tense for future meaning: 'I will call you when I arrive' (not 'when I will arrive').

**Voice — active vs. passive:** Active: subject performs the action ('The chef cooked the meal'). Passive: subject receives the action ('The meal was cooked by the chef'). Use passive when: (1) the doer is unknown ('The window was broken'). (2) the doer is unimportant ('The report was submitted'). (3) for formal/objective tone ('Mistakes were made'). Never use passive when the active is clearer and more direct.

**Modifiers — placement matters:** A modifier must be placed CLOSE to the word it describes. (1) Misplaced: 'She almost failed every exam.' (wrong — implies she nearly failed every one). Correct: 'She failed almost every exam.' (2) Dangling: 'Walking through the park, the trees looked beautiful.' (wrong — trees aren't walking). Correct: 'Walking through the park, I thought the trees looked beautiful.' Always check: does your modifier modify the right word?
confusion: Comma splice vs. correct compound sentence: 'I was tired, I went to bed' is a comma splice (two independent clauses joined by only a comma — WRONG). Fix: 'I was tired, so I went to bed' (comma + FANBOYS) or 'I was tired; I went to bed' (semicolon) or 'I was tired, so I went to bed' (conjunction). The comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

Its vs. It's — the classic trap: 'its' = possessive pronoun (the dog wagged its tail). 'it's' = contraction of 'it is' or 'it has' (it's a beautiful day). There is NO apostrophe in the possessive form. This is the most commonly tested grammar point in NEB exams.

Who vs. Whom: 'Who' is the SUBJECT form (who did something). 'Whom' is the OBJECT form (to whom did you speak). Test: replace with 'he' (who) or 'him' (whom). 'Who(m) did you call?' → 'You called him' → 'Whom did you call?' In modern usage, 'who' is accepted in both positions, but exams still test the distinction.

Restrictive vs. non-restrictive relative clauses: Restrictive (no commas, essential info): 'The boy who won the race is my brother.' (which boy? The one who won.) Non-restrictive (commas, extra info): 'My brother, who won the race, is visiting.' (which brother? The one I already identified — the clause is extra.) Mixing up commas changes the meaning entirely.

a vs. an before words starting with 'u': It depends on SOUND, not spelling. 'A university' (sound is /j/ — consonant sound). 'An uncle' (sound is /ʌ/ — vowel sound). 'An hour' (h is silent — vowel sound). 'A horse' (h pronounced — consonant sound). Always listen to the FIRST SOUND, not the first letter.

data.title: Grammar Hacks & Exam Shortcuts — the non-obvious rules
notes: **What this is:** the fast, non-general tricks that decide error-spotting and fill-in-the-blank marks — the rules examiners test repeatedly and students most often miss.
**S-V Hack #1 — of-phrases never change the subject:** 'The bouquet of roses IS...' (subject = bouquet). Cross out every 'of...' phrase between subject and verb before choosing is/are, has/have.
**S-V Hack #2 — indefinite pronouns are singular:** each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody, anything take singular verbs — 'Each of the boys WAS given a prize.'
**S-V Hack #3 — There/Here:** the real subject comes AFTER the verb — 'There ARE many reasons...'. Locate the true subject first.
**Tense Hack — the since rule:** 'since + point of time' → perfect continuous: 'It HAS BEEN raining since morning.' 'since + past clause' → perfect: 'Two years HAVE PASSED since he left.'
**Error-spotting scan order:** 1) subject-verb agreement 2) tense consistency 3) preposition 4) article 5) pronoun reference. 80% of set errors live in the first three.
**Voice Hack — only transitive verbs passivise:** state verbs (have, resemble, lack, suit) have NO passive — 'He has a car' cannot be passivised.
**Speech Hack — the backshift shortcut:** present→past, past→past perfect, will→would, can→could, this→that, now→then, today→that day, ago→before, here→there.
**Article Hack:** first mention → a/an; second mention or unique (sun, moon) → the. Zero article before meals, languages, games: 'have lunch', 'speak Nepali', 'play football'.
**Preposition Hack — direction, not translation:** IN (enclosed) / ON (surface) / AT (point): 'in Kathmandu', 'on the table', 'at Balaju'. Time: AT a clock time, ON a day/date, IN a month/year.

**Conditional ladder:** Type 1 (real): if + present, will + V1. Type 2 (unreal present): if + past, would + V1. Type 3 (unreal past): if + had + V3, would have + V3. Decide REAL vs IMAGINED first; tenses follow mechanically.

**Modifier Hack — the error sits next to the comma:** an opening participle phrase must describe the subject right after the comma. 'Walking down the road, a tree...' ❌ → 'Walking down the road, I saw a tree...' ✅
**Comparison Hack — compare like with like:** 'The population of Kathmandu is larger than THAT of Pokhara' (not 'than Pokhara').
**Question-tag Hack:** copy the auxiliary, flip polarity: 'She can swim, can't she?' No auxiliary? Use do/does/did: 'He plays well, doesn't he?'
formulas: S-V rule: the verb agrees with the HEAD noun, ignoring of-phrases.
Backshift: present→past→past perfect; will/can/may→would/could/might.
Conditional ladder: Type 1 if+present/will; Type 2 if+past/would; Type 3 if+had V3/would have V3.
confusion: ❌ 'Each of the players have a jersey.' ✅ 'Each... HAS' — each/every/either/neither are always singular.
❌ 'The scissors is on the table.' ✅ Pair nouns (scissors, trousers) are ALWAYS plural.
❌ 'He said that he will come.' ✅ Backshift after past reporting verbs: 'he WOULD come'.
❌ 'If I will see him, I will tell him.' ✅ Never put will inside the if-clause.
❌ 'One of my friend is here.' ✅ 'One of + PLURAL noun + SINGULAR verb.'

data.title: Grammar Master Mindmap — the whole of English grammar on one page
notes: **How to use this:** grammar is one connected system, not 30 separate chapters. This mindmap is the central trunk (SENTENCE) with six branches — every exam question hangs off one of them. Revise by walking the branches, not by re-reading chapters.

**CENTRAL NODE — THE SENTENCE:** every English sentence = SUBJECT + VERB + (OBJECT/COMPLEMENT) + (modifiers). Everything below is either how these parts CHANGE FORM (morphology) or how they COMBINE (syntax). If you can locate the subject and verb of any sentence, you can solve any grammar question.

**BRANCH 1 — PARTS OF SPEECH (the 8 word classes):** Noun (common, proper, collective, abstract, material; countable vs uncountable), Pronoun (personal I/we/they, possessive mine/ours, reflexive myself, relative who/which/that, demonstrative this/those, indefinite each/everyone, interrogative who?/what?), Verb (transitive vs intransitive; state vs action; regular/irregular), Adjective (quality, quantity, number, demonstrative, possessive, interrogative; degrees: big-bigger-biggest), Adverb (manner -ly, time, place, frequency, degree; also modifies adjectives and other adverbs), Preposition (in/on/at/of/by/with/for — position and direction words), Conjunction (coordinating FANBOYS: for-and-nor-but-or-yet-so; subordinating: because/although/when/if/unless; correlative pairs: either...or, not only...but also), Interjection (ouch! hurrah! — punctuation, not grammar).

**BRANCH 1 sub-node — determiners:** articles a/an/the, quantifiers some/any/much/many/few/little, and the demonstrative/possessive words that sit before nouns. The article rules and quantifier choices generate a large share of fill-in-the-blank questions.

**BRANCH 2 — TENSES (12-cell grid):** 3 times (past/present/future) × 4 aspects (simple/continuous/perfect/perfect continuous). Key cells: Simple Present = habits & universal truths ('The sun rises in the east'); Present Perfect = past action, present relevance ('I have finished'); Present Perfect Continuous = since/for duration ('has been raining since morning'); Past Perfect = the EARLIER of two past actions ('had left before I arrived'); Simple Future = will + V1. Memory hook: aspect answers HOW the action sits in time, time answers WHEN.

**BRANCH 3 — SUBJECT-VERB AGREEMENT:** the verb agrees with the HEAD of the subject. Rules cascade: of-phrases don't count ('the bouquet of roses IS'); each/every/either/neither/everyone = singular; collective nouns usually singular (team IS) but plural when members act individually; pair nouns (scissors, trousers) plural; 'one of + plural noun + singular verb'; subjects joined by and = plural (except single ideas: bread and butter IS); either...or / neither...nor → verb agrees with the NEARER subject; distances/amounts as one unit = singular ('Ten miles IS a long walk').

**BRANCH 3 sub-node — concord traps:** 'There/Here' sentences hide the subject after the verb; relative pronouns take the number of their antecedent ('one of the boys WHO play'); 'a number of' = plural, 'the number of' = singular; 'news/mathematics/physics' = singular though they look plural.

**BRANCH 4 — VOICE (active ↔ passive):** only TRANSITIVE verbs passivise. Machine: object → subject + be (in the tense of the original verb) + past participle + by + agent. Present: is/am/are + V3. Past: was/were + V3. Perfect: has/have been + V3. Future: will be + V3. Modals: can/must be + V3. Skip the agent when it's obvious/unimportant ('My bicycle has been stolen' — not 'by someone'). State verbs (have, resemble, suit, lack) have no passive.

**BRANCH 5 — NARRATION (direct ↔ indirect speech):** two operations: (a) remove quotes, add 'that'/to-infinitive/connector; (b) BACKSHIFT — reporting verb in past shifts everything one step back: present→past, past→past perfect, will/can/may→would/could/might, this→that, now→then, today→that day, ago→before, here→there, tomorrow→the next day. Statements → that +; yes-no questions → if/whether with statement word-order; wh-questions → wh-word + statement order; commands → to + V1 ('told him to go'); requests → requested + to; exclamations → exclaimed with joy/sorrow that.
**BRANCH 5 sub-node — no-backshift cases:** universal truths stay present ('the earth revolves...'); if the reporting verb is present/future ('says'), nothing shifts.

**BRANCH 6 — MODALS & CONDITIONS:** modals (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to) never take to/s/-ing and are followed by V1. Meanings: can=ability, may=permission/possibility, must=obligation/certainty, should=advice, would=past habit/politeness/unreal. The conditional ladder: Type 1 (if + present, will + V1) real future; Type 2 (if + past, would + V1) unreal present — 'were' for all persons; Type 3 (if + had + V3, would have + V3) unreal past — regret/replay.

**CROSS-BRANCH MICRO-ZONES (the marks-savers):** ARTICLES (a/an by SOUND — 'an hour', 'a university'; the = specific/second mention/unique; zero before meals, languages, games). PREPOSITIONS (IN/ON/AT for place and time scales). QUESTION TAGS (copy the auxiliary, flip polarity; none → do/does/did). NON-FINITES (infinitive = purpose; gerund = noun; participle = adjective). DEGREES (comparative + than; superlative + the; 'than that of' for like-with-like). FIXED PAIRS (no sooner...than; hardly...when; not only...but also — never mixed).

**EXAM EXECUTION LOOP:** 1) identify the branch the question lives on; 2) apply that branch's machine (the rules are mechanical); 3) in error-spotting walk the scan order: agreement → tense → preposition → article → pronoun; 4) after writing, re-check the five most-tested zones.
formulas: SENTENCE = SUBJECT + VERB + rest. Find the head pair first.
PASSIVE = object + be (same tense) + V3 (+ by agent).
BACKSHIFT = everything one step back (time, place, certainty).
CONDITIONALS: 1) if+present→will; 2) if+past→would; 3) if+had V3→would have V3.
AGREEMENT: verb follows the HEAD noun; each/every = singular; or/nor → nearest subject.
confusion: ❌ Memorising 30 disconnected 'chapters'. ✅ All of grammar is 6 branches off one trunk: the sentence.
❌ 'My team are winning' (institution sense). ✅ Collective noun as one unit → singular 'is'.
❌ 'He told that he was ill.' ✅ 'told' needs a person: 'told ME that' / 'said that'.
❌ 'a university' / 'an hour' feels backwards. ✅ Sound decides: /yuː/ → 'a'; silent h → 'an'.
❌ 'If I would have known...'. ✅ Type 3: 'If I HAD known, I would have come.'

data.title: How English Paragraphs Actually Work — the anatomy of connected writing
notes: **The big idea:** a paragraph is ONE idea, fully developed — not a fixed number of sentences. Every sentence inside exists to serve that single idea. If you start answering a new question, start a new paragraph.

**The 4-part anatomy:** 1) TOPIC SENTENCE states the main idea (usually first); 2) SUPPORTING SENTENCES give reasons, facts, examples; 3) EXPLANATION/ANALYSIS links evidence back to the idea (this is the sentence weak writers skip); 4) CONCLUDING/LINK sentence rounds off or bridges to the next paragraph.
**The MEAL formula for any body paragraph:** Main idea → Evidence → Analysis → Link. Say it, prove it, explain why the proof matters, connect onward. Works for essays, reports and answers alike.
**UNITY test:** cover a paragraph and ask 'what is this about?' If you need two answers, split it. Every sentence that cannot be traced to the topic sentence is cut material.

**COHESION — the glue devices:** pronoun reference (this policy, such measures), repeated key nouns (deliberate repetition of 'migration' anchors the paragraph), synonym chains (a student → the learner → this young person), and collocations that hold naturally in English.

**COHERENCE — logical order:** time order (first, then, finally) for narration; order of importance (most → least) for arguments; spatial order (near → far) for description; problem → cause → solution for reports. Choose ONE order per paragraph and stay in it.

**TRANSITIONS — the traffic signals:** adding (moreover, in addition), contrasting (however, on the contrary), cause/effect (therefore, as a result, consequently), exemplifying (for instance, namely), sequencing (firstly, subsequently), concluding (in short, to sum up). One or two per paragraph — a transition-heavy paragraph reads as nervous, not organised.

**WHY English paragraphs feel 'backwards' to new writers:** English is writer-responsible — the topic sentence must come EARLY and announce the point directly. Many Nepali/Asian academic styles build up to the point at the end. In English, leading with the conclusion is a feature, not rudeness.

**Paragraph shape:** the classic shape is diamond — broad opening statement, narrowing specifics in the middle, slight broadening at the close. Extremely long paragraphs (250+ words) and one-sentence paragraphs both look unbalanced in essays.
**Paragraph length rule of thumb:** 4-8 sentences for essays; 2-3 for news writing; 1 for notices and warnings. Length follows function.

**Application to exam answers:** in long-answer questions, a new marker expects a new paragraph per point: introduction paragraph → one paragraph per argument (MEAL) → conclusion. Examiners reward visible structure as much as content.

**From reading to writing — the transfer skill:** to write better paragraphs, steal structure from what you read. Take any good article, underline topic sentences, circle transitions, and notice the evidence pattern. Then rebuild the paragraph skeleton with your own content — the fastest known way to internalise how English prose works.
confusion: ❌ A paragraph is 'however many sentences the teacher said'. ✅ A paragraph is one idea developed — sentences follow the idea, not a count.
❌ Starting a new paragraph whenever you like. ✅ New paragraph = new idea, new time, new place, or new speaker.
❌ Piling transitions into every sentence ('Moreover... Furthermore... In addition...'). ✅ Use signals only where the logical relationship actually changes.
❌ Evidence without analysis ('...this shows nothing'). ✅ After every example, one sentence explains HOW it supports the main idea.
❌ Topic sentence at the end ('building up to the point'). ✅ In English, state the main idea first — early and explicitly.

data.title: Notice Writing + Formal & Informal Writing Mastery
notes: **What this covers:** the complete mechanics of notices (the shortest high-mark format) and the full contrast between formal and informal writing — so that after reading, you can produce ANY piece of English writing with the right register, structure and tone.

**NOTICE — the 5 locked components in order:** 1) the word NOTICE (top-centre, or the issuing body's name above it) 2) DATE of issue 3) HEADING (what the notice is about, centred, bold) 4) BODY (answers What/When/Where/Who in 3-4 sentences, max ~50 words) 5) SIGNATURE block (name, designation, issuing body — bottom-left).
**NOTICE — the 50-word law:** examiners deduct for length. Every word must carry information: 'The school is organising...' ❌ → 'An inter-house debate will be held...' ✅
**NOTICE — no personal touches:** no 'Dear students', no first/second person. Passive voice and third person only: 'Students are informed that...'. Signature = name + designation only.
**NOTICE — tense logic:** upcoming events → future (will be held); results → present perfect (has been selected).

**FORMAL WRITING — definition:** writing for institutions and strangers: letters to editors/principals/offices, reports, articles, notices, essays. Traits: no contractions, no slang, full sentences, objective tone, 'Dear Sir/Madam' → 'Yours faithfully/sincerely'.

**INFORMAL WRITING — definition:** writing to people you know: letters to friends/family, diary entries. Traits: contractions welcome, casual connectors (well, anyway, by the way), warmth, 'Dear Ravi' → 'With love'.

**THE REGISTER SWITCH TABLE (memorise):** Formal 'I would like to inform you' ↔ Informal 'Just so you know'; 'I am writing to inquire about' ↔ 'I wanted to ask'; 'Please find enclosed' ↔ 'I'm sending'; 'We regret to inform you' ↔ 'Bad news —'.

**FORMAL LETTER skeleton:** sender's address (top-right, no name) → date → receiver's designation + address (left) → Subject line (one line, factual) → 'Dear Sir/Madam' → 3 paragraphs (WHY you write / DETAILS / ACTION you expect) → 'Yours faithfully' + full name.
**Faithfully vs Sincerely — the rule everyone forgets:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' (no name) → Yours faithfully. 'Dear Mr Sharma' (named) → Yours sincerely.

**INFORMAL LETTER skeleton:** address (top-right) → date → 'Dear Name,' → opening (acknowledge their last letter: 'It was great to hear from you') → middle (the news, chatty, 2-3 paragraphs) → close ('Write back soon / Give my regards to...') → 'With love' + first name.

**HOW PARAGRAPHS WORK — the architecture every format shares:** 1) TOPIC SENTENCE (the paragraph's claim in one line) 2) SUPPORTING SENTENCES (evidence, example, reason) 3) LINK SENTENCE (ties back or bridges forward). One idea per paragraph — mixing ideas is the #1 structural error.

**COHESION — how paragraphs connect:** reference chains (this policy, such measures — don't repeat the noun), connectors by function (addition: moreover; contrast: however; result: therefore; sequence: firstly/finally), and one consistent tense per time-frame.

**THE COMPOSITION MATRIX:** Notice = announce an event (50 words). Formal letter = complain/apply/request an institution. Informal letter = share news with a person. Article = inform/persuade readers (title + byline + intro-body-conclusion). Report = record facts for an authority (past tense, passive-heavy). Essay = argue a thesis (intro → 3-4 body paras → conclusion). Speech = greeting + hook + body + thank-you. Story = setting → conflict → climax → resolution.

**TENSE MAP BY FORMAT:** notice → future; report → past (+passive); article/essay → present for general truths; story → past narrative (past perfect for flashbacks); informal letter → any tense (natural).

**AFTER-READING CHECKLIST (can you do all 5?):** write a compliant 50-word notice · choose faithfully vs sincerely correctly · convert formal ↔ informal · build a topic+support+link paragraph · pick the right format and tense for any prompt.
formulas: NOTICE = body name + NOTICE + date + heading + body(what/when/where/who) + name + designation; ≤50 words; no salutation.
FORMAL LETTER = address → date → receiver → subject → salutation → why → details → action → faithfully + full name.
INFORMAL LETTER = address → date → Dear Name → ack → news → warm close → With love + first name.
PARAGRAPH = Topic + 2-3 Support + Link; ONE idea per paragraph.
Register levers: no contractions + Latinate vocab + long sentences + 3rd person = formal.
confusion: ❌ Writing 'Dear Sir' in a notice. ✅ Notices have no salutation — they are impersonal announcements.
❌ Signing a notice with a first name only. ✅ Full name + designation + issuing body.
❌ 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Sir/Madam'. ✅ Unnamed → faithfully; named → sincerely.
❌ Contractions in formal writing. ✅ 'cannot', 'will not' — contractions mark informality.
❌ A 90-word notice. ✅ Stay ~50 words; extra sentences risk deduction.

data.title: Notice, Advertisement & Formal Announcements
notes: **What a notice is:** a short, formal, public announcement — one paragraph, boxed, displayed on a board or website. It must be readable in under 15 seconds. Every wasted word costs marks.

**Fixed format (5 parts, in order):** 1) the word NOTICE at top-centre; 2) date of issue (top-left or top-right); 3) HEADING announcing the event in one line; 4) BODY — what, when, where, who, (whom to contact); 5) signature block: name, designation, issuing body, in the bottom-left corner.
**The 4 W + 1 H checklist:** WHAT is happening, WHEN (date + time), WHERE (venue), WHO is issuing/is eligible, HOW to participate/register. Miss any of these and the notice fails its purpose.

**Language rules:** present or future tense only ('is organised', 'will be held'); no first-person pronouns (I/we/my) — the notice speaks for the institution; no signatures of individuals inside the body; keep it under 50 words where possible.
**Voice:** passive voice dominates notices because the actor is the institution — 'A one-day workshop WILL BE CONDUCTED by the English Club.'
**Registration/contact lines:** end the body with action — 'Interested students may register with the undersigned by 15 March.' The word 'undersigned' replaces a personal signature.
**Common exam tasks:** notice for a lost item, a meeting, a tour, a competition, a change of schedule, an appeal for blood donation. Structure never changes — only the heading and the 4W+1H content.
**Marks distribution (typical):** format ~2, content (all 4W+1H) ~2, expression (concise, formal, no errors) ~1. Format errors are the cheapest marks lost — box your notice.
confusion: ❌ Writing a notice like a letter (Dear Sir, yours faithfully). ✅ A notice has NO salutation and NO closing courtesy — it ends with name/designation only.
❌ 'Our school is organising...' ✅ Notices avoid first person: 'The school is organising...' — the issuer is the institution, not the writer.
❌ Past tense: 'A workshop was conducted...' ✅ Announcements look forward: 'will be conducted/is being organised'.
❌ Long descriptive paragraphs. ✅ A notice is compressed information — usually 40-60 words, one block.
❌ Forgetting the box/heading. ✅ The word NOTICE and the heading are structural marks — examiners award format marks for them.

data.title: Paragraph Writing — topic sentence, cohesion, exam format
notes: **What it is:** ONE controlling idea in 4–6 sentences — the engine behind every essay, letter and report.

**Structure:** (1) *Topic sentence* — main idea + your angle, specific not generic. (2) *Supporting sentences* — each adds ONE fact/example/reason, logically ordered. (3) *Concluding sentence* — restates or lands a consequence; no new ideas here.
**Unity test:** if a sentence could belong to another paragraph, delete it. **Coherence test:** the reader follows without re-reading — via connectors and repeated key words.
**Exam discipline:** 90–120 words; start with the idea, not with 'The'; end with consequence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Topic sentence — the anchor:** A strong topic sentence has two parts: the TOPIC (what the paragraph is about) and the CONTROLLING IDEA (your specific angle). Weak: 'Pollution is bad.' Strong: 'Air pollution in Kathmandu Valley has reached hazardous levels due to vehicle emissions and construction dust.' The controlling idea limits the scope — this paragraph will discuss causes (vehicles, construction), not effects or solutions. Every supporting sentence must directly support this controlling idea. If a sentence doesn't fit, it belongs in a different paragraph.

**Types of topic sentences for different purposes:** (1) *Claim + reason*: 'Online learning improves accessibility because it removes geographical barriers.' (2) *List statement*: 'Three factors contribute to traffic congestion in the valley: population growth, inadequate infrastructure, and poor traffic management.' (3) *Question as topic*: 'Why do students struggle with time management?' (Answer follows.) (4) *Transition + claim*: 'Although technology connects us globally, it often isolates us locally.' Choose the type that best organises your evidence.

**Supporting sentences — development strategies:** Develop your topic sentence using one or more of these methods: (1) *Examples*: 'For instance, last year my school…' (2) *Facts and statistics*: 'According to the 2023 census, 40% of households…' (3) *Reasons*: 'This happens because…' (4) *Process steps*: 'First, the water is heated. Then…' (5) *Comparison/contrast*: 'Unlike traditional schools, online platforms…' (6) *Cause and effect*: 'Heavy rains cause flooding because the drainage system is outdated.' (7) *Definition*: 'By "sustainable development" we mean…' (8) *Anecdote*: 'When I visited the village, I saw…' Mix these methods for depth, but keep each supporting sentence focused on ONE point.

**Coherence — the glue between sentences:** Coherence means the reader moves smoothly from sentence to sentence. Achieve it through: (1) *Repeated key words/phrases*: 'Air pollution... this pollution... such pollution...' (2) *Synonyms and parallel structures*: 'vehicle emissions' → 'exhaust fumes' → 'exhaust gases' (3) *Transition words and phrases*: Addition (furthermore, moreover, in addition), Contrast (however, on the other hand, nevertheless), Cause-effect (therefore, consequently, as a result), Example (for example, for instance, such as), Sequence (first, second, finally). (4) *Pronoun reference*: 'The government announced a new policy. It aims to reduce emissions.' (5) *Parallel structure*: 'The plan is ambitious, practical, and necessary.'

**Unity — one paragraph, one idea:** Unity means every sentence in the paragraph supports the topic sentence. Common unity breakers: (1) *Tangential details* — interesting but irrelevant facts; (2) *Multiple controlling ideas* — trying to discuss causes AND solutions in one paragraph; (3) *Personal digressions* — 'I remember when…' unless it's an anecdotal paragraph; (4) *Over-generalisation* — 'Everyone knows that…' Test unity by asking: 'Does this sentence prove, explain, or illustrate the topic sentence?' If no, cut or move it.

**Concluding sentence — the landing:** A concluding sentence does NOT introduce a new idea. It: (1) *Restates the topic sentence in different words*: 'Thus, vehicle emissions and construction dust are the primary drivers of Kathmandu's air crisis.' (2) *Synthesises the support*: 'Together, these three factors create a perfect storm of congestion.' (3) *Predicts or recommends*: 'Without urgent intervention, the situation will only worsen.' (4) *Links to the next paragraph*: 'The effects of this pollution on public health are equally alarming.' In a single-paragraph exam answer, end with a strong consequence or reflection.

**Paragraph length — quality over quantity:** For NEB exams, a paragraph is typically 90-120 words (4-6 sentences). Too short (1-2 sentences) suggests underdevelopment. Too long (8+ sentences) suggests loss of focus or multiple ideas. A well-developed paragraph: Topic sentence (1 sentence) → 2-3 supporting sentences with evidence → Concluding sentence (1 sentence). In an essay, body paragraphs are slightly longer (100-150 words) because they need more evidence.

**Paragraph patterns — organising your logic:** (1) *General to specific* (topic sentence → details): standard for most academic writing. (2) *Specific to general* (examples → generalisation): effective for persuasive or inductive writing. (3) *Chronological* (time order): for narratives, processes, histories. (4) *Spatial* (space order): for descriptions. (5) *Cause to effect* or *effect to cause*: for analysis. (6) *Comparison/contrast* (point-by-point or block): for evaluating options. Choose the pattern that makes your argument clearest.

**Topic sentence placement — where it goes:** (1) *Deductive* (topic sentence FIRST): standard for academic writing — tells the reader the point immediately. (2) *Inductive* (topic sentence LAST): builds suspense or leads to a discovery — useful for narrative or persuasive paragraphs. (3) *Middle* (bridge): connects previous paragraph's idea to new idea — rare in exams. For exam writing, ALWAYS put the topic sentence first — it signals organisation and earns easy marks.

**Common paragraph writing errors in exams:** (1) *No topic sentence* — the reader guesses the point. (2) *Vague topic sentence* — 'There are many reasons for pollution.' (3) *Too many ideas* — one paragraph covering causes, effects, AND solutions. (4) *Listing without development* — 'First... Second... Third...' with no explanation. (5) *Abrupt ending* — no concluding sentence, just stops. (6) *Repetitive transitions* — starting every sentence with 'Also', 'Also', 'Also'. (7) *Pronoun confusion* — 'it' refers to what? Fix these in your final read-through.

**From paragraph to essay — scaling up:** An essay is simply a series of linked paragraphs, each with its own topic sentence, all supporting ONE thesis. The thesis is the essay's topic sentence; body paragraphs are the supporting sentences; the conclusion is the essay's concluding sentence. If you can write a perfect paragraph, you can write an essay — just repeat the structure 3-4 times with different points, and add an introduction and conclusion. Practice writing single perfect paragraphs on different topics until it becomes automatic.
confusion: Topic sentence vs. Thesis statement: A topic sentence controls ONE paragraph. A thesis statement controls the ENTIRE essay. The thesis is broader; topic sentences are specific instances that prove the thesis. In a single-paragraph exam answer, your topic sentence IS your thesis.

Unity vs. Coherence: Unity = all sentences relate to the topic sentence (content). Coherence = sentences flow logically and smoothly (connection). A paragraph can be unified but incoherent (jumpy, hard to follow), or coherent but not unified (smooth but off-topic). You need BOTH.

Supporting sentence vs. Topic sentence: A supporting sentence develops the topic sentence with evidence, explanation, or example. A topic sentence makes the claim. If you swapped them, the paragraph would still make sense logically but would be organised backwards. Never make a supporting sentence more general than the topic sentence.

Concluding sentence vs. New topic sentence: A concluding sentence wraps up the CURRENT paragraph. A new topic sentence opens the NEXT paragraph. In exams, if you write a concluding sentence that introduces a new idea, you confuse the examiner and lose unity marks. End with consequence, not a new direction.

Paragraph vs. Essay length: A paragraph is 90-120 words; an essay is 250-400 words. Some students write 'paragraphs' that are actually mini-essays (200+ words) — this loses focus. Others write essays that are just one long paragraph — this loses structure marks. Know which format the question demands.

data.title: Report Writing and Summarisation — news & event report format
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Structure:** Headline (short, factual) → Byline ('By a Staff Reporter') + dateline ('Kathmandu, 12 May:') → Lead paragraph answering WHO did WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY in 2–3 sentences → Body in chronological order → a short quotation from the chief guest → closing outcome.
**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete event report template:**
[HEADLINE: Short, factual — 5-8 words, present simple]
By [a Staff Reporter / The Correspondent]
[City], [Date]:

[Lead paragraph: WHO attended, WHAT happened, WHERE, WHEN, WHY — 3-4 sentences max. This is the most important paragraph — write it first.]

[Body paragraph 1: Chronological sequence of events — opening ceremony, key activities, guest interactions]

[Body paragraph 2: More details — speeches given, performances, participant numbers, highlights]

[Optional: Quotation from chief guest or dignitary in reported speech]

[Closing paragraph: Outcome — results, conclusion, future plans, or next event.]

**No personal opinion. No 'I'. Past tense throughout.**

**Headline writing — the newswriter's craft:** A good headline: (1) Captures the main event in 5-8 words; (2) Uses present simple tense ('School Holds Annual Sports Day'); (3) Avoids full stops and unnecessary words; (4) Contains the who/what of the event; (5) Is factual, not sensational ('Explosion Rocks City' is tabloid; 'Annual Science Exhibition Held' is factual report). Bad: 'Incredible Day at School!' Good: 'Annual Sports Day Celebrated at St. Xavier School.'

**Dateline — the anchor of location and time:** Always format as: [City], [Day] [Month] [Date]:. Example: 'Kathmandu, 15 March:' or 'Pokhara, 2 January:'. The dateline appears immediately after the byline and before the lead paragraph. It tells the reader exactly WHERE and WHEN the event took place — essential for a news report.

**Lead paragraph — the inverted pyramid apex:** Journalists use the 'inverted pyramid' structure: most important info first, least important last. The lead (first paragraph) MUST answer: WHO (who was there/organised), WHAT (what happened), WHERE (location), WHEN (date/time), and WHY (purpose). Combine all five in 2-3 sentences. Everything that follows adds detail. If the report is cut short from the bottom, the lead still makes sense.

**Body paragraphs — chronological reporting:** Report bodies follow time order: 'The event commenced at…', 'Following the inaugural address, the chief guest…', 'After the prize distribution, the guests…', 'The programme concluded with…' Use time markers: 'first', 'then', 'afterwards', 'meanwhile', 'later', 'finally'. Each body paragraph covers one phase of the event. Be specific: '200 students from 12 schools' is better than 'many students'.

**Quotations — using reported speech in reports:** Reports use reported (indirect) speech for quotes, not direct speech with quotation marks. 'The chief guest, in his address, said that education was the key to national development. He added that students should read beyond the textbook.' Never: 'The chief guest said, "Education is the key to national development."' In exams, this distinction is often tested. Keep the verb tense consistent: past tense ('said that… was…') in reports.

**Passive voice — the report's natural voice:** Reports prefer passive voice for actions performed on objects: 'The prize money was distributed among the winners', 'Certificates were handed over by the chief guest', 'The flag was hoisted by the principal'. Use active voice when the person matters: 'The principal delivered the welcome address' (person is important). The rule of thumb: passive for ceremony/objective facts, active for people/speakers.

**Summarisation — the partner skill:** A summary condenses a passage into its essential meaning in your own words. Method: (1) Read the passage fully once; (2) Identify the main idea (usually in the first or last sentence of each paragraph); (3) Note key supporting points; (4) Draft by combining main ideas + key supports in your own words; (5) Cut to fit word limit (usually 80-100 words for a 300-word passage); (6) Check: is every word essential? Could it be shortened? NEVER copy whole sentences. NEVER add opinion. NEVER include examples or anecdotes.

**Summary word-count discipline:** If asked to summarise in 'about 80 words', 70-90 is acceptable. 60 is too short (you've omitted key ideas); 100 is too long (you've included non-essentials). Count your words. Practice counting accurately — it's a skill tested in NEB exams. A summary should be approximately 1/4 to 1/3 the length of the original passage.

**Summarisation techniques for exam mastery:** (1) *Generalisation*: 'The boy ate apples, oranges, and bananas' → 'The boy ate various fruits.' (2) *Nominalisation*: 'The government decided to reduce taxes' → 'The government's tax reduction decision.' (3) *Merging*: Combine two related sentences into one. (4) *Omission*: Delete examples, repetitions, anecdotes. (5) *Simplification*: Replace complex descriptions with single words. (6) *Abstraction*: Replace specific lists with categories.

**Note-making — the structured summary:** Notes are a visual summary of a passage. Format: TITLE (in caps) → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3) for each paragraph/section → lettered points (a, b, c) under each sub-heading → abbreviations list at bottom. Keep each point to under 7 words. Use arrows (→), ampersands (&), etc. Notes are tested for: accuracy of sub-headings, completeness of key ideas, conciseness of points, correct abbreviation usage.

**Note-making rules and conventions:** (1) Title: UPPERCASE, capture the main theme. (2) Sub-headings: Numbered (1, 2, 3), in NOUN PHRASE form (not sentences). (3) Points: Lettered (a, b, c), in KEY PHRASES (not full sentences). (4) No full stops in sub-headings or points. (5) Abbreviations defined at bottom (govt., approx., vs., etc.). (6) Each point under 7 words. (7) Maintain the original order of ideas. (8) Do not add your own interpretation.

**Common report writing errors:** (1) First-person narration ('I attended the function') — never 'I' in a report. (2) Past tense used inconsistently — switch between past and present. (3) Opinion or commentary ('It was the best event ever') — reports are objective. (4) Direct speech quotes instead of reported speech. (5) Missing headline or dateline. (6) Chronological confusion — jumping between time periods. (7) Too much detail / missing key facts. (8) Emotional language ('Heartbreaking tragedy', 'Amazing success').

**Report vs. Story — the key difference:** A report tells WHAT happened; a story tells HOW it felt. A report is objective and external; a story is subjective and internal. A report uses past tense, third person, and passive voice; a story uses past tense, first/third person, and active voice. A report includes facts, numbers, and quotes; a story includes emotions, dialogue, and sensory detail. In exams, confusing these loses the 'form' marks immediately.

**Note-taking with abbreviations — speed writing:** In exams, abbreviations earn marks when defined. Standard abbreviations: acc. (according), approx. (approximately),Assoc. (Association), b/c (because), Dept. (Department), e.g. (for example), Govt. (Government), in (in), i.e. (that is), incl. (including), opp. (opposite), org. (organisation), ppl (people), resp. (responsible), sq. km (square kilometre), vs. (versus), wrt (with regard to). Never use abbreviations in the TITLE or SUB-HEADING — only in the bullet points.

**Event report practice checklist:** Before submitting your report, verify: [ ] Headline present and factual [ ] Byline + dateline present [ ] Lead answers WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY [ ] Body is chronological [ ] Quotation in reported speech [ ] No first person, no opinion [ ] Past tense throughout [ ] Closing paragraph with outcome [ ] Within word limit [ ] Spelling checked.
confusion: Report vs. Summary: A report writes about an EVENT that happened (news report). A summary condenses a GIVEN PASSAGE into fewer words. Both use third person and past tense, but they have different purposes and structures. Reports create new content from observed facts; summaries repackage existing text.

Reported speech vs. Direct speech in reports: Reports use reported speech ('The guest said that…') for quotes. Direct speech ('The guest said, "Education is key."') is for feature articles and stories, not formal event reports. This distinction is frequently tested in NEB exams.

Note-making vs. Summary: Notes are a VISUAL, STRUCTURED format with numbered sub-headings and lettered points. A summary is a PARAGRAPH of continuous prose. Notes use abbreviations and fragments; summaries use full sentences. Both condense the same passage, but the output format differs.

Lead paragraph vs. Introduction: In a report, the lead paragraph is the FIRST paragraph — it must answer all five Ws (who, what, where, when, why). In an essay, the introduction sets up the topic and thesis. The report lead is factual and dense; the essay introduction is engaging and argumentative.

Dateline vs. Date in letter format: In a report, the dateline is part of the header format: 'Kathmandu, 15 March:' — it runs inline with the byline. In a formal letter, the date is on its own line below the sender's address. Never format a report date like a letter date.

data.title: Speech Writing — salutation, hooks, persuasive devices
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete speech template:**
[Salutation — seniority order: 'Respected Chairperson, distinguished judges, learned teachers, and my dear friends –']

[Self-introduction (if required): 'My name is… from Class… I stand before you today to speak about…']

[Hook: A striking fact, a powerful question, or a memorable quotation]

[Point 1: 'Let me begin with…' / 'First, let me tell you…']

[Point 2: 'Secondly…' / 'But there's more…']

[Point 3: 'Finally…' / 'And most importantly…']

[Closing: Emotional appeal + call to action + 'Thank you.']

**Salutation — the etiquette of order:** Speeches in exams always start with a salutation listing people in ORDER OF SENIORITY: (1) Chairperson/Principal → (2) Judges → (3) Teachers → (4) Fellow students → (5) Guests. Example: 'Respected Chairperson, learned judges, dear teachers, and my fellow students — Good morning to you all.' Do NOT skip anyone mentioned in the prompt. Do NOT reorder them. The salutation shows respect and awareness of protocol.

**Self-introduction — when and how:** Include only if the question says 'introduce yourself'. If required: 'My name is Ram from Class 11-A. Today I wish to speak about…' Keep it to ONE sentence. If not required, skip it — wasting words on self-intro eats into your argument time. In formal speech competitions, the introduction comes after the hook; in exams, before.

**Speech hooks — grab attention in the first 10 seconds:** (1) *Rhetorical question*: 'What would you do if you lost everything today?' (2) *Startling fact*: 'One billion people globally go to bed hungry every night.' (3) *Quotation*: 'Mahatma Gandhi once said, "Be the change you wish to see in the world." But how many of us actually try?' (4) *Direct address*: 'Look around you. What do you see?' (5) *Story*: 'Last Tuesday, a five-year-old girl in a remote village walked 10 kilometres to school. Her name is Sita.' (6) *Quote with twist*: 'They say knowledge is power. But I say knowledge without action is merely information.' Pick the hook that best suits your topic's tone.

**Speech body — three points max:** You have about 2-3 minutes in a speech. Cover 2-3 points maximum. Each point should: (1) Have a clear heading signal ('First…', 'Second…', 'Finally…'); (2) Explain one idea with a short example or story; (3) Connect back to your main argument. Never try to cover 5 topics in 200 words. Depth beats breadth every time in speech writing.

**Persuasive devices — the orator's toolkit:** (1) *Triads* (rule of three): 'Education builds character, creates opportunity, and transforms communities.' (2) *Repetition*: 'We must act now. We must act together. We must act with conviction.' (3) *Rhetorical questions*: 'Is this the Nepal we want for our children?' (4) *Direct address*: 'You have the power to change this. YOU have the responsibility.' (5) *Triadic structure*: 'Not because it is easy, but because it is necessary.' (6) *Anaphora*: 'I dream of a Nepal… I dream of a generation… I dream of a future…' These devices create rhythm, emphasis, and memorability.

**Speech vs. Essay — the fundamental difference:** An essay is READ; a speech is HEARD. This changes everything. Speech sentences should be SHORTER (15-20 words maximum). Use MORE contractions ('don't', 'it's', 'we'll') — speech is oral, not written. Use MORE repetition — the audience can't go back and re-read. Use MORE direct address ('you', 'we') — the speaker is talking TO people. Use LESS complex subordinate clauses — keep the grammar simple and clear.

**The read-aloud test — your best editing tool:** After writing your speech, read it ALOUD to yourself. Mark anywhere you: (1) Run out of breath — split that sentence; (2) Stumble over words — rephrase; (3) Feel bored — add emotion or a question; (4) Lose the audience's attention — cut that sentence. A speech that reads well on paper but sounds awkward when spoken is a failed speech. This test catches 80% of speech-writing errors.

**Closing a speech — the power moment:** The last 20 seconds determine how your speech is remembered. Close with: (1) *Call to action*: 'Let us all pledge to plant one tree this month.' (2) *Rhetorical question*: 'What legacy do you want to leave?' (3) *Repetition of theme*: 'Education is not just a right. Education is a revolution. Education is hope.' (4) *Quotation*: End with a powerful quote that reinforces your message. (5) *Final 'Thank you'*: Always end with 'Thank you.' — it signals the speech is over and allows applause.

**Speech vocabulary — power phrases for oratory:** Opening: 'I stand before you today to…', 'Let me begin by asking…', 'How many of you have ever…' Body: 'Consider this…', 'Think about…', 'Picture this…', 'Let me give you an example…', 'Here's the thing…' Closing: 'Let us not forget…', 'The choice is ours…', 'Together, we can…', 'I urge you all to…', 'Thank you for your time and attention.'

**Common speech writing mistakes:** (1) No salutation or wrong order. (2) Starting with 'Good morning everyone' without listing dignitaries first. (3) Long, complex sentences that are hard to speak. (4) No rhetorical devices — dry and forgettable. (5) No clear call to action. (6) Ending abruptly without 'Thank you.' (7) Too formal — 'One should consider the implications…' (8) Too casual — 'So basically, stuff is bad.' (9) Ignoring the given first line (if provided). (10) Over-running the word limit.

**Speech delivery tips (for oral exams):** Make eye contact with different sections of the audience. Vary your tone — don't speak in a monotone. Pause after important points. Use hand gestures naturally. Speak slowly and clearly. Breathe between sentences. Smile when appropriate. Your BODY LANGUAGE matters as much as your words. A confident delivery can turn an average speech into a winning one.
confusion: Speech vs. Essay — key structural differences: Speeches have salutations, direct address ('you', 'we'), shorter sentences, repetition, and rhetorical devices. Essays have no salutation, use 'one/it is said', longer sentences, logical transitions, and no repetition. Don't write a speech like an essay, or an essay like a speech.

Rhetorical question vs. Direct question: A rhetorical question ('Have you ever felt truly alone?') does NOT expect an answer — it makes the audience THINK. A direct question ('How many students feel alone?') expects a show of hands or verbal response. In speech writing, rhetorical questions are the standard tool. Direct questions sound interrogative and aggressive.

Quotation in speech vs. quotation in essay: In a speech, quotations are SPOKEN — keep them short (one sentence max) and deliver them with emphasis. In an essay, quotations can be longer and embedded in analysis. Also: in a speech, introduce the quotation ('As the great Dr. Koirala said…') before delivering it. In an essay, you can weave it into your sentence.

Point of view in speech vs. narrative: Speeches use 'I' (speaker) and 'you' (audience) and 'we' (shared identity). Narratives use 'I' or 'he/she' but NOT 'you' (unless second-person narrative, which is rare). The speech 'you' creates intimacy; the narrative 'you' creates confusion. Never write 'You walked into the room and felt scared' in a speech.

Thank you placement — before or after closing point: In a speech, 'Thank you' is the ABSOLUTE LAST WORD. It comes after your closing appeal, not before. Correct: 'Let us act together. Thank you.' Incorrect: 'Thank you. Let us act together.' The final words must carry your message, not your politeness.

data.title: Story Writing — complete arc from a given outline
notes: **What it is:** a COMPLETE narrative arc judged on plot — situation → problem → turning point → resolution → (often) a quiet moral.

**Structure:** Opening (if the prompt gives a first line, USE it verbatim and continue) → Complication → Rising action → Climax (the decisive moment — slow down here) → Resolution + realisation/moral.

**Tense machinery:** past simple drives the plot; past continuous paints background ('I was dawdling home'); past perfect marks earlier events ('which she had lost'); direct speech at the climax adds life.
**Keep ONE tense zone and ONE narrator** — drifting between present and past, or I/he, breaks the story.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete story arc with word budget:** Total ~250-300 words. Opening (50-60): set scene, introduce character. Rising action (80-100): build tension, present problem. Climax (50-60): the decisive moment, slow down, use direct speech. Resolution (40-50): what happens next, the change. Moral/reflection (20-30): the quiet lesson learned.

**Opening strategies — the in medias res technique:** Start as close to the action as possible. (1) *In medias res* (into the middle of things): 'Ramesh ran harder than he ever had in his life, the stone hitting his foot with every step.' (2) *First line continuation*: If given 'The box arrived on a Tuesday morning…', continue that exact sentence. (3) *Atmospheric opening*: 'The rain had not stopped for three days, and the village was drowning in mud and silence.' (4) *Character opening*: 'Anita had always been the quiet one — the kind of girl who blended into walls.' The key principle: start with ACTION or a SENSORY DETAIL, not background information.

**Rising action — the tension engine:** Each sentence in the rising action should increase tension. Use: (1) *Complications* — 'Just as she thought she had solved the problem, another appeared.' (2) *Obstacles* — 'The path was blocked by fallen trees.' (3) *Time pressure* — 'She had only an hour before the exam began.' (4) *Stakes* — 'If he failed, the family would lose everything.' (5) *Conflict with others* — 'Her brother disagreed, saying…' Every paragraph should make the problem HARDER, not easier.

**Climax — slow down at the turning point:** The climax is where the story changes direction — the moment of highest tension. Slow down your prose here. Use SHORT sentences. Use DIRECT SPEECH. Make the reader feel the moment. 'The door creaked open. A shadow moved across the floor. Her breath caught. "Who's there?" she called out. Silence. Then a voice: "I've come to return your book."'" "This paragraph could have been one sentence — but it's five, each one a beat. That's the technique.

**Resolution — the quiet landing:** The resolution shows what happens AFTER the climax. It should: (1) Resolve the main problem; (2) Show character change or realisation; (3) Create a sense of closure. 'The next morning, Anu woke to sunlight streaming through the window. She picked up the book, opened it, and found a note in her father's handwriting: "I'm proud of you." She smiled — not because the problem was solved, but because she had faced it.' The moral emerges from action, not from being stated outright.

**Moral — show, don't preach:** Never end a story with 'And the moral of the story is…'. That's for fables, not short stories. Instead, let the reader infer the moral from the events. 'Kiran looked at the broken vase, then at his mother's tired hands. He knew he should have been honest from the beginning.' The moral (honesty is better than hiding) is clear without being stated. This is called 'thematic resonance' — a hallmark of good storytelling.

**Direct speech — bringing characters to life:** Direct speech makes stories vivid and earns marks. Rules: (1) Use quotation marks for every spoken line. (2) Dialogue tags: 'said', 'whispered', 'exclaimed', 'replied'. (3) Mix dialogue with action: 'I don't believe you,' she said, turning away. 'Not without proof.' (4) Keep each line short — 1-2 sentences maximum. (5) Each character should have a distinguishable voice — one formal, one casual. (6) Don't overuse — one or two lines at the climax is enough.

**Tense mastery in stories — the three past tenses:** (1) *Past simple* (walked, said, saw) — the main tense for plot events. (2) *Past continuous* (was walking, were talking) — for background and setting. (3) *Past perfect* (had walked, had said) — for events that happened BEFORE the main story. Common error: 'I am walking to the market when I saw…' — should be 'I WAS walking… when I saw'. Keep one tense zone per paragraph.

**Narrator consistency — the invisible rule:** Choose a narrator: first person ('I walked…') or third person ('He walked…'). NEVER switch. Never write 'I walked to the door and she opened it' — mixing I and she in one story. Also: if third person limited (follows one character), don't reveal what OTHER characters are thinking. Stay inside one head throughout. Breaking this rule is the #1 story-writing error in exams.

**Showing vs. Telling — the golden rule:** Tell: 'He was angry.' Show: 'His face flushed red, his fists clenched, and his voice dropped to a whisper.' Tell: 'She was sad.' Show: 'She stared at the empty chair, her tea growing cold, and wiped at her cheek with the back of her hand.' In exams, 'show' writing consistently earns higher marks because it demonstrates control of language. Always convert a 'telling' sentence into a 'showing' description.

**Story from outline — working with prompts:** When given an outline (three bullet points or numbered events), expand each into a paragraph: (1) *First bullet* → opening + setup; (2) *Second bullet* → rising action + complication; (3) *Third bullet* → climax + resolution. Add connecting tissue — transitional sentences, sensory details, and internal thoughts. Don't just paste the outline points — weave them into a flowing narrative.

**Story from a given first line — the continuity rule:** If the prompt gives a first line (e.g., 'The letter arrived just as she was about to leave for school'), YOU MUST use it verbatim as the first sentence of your story. Do not modify it. Do not repeat it. Continue directly from that line. Your story must follow logically from the given line. Check: does your story START with the exact given line? If not, you lose format marks immediately.

**Common story-writing mistakes:** (1) Changing tense mid-story — 'He walked… he runs… he had gone'. (2) Switching narrators — 'I was afraid, and she smiled'. (3) No climax — the story peaks early and then trails off. (4) Preachy moral — 'The moral is honesty is the best policy'. (5) Too many characters — hard to manage in 250 words. (6) Forget the given first line — catastrophic for marks. (7) No dialogue — makes the story flat. (8) Ending with 'And then they lived happily ever after' — too generic.
confusion: Story vs. Narrative essay: A story is pure fiction — invented characters and events. A narrative essay is typically based on a REAL personal experience. In exams, if asked to 'Write a story', invent it. If asked to 'Write a narrative essay about a personal experience', draw from your own life. The structures are similar but the source material differs.

Moral vs. Theme: A moral is an explicit lesson ('Honesty is the best policy'). A theme is an implicit idea (the destructive power of greed, the value of perseverance). Short stories should have themes, not morals. Fables have morals. In exams, ending with a moral is accepted but less sophisticated than thematic resonance.

Climax vs. Turning point: The turning point is the moment the story's direction changes. The climax is the highest point of tension, often just before or at the turning point. They can be the same moment ('He opened the letter and read…' — tension peaks, direction changes) or separate moments (climax = the moment of decision; turning point = the consequence).

First person vs. Third person story: First person ('I') creates intimacy and immediacy but limits knowledge to one character's perspective. Third person ('he/she') creates distance but allows omniscience — you can describe other characters' actions and settings freely. For exams, third person is safer: fewer perspective errors. But first person, done well, is more emotionally powerful.

Opening line given vs. opening line invented: If the examiner GIVES you a first line, you MUST use it exactly. If they don't, you invent your own. Some students waste the given line by repeating it or modifying it slightly — this is an immediate format error. Always copy the given line word for word as your first sentence.

data.title: Summary and Note-making — condensing any passage
notes: **Summary:** read for gist → underline key ideas → draft (author's main idea first, then 2–4 key supports) → cut modifiers/examples to fit the word limit → verify meaning is unchanged and nothing is copied.

**Summary grammar:** four paraphrase moves — synonym swap (threat→danger), word-class change (pollute→pollution), voice change (active↔passive), sentence merge; report verbs frame it ('the passage argues…'). Never add your own opinion.
**Note-making:** TITLE in caps → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3 — noun phrases, one per paragraph) → lettered points (a, b, c) → abbreviations (&, →, e.g.) with an 'Abbreviations used' note.
**Note grammar:** nominalise verbs for headings ('agricultural expansion'); drop articles/auxiliaries in points; every point under 7 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Summary — the complete method:** (1) Read the passage TWICE — once for gist, once for detail. (2) Identify the MAIN IDEA (usually in first or last sentence of each paragraph). (3) Note KEY SUPPORTING POINTS (2-4 per paragraph, max 5-6 total). (4) DRAFT — start with the main idea, add supporting points in logical order. (5) PARAPHRASE — every sentence must be in your own words (synonyms, voice change, clause merge). (6) CUT — remove examples, repetitions, elaborations until within word limit. (7) VERIFY — check: is every word essential? Is the meaning unchanged? Is anything copied? (8) COUNT — ensure you're within the limit (usually ±10% is acceptable).

**Summary word-count discipline:** If asked to summarise in 80 words, your target is 70-90 words. 60 is too short (you've omitted key ideas). 100 is too long (you've included non-essentials). PRACTISE counting words accurately. Count each word as you write: "The passage discusses (3) the problems of (6) air pollution (9) in Kathmandu (12) valley (14) caused by (17) vehicle emissions (20) and construction dust (23)." Practice until counting is automatic.

**Summary techniques — the four moves:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'danger' → 'risk', 'important' → 'significant', 'show' → 'demonstrate'. (2) *Word-class change*: 'The government decided to reduce' → 'The government's decision to reduce'. (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built'. (4) *Sentence merge*: 'The factory emitted smoke. The smoke polluted the air.' → 'The factory's smoke pollution contaminated the air.' Master all four moves — they are your paraphrasing toolkit.

**Summary — what to keep and what to cut:** KEEP: main ideas, key facts, cause-effect relationships, the author's stance. CUT: examples, anecdotes, statistics (unless central), repetition, elaboration, specific names/dates (unless critical), direct quotes. Rule of thumb: if removing a sentence doesn't change the core meaning, remove it. After cutting, re-read: does the summary still convey the full meaning of the passage?

**Summary report verbs — framing your summary:** Frame your summary using reporting verbs that attribute ideas to the author: 'The passage argues that…', 'The author contends that…', 'According to the passage, …', 'The text explains that…', 'The writer suggests that…', 'The passage highlights that…'. These verbs make it clear the ideas belong to the original author, not to you. NEVER say 'I think' or 'In my opinion' — this is a summary, not an essay.

**Note-making — format mastery:** Format: TITLE (UPPERCASE, on its own line) → 1. Sub-heading 1 (noun phrase, from paragraph 1) → a. Point a (under 7 words) → b. Point b → c. Point c → 2. Sub-heading 2 (noun phrase, from paragraph 2) → a. Point a → b. Point b → Abbreviations used: (list any abbreviations you created). Every sub-heading = one paragraph. Every lettered point = one key idea. No full sentences. No full stops in sub-headings or points.

**Note-making — abbreviations that earn marks:** Use standard abbreviations freely in note-making: & (and), → (leads to/causes), vs. (versus), approx. (approximately), assoc. (association), dept. (department), e.g. (for example), gov. (government), incl. (including), resp. (responsible), sq. km (square kilometre), w/ (with), w/o (without), yr. (year). List them in an 'Abbreviations used' section at the bottom. This shows skill and saves space.

**Note-making — common errors:** (1) Sub-headings as full sentences — should be NOUN PHRASES. (2) Points as full sentences — should be PHRASES under 7 words. (3) Missing abbreviations list. (4) Sub-headings not matching paragraphs. (5) Too many sub-headings (more than the passage has paragraphs). (6) Using abbreviations in sub-headings (only use them in points). (7) Full stops at end of sub-headings or points. (8) Copying whole sentences instead of condensing.

**Summary vs. Note-making — key difference:** A SUMMARY is a PARAGRAPH of continuous prose (complete sentences, flowing text). A NOTE-MAKING is a VISUAL STRUCTURE (numbered headings, lettered points, abbreviations). Both condense the same passage, but the OUTPUT FORMAT differs. Exams sometimes ask for both from the same passage — know which format to use for which task.

**Combined summary and note-making — exam strategy:** When asked to do BOTH from the same passage: (1) Read the passage ONCE and identify key ideas. (2) Write the summary FIRST (paragraph form) — this ensures you understand the full meaning. (3) Write the notes SECOND (visual form) — this ensures you can structure the information. (4) Time: 15 minutes for summary, 10 minutes for notes. Total: 25 minutes for a 30-mark question. Practice doing both from the same passage in one sitting.

**Note-making with title — the first decision:** The TITLE must capture the MAIN THEME of the entire passage. Not the first paragraph, not the last — the WHOLE passage. Example: If a passage has 3 paragraphs about air pollution causes, effects, and solutions, the title is NOT 'Causes of Air Pollution' — it's 'Air Pollution: Causes, Effects & Solutions' or 'Understanding Air Pollution in Urban Nepal'. The title should be broad enough to cover all sections.
confusion: Summary vs. Paraphrase: A summary CONDENSES a passage into a shorter version (reducing length). A paraphrase RESTATES a single sentence or idea in different words (same length). Summary = shorter, paraphrase = same length. You can paraphrase as part of a summary, but a summary is a larger task involving condensation.

Note-making vs. Summarisation: Notes are STRUCTURED (numbered headings, lettered points, abbreviations). Summaries are CONTINUOUS (paragraph form, complete sentences). Both compress the same passage. The format difference is what distinguishes them. Notes are visual; summaries are prose.

Noun phrase vs. Sentence as sub-heading: A sub-heading must be a NOUN PHRASE: 'Causes of air pollution' (correct). 'Air pollution is caused by vehicles' (wrong — this is a sentence). Drop articles, verbs, and prepositions where possible. Keep it to 3-5 words maximum.

Point as phrase vs. Point as sentence: A note point must be under 7 words and NOT a complete sentence. 'Vehicles emit smoke' (wrong — this is a sentence). 'Vehicle emissions' (correct — this is a phrase). 'Pollution from vehicles' (correct). Drop 'is/are/was/were' and articles (a/an/the) in note points.

Title vs. Sub-heading: The TITLE covers the entire passage (one phrase). Sub-headings cover individual paragraphs (one per paragraph). The title is broader; sub-headings are specific. A passage about 'Health' might have sub-headings 'Nutrition', 'Exercise', and 'Mental Health'. The title is the umbrella; sub-headings are the ribs.

data.title: Q: Why does the sign of a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ determine which bisector is acute vs obtuse?
notes: a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ is proportional to the cosine of the angle between the two lines' normal vectors (a, b), since a·a' + b·b' = |n₁||n₂|cos θ for normal vectors n₁, n₂

When this dot product is negative, the normals point in 'opposing' directions relative to each other, which flips which bisector formula (+ or −) ends up bisecting the acute angle between the actual lines rather than the obtuse one
This is why the rule reverses depending on the sign — it's tracking the relative orientation of the two lines' normals, not just their raw coefficients

data.title: Q: In the worked example, both methods agree — is checking both methods necessary, or is one sufficient?
notes: The a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method alone is sufficient and is the standard fast method for exams — it requires no slope calculation or angle formula

The tan θ method is more computationally heavy but is useful as an independent verification, or when the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method feels error-prone (e.g. after a sign mistake while normalizing the constant terms)
In practice: use a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ to solve quickly, and only fall back to tan θ if you want to double-check a specific answer

data.title: Q (worked example): Determine which of the two angle bisectors is acute for 3x + 4y − 5 = 0 and 5x + 12y + 13 = 0
notes: Both constants (−5 and +13) — the second line already has a positive constant; for the first, multiply through by −1 so the constant is positive: −3x − 4y + 5 = 0, giving a₁ = −3, b₁ = −4
For the second line: a₂ = 5, b₂ = 12
Since this is negative, the **(+) sign bisector is the acute angle bisector**, and the (−) sign bisector is the obtuse angle bisector
